News.title: Bereaved parents tell Lisa Nandy she needs 'political courage' to stand up to social media bosses
News.content:
Bereaved parents tell Lisa Nandy she needs 'political courage' to stand up to social media bosses

Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy apologised to the Bereaved Families for Online Safety group for slow progress in tackling online harms when she met them for the first time this week

View 5 Images Some of the families who attended the meeting with Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy gathered outside Parliament afterwards (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

The parents of more than a dozen children whose deaths are linked to social media have told Lisa Nandy she needs “political courage” in standing up to the tech firms.

‌



‌



The Digital Secretary, who picked up the online safety brief in July, apologised to the Bereaved Families for Online Safety group for slow progress in tackling online harms when she met them for the first time this week.

‌



Some of the families, who spoke to The Mirror outside Parliament after the meeting on Tuesday, said they warned her they need tough action to tackle the crisis after years of warm words from politicians. Ms Nandy promised parents the social media ban for under 16s is on track to come into force in spring next year.

‌



Lisa Kenevan, who believes her son Isaac, 13, may have died in an online challenge that went wrong in 2022, said: “We have been sitting around the table before with other SOSs (Secretary of States) and she did apologise and she did say that she was going to be doing more action and that she would like us to be more involved, almost like lived experiences, so that was quite encouraging."

Ruth Moss, whose 13-year-old daughter Sophie Parkinson took her own life in 2014 after being exposed to dangerous material online, said the Government has an “opportunity to crack this”. Ms Moss, who has been campaigning on this for a decade now, admitted she has become a bit of a "cynic" amid the lack of progress.

Tech firms could earn social media ban exemption if they make their platforms safe READ MORE :

5 View 5 Images Ruth Moss said the Government has an 'opportunity to crack this' (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror) 5 View 5 Images Lisa Kenevan said Nandy said she wants bereaved families to be more involved going forward (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



She told The Mirror: " I've become a bit of a cynic, so for me, it's about action now. But she did commit to the timeline for bringing in the social media ban. That was really positive. She has listened to us when we've said it should be feature-based rather than actually banning or naming platforms, so that's really positive."

She continued: “They have an opportunity to crack this. One thing I did say to her was it will take political courage. One of the questions I asked was, how does she balance the fact that they want to keep children safe, but the moment they bring in legislation, geopolitically, that will be hard.

‌



"That will be a challenge because the tech companies aren't going to sit and take that lying down. And she said she was up for the challenge. So let's hope she actually carries on and pulls through with that.”

Stuart Stephens, whose 13-year-old son Olly was stabbed to death after an online dispute in 2021, said the meeting with Ms Nandy had been "very emotional", adding: " These meetings always are because we're telling our stories, but the focus wasn't really on our stories today. It was about what needs to be done next.

‌



"I was very pleased with the way the meeting went, but I wish this was done 10 years ago. All of us here, our children would still be here had we had the information 10 years ago that we had now."

George Nicolaou, whose 15-year-old son Christoforos took his own life after being sent “horrific messages” on an online forum in 2022, said he hopes Ms Nandy's "words become actions". He said: "Lisa Nandy is a lovely lady, and she has given us lots of assurances. She's made lots of promises. And we just all of us speaking for the entire group hope that her words become actions, and we gain what we want to achieve."

‌



5 View 5 Images Mariano Janin said he felt reassured that Nandy knew all the families' stories (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror) 5 View 5 Images George Nicolaou said he hopes Nandy's 'words become actions' (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



Gemma Best, whose 13-year-old daughter Blake Gallier took her own life in 2025 after being bombarded with suicide content online, said it was "hugely" important bereaved parents are involved in conversations about social media safety, saying: "I don't think a lot of parents, probably like myself, thought it would ever happen to them.

"So I think being a parent who's now going through it and being part of a group that has experienced it, it's so important because we're currently going through it. So we want to support parents to not go through this horrific, tragic journey we'll come across."

‌



Michelle Gardner, whose step-daughter Kibi Wade took her own life in 2024 after being bullied online, outlined the urgency of the issue, saying: "T hey really, really need to do something very quickly because every day more and more children are being harmed, and sadly, in our case, children are losing their lives."

Mariano Janin, whose 14-year-old daughter Mia died took her own life in 2021 after she was relentlessly bullied, said it looks like the Government is committed to creating a "safer internet" and following through with promises made under Mr Starmer. He said he felt reassured that Ms Nandy knew all the families' stories, adding: "I think she knew who we were, all of them sitting there, every case in particular, and she showed us, reassured in a way, that we carry on with the same route."

Article continues below

The Government has promised to publish the social media ban’s legislation by the end of the year. It has meant parents have been waiting for details since Keir Starmer announced the ban in June.

Ms Nandy last month suggested tech firms could earn an exemption to the incoming ban in the UK if they make their platforms safe for teens. Teens aged 16 and 17 also face a default overnight curfew and a block on infinite scrolling - an addictive design feature - to prevent a cliff edge when the social media ban lifts.

News.title: Russian fighter jet crashes in huge fireball near cemetery in blow to Putin’s war effort
News.content:
Russian fighter jet crashes in huge fireball near cemetery in blow to Putin’s war effort

A Su-30M fighter jet was seen going up in flames near the town of Chernyakhovsk in the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad while on a training flight

View Image Flames coming from the crashed plane (Image: east2west news)

A Russian fighter jet has crashed in a huge fireball near a cemetery in a fresh blow to Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

‌



‌



Images taken from a graveyard show the moment that the Su-30M went up in flames in the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad region on the Baltic.

‌



The £40 million warplane which is understood to have belonged to the Russian navy was on a training flight when it crashed today near the town of Chernyakhovsk.

‌



Initial reports said that both pilots successfully ejected and are receiving medical treatment with their conditions unclear but it is not believed that their lives are in danger.

Witkoff salutes Putin as 'humanitarian' 48 hours after Russian strike killed baby READ MORE :

Private jet evacuated as smoke pours out and plane veers off runway during landing READ MORE :

The aircraft exploded close to a cemetery where uniformed servicemen appeared to be attending a funeral. A cloud of thick black smoke rose from the woodland where the aircraft crashed.

‌



“On 21 October, a Su-30 aircraft crashed in the Kaliningrad Region while carrying out a scheduled training flight," stated the Russian defence ministry.

“The aircraft crashed in an uninhabited area. The flight was carried out without ammunition.”

‌



Some servicemen in the cemetery were carrying musical instruments, perhaps members of a military band attending a funeral. The necropolis appeared to have civilian and military graves, possibly including war dead from Putin’s conflict in Ukraine.

The Sukhoi Su-30SM is a Russian twin-engine, two-seat, multirole supersonic fighter jet. The aircraft has been used extensively in the war against Ukraine and the crashed plane was part of the 4th Naval Aviation Regiment.

‌



In the war, the plane is deployed for air defence, escorting bombers, attacking Ukrainian targets and operations over the Black Sea.

It is reported that Russia has now lost more than 20 combat planes this year. Last month a nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, the defense ministry said.

‌



It added in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, with one crewmember surviving the crash and was hospitalized with injuries.

And a Russian military plane crashed in annexed Crimea in April, killing 29 people on board, officials said.

‌



The An-26 military transport plane went missing while flying over the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014. The Russian defence ministry then said in an update that the plane crashed, killing six crewmembers and 23 passengers.

Meanwhile, Putin has agreed today to resume trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kyiv on ending the war in Ukraine, a Kremlin official said.

‌



The Russian leader has agreed “in principle” to resume the talks after November 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters following a meeting in St Petersburg between Putin and Donald Trump ’s envoy Steve Witkoff.

The trilateral talks will focus on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends,” Ushakov said.

Article continues below

Witkoff’s talks with Putin about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine came as Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted only a summit of leaders can break the impasse.

News.title: Dad spared execution after decades on Death Row as governor questions murder evidence
News.content:
Dad spared execution after decades on Death Row as governor questions murder evidence

Toforest Johnson's daughter cried tears of joy after his death sentence was reduced to life without parole. She vows to keep fighting for his freedom, as his original prosecutor backs a new trial

View 3 Images Toforest spent almost three decades on Alabama's death row (Image: Johnson Family via AP)

A man convicted of murdering a deputy despite no physical evidence tying him to the killing has been spared execution after almost three decades on death row.

‌



‌



Toforest Johnson was sentenced to death in 1998 for the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy William Hardy, who was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel in Alabama. Johnson has maintained he was at a nightclub when the shooting happened. No physical evidence linked him to the killing, while more than 10 witnesses placed him on the other side of town.

‌



A key witness testified at his 1998 trial that she had overheard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime during a phone call. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony. Johnson’s lawyers argued that the state withheld evidence of her financial motivation.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images No physical evidence linked Johnson to the killing (Image: AP)

In a major development, Governor Kay Ivey commuted his death sentence to life imprisonment without parole on Tuesday, October 20. However, his conviction remains in place.

‌



The decision marked a breakthrough for his daughter, Akeriya Terry, who has spent much of her life fighting to save her dad. As tears of joy streamed down her face, she said: “I was like, OK, somebody’s listening. We’re making some moves, we’re making some waves.”

She added: “I’m going to cry, because that’s what we’ve been saying this whole time, there’s nothing there that would tie him to this case.”

‌



Governor Ivey said she had reviewed the case and concluded there was insufficient direct evidence to carry out the death penalty. She stressed that her decision was not a finding of innocence.

She said: “My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.”

‌



Calls for a new trial have come from both Jefferson County district attorney Danny Carr and Jeff Wallace, the original trial prosecutor, who believes Johnson deserves a new trial in light of information he did not know when he prosecuted him.

View 3 Images Kim Kardashian thanked Johnson's legal team for their years of work on his case (Image: KimKardashian/Instagram)

‌



Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley and former chief justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers have also supported calls for a new trial, alongside other former judges and prosecutors.

But, Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall urged Ivey to reject the clemency request in an October 16 letter. He called on her to “respect the jury’s decision” and the decisions of the courts that had reviewed the case.

‌



For the family, the commutation lifted the looming fear of an execution date being set. Terry was a young girl when her father went to prison, and their relationship has continued through visits behind glass, phone calls and letters.

She explained that being in prison had not prevented him from being an active father. She said: “If I have a problem, I can call him and he can just talk me off the ledge. Having a father in prison but still be an active father is something I just praise him the most for.”

‌



Ty Alper, one of Johnson’s attorneys, said they were grateful to Ivey for “diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution”. His lawyers vowed to continue fighting to overturn the conviction and reunite him with his family.

Alper said: “Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family.”

‌



Kim Kardashian also welcomed the commutation. Writing on her Instagram stories, she said: “Today, Toforest Johnson’s death sentence was commuted to life without parole after decades on Alabama’s death row. I’m so grateful that Toforest will no longer face execution, but his fight for justice is far from over.”

She added: “I want to give a special thank you to his incredible legal team, who have spent years fighting for him and never gave up. Their dedication and persistence have been nothing short of extraordinary.”

‌



Terry will also continue fighting to bring her father home. For decades, she has followed a ritual and blown a kiss whenever she sees a redbird and wished for his freedom.

She said: “Just look at a redbird still and just keep hope alive. Just praying and wishing that all of this will come to an end soon - my wish is making its way, because we’re almost to the finish line.”

Article continues below

“It’s been a long fight, and this is just the beginning, getting this news today, so we’re going to keep fighting.”

News.title: Prince William has no intention of engaging with Harry - despite brother's hope for reconciliation
News.content:
Prince William “has no intention of engaging” with Prince Harry, despite his estranged brother's plea for reconciliation.

The Prince of Wales is committed to his public role and sees no scenario in the future where he would restore the fractured relationship with his brother, sources close to the heir have said. Prince Harry this week suggested that “some people don't want” him to repair his once close bonds with his family, following his departure from royal life.

Harry and his wife Meghan quit their royal roles in March 2020, to pursue a range of big money deals in the commercial world, including a tell-all series on Netflix and his bombshell memoir. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex relocated in August, from their home in the California to Britain, with Harry revealing that the family moved back for “opportunities”, such as having their children educated in the UK.

However, the couple have had only sporadic contact with the King and have not spoken to the Prince and Princess of Wales for years.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Prince Harry has issued a call for reconciliation with his family after years of being estranged from them

King Charles heaps praise on Prince William just hours after Harry reconciliation plea READ MORE :

A source close to William said: "There isn't a world right now where the Prince of Wales can imagine repairing the relationship with his brother. He remains deeply hurt over the many things the Duke of Sussex has said publicly about him and other family members.

"Look at what the family is doing just this week: a significantly important State Visit, commemorating the tragedy that occurred in Aberfan 60 years ago, and preparations being made for major royal tours in the immediate future.

‌



“This is what matters to the Prince and Princess of Wales, and the King and Queen - and that certainly doesn't include responding to the Duke of Sussex every time he pops up doing yet another interview.”

Harry made the comments during an on-camera interview with GQ, which was recorded in late September but released yesterday on the day senior royals welcomed the Sultan of Oman to a state visit at Windsor Castle.

View 3 Images The King, Queen and Prince William are getting on with their public roles, such as paying their respects at the Aberfan Memorial Garden today (Image: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock)

Harry, who moved his family back to the UK in August, said his attitude had changed and that he felt "optimistic" about his return.

‌



Asked whether he was grieving over the complicated relationship with his brother and father, Harry said: "Yes, of course." He then described complicated family dynamics as a "massively relatable issue" for so many people.

"Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out," he said. "Of course I do. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point."

Royal sources have revealed that despite Harry and Meghan now living in the UK, the royal family remain incredibly cautious over engaging with him after the controversies of the last few years, including the Sussexes' decision to take part in a tell-all interview with Oprah Winfrey and produce a documentary series on Netflix where they bemoaned their treatment by the institution.

‌



Harry was asked whether he thought he could repair his relationships with the King and William, responding: "Of course. Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, certainly letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do."

The source added: "Harry was advised in no uncertain terms to cease making public statements about issues which are deeply private. The way things are right now, he (William) has no intention of engaging with Harry."

A spokesman for the Sussexes said it was GQ's decision to publish the interview yesterday, adding that Harry's comments were "absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other member of his family. The comment was made in a general context and was not directed at his family in any way."

News.title: Should William forgive Harry and reconcile with his brother? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should William forgive Harry and reconcile with his brother? Take our poll and have your say

The Duke of Sussex has issued a plea to reunite with his family, after admitting he is ‘grieving’ the broken bond with the royals

Prince Harry admits he wants to reconcile with William and King Charles after royal rift - 'I want to work it out'

Prince Harry has made yet another public plea to reunite with his estranged brother Prince William, after the two warring brothers are believed to have not spoken in four years. The Duke of Sussex spoke candidly in a recent interview with GQ magazine about the ongoing rift with the Prince of Wales, as he admitted that he was 'grieving' their broken bond and that there is "enough drama in the world to continue with issues with family".

‌



‌



While he issued a plea to reconcile with his family, he claimed "some people don’t want it to work out". Harry continued: "With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point... scars stick around forever.”

‌



View 3 Images Harry has spoken about his family relationships in a new interview (Image: Aaron Chown/POOL PA via AP)

‌



Harry and William’s rift came to a head in 2020 when the Duke and Duchess of Sussex made the shock decision to quit their royal roles and relocate to the United States in search of personal and financial freedom from the Firm.

In the years that followed, both Harry and Meghan spoke freely about their grievances with the Royal Family and the institution as a whole, most notably in their 2021 tell-all interview with Oprah, their 2022 Netflix docuseries, and Harry’s memoir Spare, released in 2023.

Amidst these public jibes, Harry claimed he got in a physical altercation with his brother, and alleged they argued over disputes between Meghan and the Princess of Wales.

‌



It is believed Harry has not seen his brother since 2022 when they both attended the funeral of their late grandmother Queen Elizabeth. In the years since, Harry has spoken about wanting to reunite with his older brother. Despite moving back to the UK in late August, it is believed Harry and William have still not reconciled.

‌



Following the release of the GQ interview, a friend of Harry’s told news.com.au that the intention of his interview was clear, as he hopes to send a message to the Royal Family that he is laying down his sword and is finished with fighting.

The friend told the publication: “Harry’s come back to the UK with a very different perspective on things, given everything that’s happened since 2020. He’s genuinely very keen to find a way to make things work here, he wants to be here, and part of that is rebuilding a relationship with the media … and in a way that works for everyone on all sides.”

‌



View 3 Images William and Harry have not spoken for several years (Image: DOMINIC LIPINSKI, POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

They continued: “There’s just no point pretending the environment wasn’t incredibly toxic before they left, but I think he’s clearly now keen to move forward from that.”

‌



While Harry has continued to mend his relationship with King Charles in the last year - after meeting in person several times, along with Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet - William has yet to comment on the status of his relationship with his brother.

And according to former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond, William could find it “increasingly difficult to ignore" any reconciliation between the King and the Duke.

‌



View 3 Images The King with his two sons, William and Harry

She told the Mirror : “William, as far as we can see, seems set on concentrating on his own family and his work without the angst of dealing with his rift with Harry. But it’s going to become increasingly hard for William to ignore the situation [between Harry and Charles].”

‌



Dai Davies, former the head of Scotland Yard’s Royal Protection Command from 1994 to 1998, added about the brothers one day burying the hatchet: “Well, never say never, as we’ve now seen him meet with his father and stepmother [during their private Highgrove meeting].

“But when you think about the things he has said in public about his brother, he [Harry] has to remember that if you wash your dirty linen in public, and it was pretty dirty linen, then you shouldn’t expect the fees for your laundry to be met.”

News.title: Radiators will run warmer in autumn and winter if you do 10-minute task now
News.content:
Radiators will run warmer in autumn and winter if you do 10-minute task now

Keep your home warm throughout the cold months by doing a simple task this month

View 4 Images This trick helps prepare your home for winter (Image: PIKSEL via Getty Images)

Autumn is well and truly here in the UK, and now is the perfect time to get your radiators ready for the chilly months ahead, keeping your home as snug and comfortable as possible. Most British households tend to flick the heating on once outdoor temperatures consistently drop below 15°C, which usually occurs around the start of October.

‌



‌



Journalist Katherine McPhillips has revealed the one trick she swears by to keep her home warm throughout the winter. She said: "I live in an old Victorian house in Scotland, where it can be really draughty, so it is really important to me that my radiators are working properly."

‌



Radiators push warm air outwards, which can trap dust within the fins. Left unchecked, this dust will block heat from circulating around a room, leaving it feeling bitterly cold.

‌



The thought of cleaning a radiator might seem like a big job, but it generally takes less than 10 minutes, as all that dusty build-up can be cleared away simply by using a hair dryer.

View 4 Images Dust tends to collect inside radiators and stop them from heating up a room properly (Image: Katherine McPhillips)

Why use a hair dryer to clean a radiator?

It might sound a little unconventional, but over the course of a year, dust, pet hair and fluff can gather inside radiator fins, which are notoriously difficult to get to.

‌



This accumulation can act as an insulator, preventing warm air from flowing into a room, meaning not only will it struggle to heat up properly, but the radiator will also have to work considerably harder — ultimately pushing your energy bills higher. A hairdryer can help shift any debris that's become trapped inside or behind the radiator by blasting a powerful stream of air through it, forcing the dust down onto the floor.

Katherine explained: "I like to clean out my radiator now in late September, before I need to switch it on, and then do it once a month during the colder months to make sure it stays as hot as possible."

‌



View 4 Images It takes Katherine about 10 minutes to carry out this task on all of her radiators (Image: Katherine McPhillips)

How to remove dust from inside a radiator

To begin, lay a towel underneath the radiator — it makes gathering up any falling dust far simpler.

‌



Then, set your hairdryer to its lowest heat setting and highest speed option. Steer clear of using a hot setting, as this won't help with dust removal and can actually make the debris give off a slightly burnt odour.

Point the hairdryer nozzle at the top air vents and grille of the radiator to push the dust downwards and outwards.

‌



View 4 Images Katherine likes to use a hair dryer to quickly clean radiators before turning her heating on (Image: Katherine McPhillips)

Once done, simply throw away any dust that's gathered on the towel and use a vacuum to pick up any fluff that's ended up on the floor.

Article continues below

Katherine added: "I then like to use a wet cloth to wipe the outside of the radiator if there is any dust, and then my radiators are ready just in time for the colder seasons ahead."

News.title: UK's hidden treasure capital revealed after £20k gold cross discovered - check your area
News.content:
UK's hidden treasure capital revealed after £20k gold cross discovered - check your area

Impressive treasure finds have been dug up across Britain with dozens being found in some regions alone - it comes after a grandmother uncovered a gold cross while metal detecting in a farmer's field

View 2 Images Dozens of treasures have been found by treasure seekers in the UK (Image: Unsplash)

Britain is home to a trove of unearthed treasures, with thousands being discovered by amateur detectorists each day, including a £20,000 gold cross that was recently found.

‌



‌



Seaside favourites and holiday hotspots were among the top sites for treasure hauls in the UK. Research found the best place for those looking for buried riches is the Isle of White, where 118.7 recorded treasure finds were made per 38.6 miles.

‌



It is more than three times the rate in Midlothian, where the next-highest concentration of treasure finds is located at 33.6 per 38.6 miles. But they are far from the only places with artefacts worth finding.

‌



View 2 Images The Isle of Wight is known for its treasure finds (Image: Zoe Falk/Sustrans)

Rare signed menu with infamous spelling mistake from 1943 Dambusters victory dinner up for auction READ MORE :

Dorset and Wiltshire took second and third place in the overall ranking respectively, while Midlothian came in fourth. The study comes after grandmother Shelley Couzins was stunned after coming across a rare gold cross worth £20,000 while metal detecting in a farmer's field in Kent.

Cornwall, a county famous for smuggling and stories of buried treasure, has just 6.1 recorded treasure finds per 38.6 miles.

‌



Despite this, it does boast the highest concentration of protected historic monuments anywhere in the research study by gold investment platform BullionVault. Cornwall has an impressive 1,589 scheduled monuments, from ancient burial sites to historic ruins.

‌



East Lothian in Scotland boasted the second-highest concentration of scheduled monuments in the research, despite relatively few recorded treasure discoveries.

Dan Jay, director at BullionVault, said: “Britain has an extraordinary history beneath its feet, but looking only at where the most treasure has already been found gives us a very incomplete picture. We wanted to look at two sides of the story: where treasure discoveries have been concentrated and where the landscape shows particularly strong evidence of historic human activity.

Article continues below

“The Isle of Wight is the clearest example. Its concentration of treasure finds is extraordinary, but it also has a very high concentration of scheduled monuments, so it performs strongly whichever way you look at the data.

“Perhaps most interesting are places such as Herefordshire, East Lothian and Cornwall. They have comparatively fewer recorded treasure finds, but their historical footprint means they stand out as areas where the story may be far from finished.”

News.title: Private jet evacuated as smoke pours out and plane veers off runway during landing
News.content:
Private jet evacuated as smoke pours out and plane veers off runway during landing

Dramatic footage shows a private jet veering off a runway at Toluca International Airport in Mexico after suffering an electrical failure while landing

Private jet passengers evacuated on runway after electrical failure

A private jet was evacuated on the runway after suffering an electrical failure while landing.

‌



‌



Eleven people were on board flight XA-CBQ when it made an emergency landing at Toluca International Airport, near Mexico City, and veered off the runway on Tuesday. The pilot had reported electrical problems affecting the aircraft's steering and braking systems beforehand.

‌



The jet landed in Toluca at 12.04pm local time after departing Aguascalientes, in north-central Mexico, about an hour earlier. Airport staff activated emergency procedures and sent fire and rescue crews to the scene.

‌



Footage of the incident showed smoke billowing from the aircraft on the runway. None of the nine passengers or two crew members on board were injured, Toluca International Airport said in a statement.

View 2 Images The jet experienced an electrical failure and veered off the runway (Image: Jam Press)

The runway was temporarily closed while the aircraft was removed and safety checks were carried out.

‌



Authorities have not confirmed the type of aircraft involved, but aviation outlets have suggested it was a Gulfstream G200, a super-midsize, twin-engine business jet. Most G200s can accommodate between eight and 11 passengers.

An investigation into the cause of the electrical failure is under way.

‌



View 2 Images The aircraft is seen landing at Toluca International Airport (Image: Jam Press)

It comes after a private jet issued a "mayday" distress call shortly after taking off from Nigeria's capital after its cabin door came open and detached mid-flight.

Article continues below

The Bombardier Challenger CL60 business jet departed Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja at 4.17pm UTC on Thursday, bound for Murtala Muhammed Airport in Lagos. The crew of flight DWC052 declared an emergency just three minutes after take-off, according to an incident report.

The report, obtained by Nigerian newspaper the Daily Trust, said the crew informed air traffic control that a door had opened during the flight. The aircraft was instructed to return to Abuja for an emergency landing, where a duty controller observed that the door was missing. There were no reports of injuries.

News.title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
News.content:
Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.

The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.

Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.

The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.

While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.

It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.

"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.

She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.

On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.

But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.

Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London was raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year.

A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.

Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

News.title: Aberfan disaster 'most tragic of days imaginable' says King on 60th anniversary
News.content:
The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary.

Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school.

The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit".

Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing

About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside.

Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris.

News.title: 'I was only 8 but I realised my friend was dead' - Aberfan survivor recalls moment of disaster
News.content:
Four people who were children at the time of the Aberfan disaster recall the moment when a coal waste tip collapsed on schools and homes 60 years ago.

Gerald Kirwan told BBC Newsnight he thought it was an earthquake and found his classmate unresponsive, while his other classmate Gaynor Madgwick recalled waking up to finding herself buried up to her chest in the massive slurry.

Read more about this story here.

News.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
News.content:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.

The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were assessing potential impacts to government systems and critical infrastructure, and it was working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.

And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.

They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.

News.title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
News.content:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

News.title: Teenage boy guilty of trying to murder girl, 15, in school
News.content:
A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.

The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.

Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.

The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.

Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.

The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.

The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

News.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
News.content:
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than Â£284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.

He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.

The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had other jobs.

At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid Â£11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

News.title: Don't Stop Believin' - high school musical Glee set for reboot
News.content:
In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.

He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members".

"It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see."

He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it."

It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return.

"I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes."

Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera, who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez.

"It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school.

"But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it."

Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning.

Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.

Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges.

A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside.

Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars.

News.title: Woman told Russell Brand he 'treated her like an animal', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

One of the women who claims Russell Brand raped her later told him he had "treated her like an animal", a court has heard.

The comedian's trial at Southwark Crown Court in London has been hearing recorded police interviews with a female complainant, who claims she did not consent to anal sex with him at his house in 2009.

Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. He has said he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

On Wednesday, the jury heard an interview with a woman who says she first met Brand at one of his comedy shows at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

She said she had a boyfriend at the time but went to his dressing room, where she performed a sex act on him.

The woman said it was during their next meeting at his house when the sex was not consensual and she had only agreed to vaginal sex.

Asked by the detective in the interview whether there was ever a conversation about anal sex, she replied: "No."

She said she was surprised to receive a "random" text message from Brand six months later, saying he wanted to "push her further".

She said she replied asking: "Why are you even messaging me?"

"I remember his response, saying, 'Because you're dirty and I want to push you further'."

The jury heard that the woman did not respond straight away because she was upset, but then replied saying: "I think you've pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal."

The woman added: "I do remember his response was immediate. He said, 'I'm sorry'."

News.title: Crystal Palace urged to retire bald eagle mascot
News.content:
An animal rights group is urging Crystal Palace to retire their live bald eagle mascot with immediate effect, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals".

In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) asked the Premier League club to stop using the eagle, named Phoenix, in pre-match displays at Selhurst Park and to never use live animal mascots again.

The London team, known as the Eagles since 1973, introduced a live eagle to matchdays in 2010. Kayla, who died in 2020, performed the role for 10 years and her replacement Phoenix made her debut against West Ham in August 2024.

Peta says birds can become "frightened, disoriented and panicked" in stadium environments, putting themselves and fans at risk.

Using them for displays and entertainment also denies the animals, who "would naturally avoid humans", the opportunity to engage with their natural instincts, leading to "frustration and stress", the group said.

The organisation has "detailed records" of incidents involving live mascots, including birds, being injured or killed in collisions with walls, windows and match balls, as well as a falcon embedding its talons in a spectator's scalp after landing on his head.

In 2017, a Charlton Athletic fan was found guilty of trying to punch Kayla the eagle at a League Cup fixture two years earlier.

"Many professional sports teams use only willing humans as mascots and the club already has Pete the Eagle to excite the crowd," said Dr Carys Bennett, Peta's senior corporate projects manager.

"Bald eagles are widely recognised as symbols of freedom. They deserve better than to be used as an entertainment prop to amuse the Eagles' fans."

BBC Sport has contacted Crystal Palace for comment.

News.title: Amber warning issued as Storm Austen threatens UK with strong winds and heavy rain
News.content:
The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.

The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.

Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.

Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings.

A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible.

Southern and eastern Scotland is also covered by a Met Office yellow warning - this one for heavy rain which could bring the risk of flooding.

News.title: Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life
News.content:
A student has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years for murdering his university housemate after lying in wait and stabbing him 30 times.

Zack Coughlan, 23, ambushed Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near Bristol on 8 April and left him dying in the alleyway to dispose of bloodstained evidence. He called police eight hours later.

Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol Crown Court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.

In a statement read in court, Collins' step-mother Lisa Jane Collins said his death had "affected our family in a deep, lasting and profound way. From now on, we will always be the couple whose boy got murdered".

Both men were final-year University of the West of England (UWE) students and lived together in a house in Filton.

Collins only had two pieces of coursework to complete before he would have returned home to his family in Swansea, where his dad already had an engineering job set up for him.

News.title: Giant tunnel proposed to clean up Windermere's sewage problem
News.content:
A Â£3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.

The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.

At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.

It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the Â£3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.

Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.

News.title: Hackers steal children's data after company used 'Password1' to protect old account
News.content:
A cyber-attack stole information belonging to thousands of children by accessing an account that used the password "Password1", a data watchdog has said.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and Data Cymru after the attack on 1 November 2024.

The hackers exposed personal information belonging to 3,300 people, mostly children, by using a test account, known as Test2, which had existed for more than 12 years and was protected by the password that could be compromised in less than a second.

ONL said the account "should have been removed long before criminals were able to use it", adding it had brought in independent cyber-security specialists.

The company, which provided IT services to Data Cymru, said it accepted the ICO's findings and had "acted on them".

Data Cymru merged with the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) in 2025, who said there was no evidence the stolen information was "shared further or misused".

ONL and Data Cymru were found to have breached UK GDPR rules, external by failing to properly protect their systems and by not regularly checking whether their security measures were effective.

During the ransomware attack, the hackers encrypted 182.7GB of data and stole 42GB from Data Cymru's systems. It exposed the personal information related to two projects supporting children and families.

David Doodson, head of investigations at the Information Commission's Office, said: "Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors.

"This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands."

Doodson added the responsibility for "these failures did not sit with one organisation alone".

According to the watchdog, ONL created a test account in 2012 and used the password "Password1" to protect it, failing to audit it or remove it for more than 12 years.

It also did not review local administrator accounts after they were first deployed, with accounts on three affected systems using the same password, for the same period of time.

The watchdog said Data Cymru failed to put a data protection agreement in place with ONL, and that there was a gap in responsibility between the two organisations.

It also said Data Cymru failed to ensure the dormant test account was identified and removed, or updated to meet stronger password requirements.

The ICO added it was a lesson for every organisation to "use strong passwords, protect remote access with multi-factor authentication, regularly review every user account, and be completely clear about who is responsible for cyber-security when services are outsourced".

Following the cyber-attack, both organisations introduced stronger security measures.

ONL introduced a process prompting customers to review active accounts periodically and providing recommendations about accounts that should be removed, the ICO said.

It also strengthened its account access controls, including the use of multi-factor authentication.

On 30 April 2025, Data Cymru and ONL entered into a legally compliant data processing contract.

Data Cymru also introduced periodic account reviews and strengthened account access controls, including using multi-factor authentication.

A spokesperson for ONL said: "Within a week of the attack, we'd worked with Data Cymru to check every account on its network and switched off the ones it no longer needed that same day.

"We also brought in independent cyber-security specialists to investigate."

They added: "Since then, we've protected remote access with multi-factor authentication and introduced regular account reviews for the customers whose networks we look after, so accounts that aren't needed are found and removed.

"This was limited to the server we hosted for Data Cymru. No other customer information held by ONL was affected."

A WLGA spokesperson said it remained "committed to maintaining robust information governance standards and continually reviewing the measures we have in place".

"We recognise the fundamental importance of strong information governance and of protecting the information entrusted to organisations working on behalf of local government.

"Since the incident, measures have been put in place to strengthen the arrangements identified by the ICO, including the removal of dormant user accounts, strengthened password and remote user access controls, and improved data processing arrangements to clearly define contractual responsibilities for security and audit activities," the spokesperson added.

News.title: Belfast comedian criticised for rape 'joke' about assault victim
News.content:
A Belfast comedian has been criticised for making a rape "joke" about a woman who had recently spoken publicly about being the victim of a sexual assault.

Vittorio Angelone, who has since apologised on social media, referred to content creator Rebecca Goodwin in a remark about rape which he made in a podcast episode in 2025.

Goodwin, who had previously reported a rape to police, said it will "forever live with me that it was allowed for my name to be used as the punchline of a malicious 'joke' about such a serious issue".

Angelone said he has reached out to Goodwin and apologised directly.

Goodwin had claimed that Angelone posted videos of the "joke" on his social media accounts in recent days.

Rape Crisis Northern Ireland and Dublin Rape Crisis Centre have both criticised the remarks.

The makers of the podcast have been contacted for comment.

During a 2025 episode of the 'Have a Word' podcast, Angelone asked of fellow comedian Freddy Quinne "if you're here, who's raping Rebecca Goodwin?".

British OnlyFans creator Rebecca Goodwin had previously spoken publicly about being the victim of sexual assault.

The comments were made during a "roast" episode of the podcast posted in December 2025.

The episode, which Goodwin was not involved in, contained comedians taking turns insulting each other in front of an audience.

News.title: Man in court after three Jewish women assaulted
News.content:
A 33-year-old man accused of assaulting three Jewish women in north-east London allegedly attacked one of the victims while she was pushing her baby in a pram, a court has heard.

Abdisamad Siad, of no fixed abode, appeared at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court charged with three counts of assault by beating.

Magistrates heard the alleged offences took place on Clapton Common, Hackney, on Monday when the first victim reported being "slapped across the face" by a man at about 13:30 BST.

Siad entered not guilty pleas to the three charges and was remanded into custody.

The court was told the second complainant was pushing her baby daughter in a pram when, at about 13:36, she was allegedly punched twice in the face by the defendant.

Shortly after, the defendant allegedly punched the third victim "three to four times" before running away.

News.title: Como v Man United LIVE: Carrick battles injury crisis and winless run in Champions League
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Carrick travels to Italy without up to eight first-team players ( Getty )

Manchester United seek to end a six-game winless run as they travel to face Como in the Champions League.

But Michael Carrick is battling an injury crisis in defence as he bids to turn the club’s fortunes around, with Luke Shaw, Lisandro Martinez and Patrick Dorgu all out, Ayden Heaven unavailable due to illness and Leny Yoro suspended following his sending off in the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid last week.

Carrick said he was hoping for a “fresh start” following the 1-1 draw against Leeds on Sunday but United could face a tough evening against the Italian side, who are led by Cesc Fabregas and demolished RB Leipzig 4-1 on their Champions League debut at the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium last month.

Follow live updates from Como v Man Utd with our live blog below:

News.title: Driver is fatally shot while crossing the George Washington Bridge
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A 46-year-old man was shot and killed while driving across the George Washington Bridge near the end of the evening rush, snarling traffic for hours on the busy span that connects New York City and New Jersey.

Authorities said that while responding to calls about the shooting on the New Jersey-bound side of the bridge's upper level just after 7 p.m. Tuesday, they found the man unconscious with a gunshot wound in the driver's seat of a vehicle.

The man, whose name hasn't been released, was later pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. No arrests have been made, and authorities haven't given a possible motive for the shooting.

Closed lanes reopened about five hours after the shooting, said the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates the bridge.

Opened to traffic in 1931, the iconic, double-decked bridge spans high over the Hudson River, carrying around 100 million vehicles between New Jersey and Manhattan each year, according to the Port Authority, which calls it the world's busiest. The bridge and its entrances are teeming with cameras.

Its entrances can be difficult to navigate, as drivers often veer across packed lanes, causing heavy traffic even under normal circumstances.

News.title: Macron criticizes Trump's ‘stupid’ comments about French riots and 'false' AI images
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

French President Emmanuel Macron has hit back at Donald Trump and foreign leaders, accusing them of trying to exploit France's tense social climate for political gain after a weekend of violence and looting drew worldwide attention.

Protests over the soaring cost-of-living led to widespread rioting and looting that shocked many French citizens. US President Donald Trump used the violence to rally his political supporters at campaign events.

He made unsubstantiated claims that Muslim migrants are responsible for the unrest and urged Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late!”

Macron responded by saying there “has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting in Paris and other French cities last weekend. “And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said.

Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.”

open image in gallery A protesters holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Lyon, France, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 ( AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani )

He added that there have been “AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.” Macron did not specify which AI-generated images he was referring to, nor how he knew the content was false.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said his office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, “to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media.”

Macron and Trump once enjoyed a good relationship, but Trump regularly mocks the French president in his public speeches.

“The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country,” Macron said. “So those people really bother me.”

“When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic — who sometimes naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote about what happened in France — they’re using our country for their own political campaigns,” said Macron.

“And we don’t need that.”

More protests planned this week

New protests are planned in France on Thursday and Saturday, following calls from student unions and groups within the “yellow vest” movement whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a "massive" security operation was planned for Saturday. The aim, he said, was to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.

France has had two consecutive quiet nights since the weekend's unrest. Curfews have been imposed in parts of several major cities, including small areas of Paris.

open image in gallery Protesters confront police during a demonstration against rising living costs and in support of students’ grievances in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 ( AP Photo/Emma Da Silva )

High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also say school days, which often run from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., are exhausting, and that the university admissions system is complex and unfair.

Petrol, energy and food prices have surged in recent months, and it remains to be seen whether Macron's announcement will ease protesters' anger. He said the additional diesel supplies addressed “some of the anxieties.”

“I also hear the concerns of our high school and university students. Those concerns stem from other factors, but in any case, I think things are moving in the right direction,” he added.

Macron secures diesel supplies

Macron was speaking in Qatar at the end of a tour of key energy suppliers in Gulf Arab states. On the tour, he secured an additional 100,000 metric tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates, with a further 100,000 tons to be confirmed in Bahrain.

Macron's office said he traveled to the Middle East to find solutions to the energy crisis and rising energy prices, and to secure supplies of oil, gas, diesel and jet fuel. The Élysée said nearly 295,000 additional tons of diesel per month could be secured, including supplies from Saudi Arabia. That figure is equivalent to more than 10% of France's monthly diesel consumption.

Macron later traveled to Saudi Arabia to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman “to continue efforts to secure and diversify oil and gas supplies,” according to his office.

Earlier this month, the Group of Seven wealthy democracies agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products. The releases will begin with substantial quantities of diesel, after the fuel's price hit a record high in the United States.

“I would remind you that France initiated the G7 meeting that led to the release of strategic reserves, which, through implementation at the national level, will help bring down prices starting in early November,” Macron said.

“We are using the legal means at our disposal to prevent further incidents of this kind,” Macron said. “Those who intend to cause disturbances in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so. Tomorrow, we will also have a very detailed update on the implementation of these measures, including anticipation, intelligence gathering, and security, not just for Saturday, but also for the coming weeks.”

News.title: I understand why only a third of LGBTQ+ people are ‘out’ when they travel – and that’s the problem
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It happens at the hotel check-in desk: the booking for one bed, the receptionist's glance, and the split-second decision of whether to say "partner" or "friend". Last month, research from Booking.com finally put a number on it. Just 34 per cent of British LGBTQ+ travellers say they're out when they travel, despite 76 per cent of us being out to our close friends. Somewhere between the departure board and the check-in desk, more than half of us quietly fold a part of ourselves up and tuck it into the overhead locker for the duration of our stay.

I understand it completely, because I've done it myself. Every queer traveller knows the dial, and my day job as a travel presenter and journalist means I've turned mine up more than most. The first few times I found myself in the Middle East for work, the discomfort caught me off guard. Here in the UK, for all our challenges, I can exist as a gay man. Yet there I was, slipping the pride flag wristband off my hand before landing while checking my screensaver wasn't a photo of me and my boyfriend at the time. You feel it in small moments, like the taxi driver's eyes lingering in the wing mirror a beat too long. The worst of it, however, comes at the hotel desk. I remember the bead of sweat running down my back as it dawned on me that the booking said one double bed, there were two of us, and we’re both men. The clerk repeated "we have single rooms available, sir" and I could barely take it in, because somewhere in the back of my mind, the police were already on their way, and in a country where the way you love carries a prison sentence, that thought is not just paranoia.

The research confirms what so many of us have always known in our bones. More than a third of us would hide who we are entirely if it meant seeing a bucket-list destination, and 37 per cent now take more precautions than a few years ago. One statistic that has remained lodged in my mind, is the 46 per cent of us who scan our surroundings before showing affection, a practised sweep of the room before a hand is held. Romance, for so many of us it seems, comes with a risk assessment attached. Grimmest of all, the travellers who stay in the closet report by far the fewest negative experiences and the least anxiety. Hiding, in other words, works. Which might be the saddest sentence I've typed all year.

open image in gallery Aidy Smith ( Aidy Smith )

The world is quietly teaching our community that the price of seeing it is ourselves, and trans travellers, whose anxiety is rising on an exponential scale, are paying the highest fare of all. A holiday is supposed to be the exhale, yet instead you're running a second job in the background, remembering which version of yourself you checked in as. How are you meant to relax when you are constantly on guard. Just waiting for one slip up, one wrong word to foil your disguise, and in certain countries, put you at genuine risk of danger.

Would it put me off traveling to these countries? Truthfully, it starts an argument I keep having with myself more and more often these days, and I'd like to hear your thoughts upon reading this to see if you questioned your original perspective too.

The first instinct is point-blank refusal: why hand my money to a country that treats my community as though it shouldn't exist? Then the guilt arrives, because our immediate yet justifiable reaction fails to consider the most critical part of this whole conversation. What about the queer people who live there and have no choice? Does my absence make their lives easier, or lonelier? Perhaps the braver action is to actually go, to be visibly and calmly ourselves in front of ordinary people, so those people can see we're not the cabal they've been warned about. We're simply humans, who happen to love differently to them, and love harmlessly all the while.



On every one of these trips, I ask myself the same question: do the people here actually care who I love, or is this the work of governments who need a common enemy to hold onto power? In my experience the two are often not the same thing. Stay at almost any resort in various countries where being LGBTQ+ is a legal offence and the staff couldn't care less. They're simply happy that you're happy. Mention a boyfriend in passing to a tour guide or driver and the reaction isn’t immediate horror; many times, it's actually curiosity. Which then leaves you wondering how much of this is really a people problem, and how much of it is a hierarchy problem wearing the people as a costume.

Right now, Turkey is an example. Friends of mine have holidayed there for years; the sunshine is glorious, the lira goes far, and the welcome has always been incredibly warm. Yet since September, authorities there have raided gay bars, LGBTQ+ organisations and activists' homes, arresting more than 160 people under a campaign the government calls "My Family is Safe".

The first thought is to abstain and take the money elsewhere. Then I read an article by my colleague, Gary Nunn. Gary has visited Turkey annually for 20 years as an openly gay man and went back days after the raids to find Istanbul's gay bars rammed, the community defiant and dancing, and with that my thinking began to shift. Perhaps the answer isn't avoiding Turkey at all but going precisely to put my money behind those venues and the people keeping the lights on through the hardest of times. That, honestly, is what's on my mind now. There is a line I'd draw, though: travelling somewhere to stand with its queer community for a few days is one thing, while two weeks impersonating a straight man on my own holiday is entirely another. Quite honestly, at that point the trip has lost the very thing it was for.

There is some good news too. The same research found 75 per cent of us had at least one positive experience linked to our identity while travelling, and almost half believe acceptance is improving. The signals that land are beautifully small: pronouns got right, a flag in a window. Schemes like Booking.com's Travel Proud badge exist precisely so we can find those places without the guesswork and just be ourselves. Lovingly, openly, unapologetically.

Being out on holiday isn't a luxury or an add-on. It's the entire point of going away in the first place: to relax, to be free, to be fully yourself. The tan fades within a fortnight of landing, but coming home having spent two weeks as yourself, all of yourself, is the only souvenir that lasts.

News.title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.

The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.

Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced.

The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.

Trump's order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”

The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.

Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.

The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified.” A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.

About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote.

The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.

News.title: In Honduras, hard hit by drought, authorities hope to make it rain using contentious tactic
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Victor Torres is on the hunt for clouds as he flies over parched corn fields ravaged by months of drought in the rugged Honduran mountains.

“We’re seeing strong cloud cover over here,” the pilot says, pointing to a map on the dashboard as he banks the small plane sharply into a patch of dark gray.

Behind him, a technician cranks the knob of a large metal tank, which hisses as it sprays yellow silver iodide particles into the skies. This “cloud seeding” is a gamble by the Honduran government, aiming to induce enough rain over enough fields to help farmers and their crops survive.

The El Niño climate pattern, scrambling weather worldwide and now exacerbated by warming seas, has devastated communities across the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid region from southern Mexico through Panama.

The effects are particularly acute in the dry forests of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua, where corn and bean crops have dried up, leaving subsistence farmers without food. Cattle have either died or been sold off. Coffee plantations have withered and shrimp farms have lost production.

“Families are going to bed with one or two meals a day, and that’s after turning to other survival strategies like selling off their animals, their tools … just to get by,” said Aníbal Zúñiga, who coordinates World Food Program aid distribution in Nueva Concepcion, a 250-person village tucked in the mountains 90 minutes north of Honduras’ capital, Tegucigalpa.

The WFP estimates that nearly 50 million people globally could be pushed into acute food insecurity now that El Niño is expected to last into 2027. Central America is among the places to be hit the hardest.

Meteorologist says cloud seeding is an expensive ‘experiment’
