Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.

Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.

Is this legal, and why is it controversial?

Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.

“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”

But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.

Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television s for a candidate.

Has anyone done this before?

Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.

Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.



He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.

Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

World.title: US envoy Witkoff calls Russia’s Putin a ‘humanitarian’
World.content:
NewsFeed US envoy Witkoff calls Russia’s Putin a ‘humanitarian’

US envoy Steve Witkoff praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a ‘humanitarian’ while thanking him for the release of American Stephen Hubbard, who spent more than four years in Russian detention after being convicted of mercenary activity in Ukraine.

World.title: Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard after four years in prison
World.content:
Hubbard was jailed after Russia said he fought alongside Ukrainian forces against Russia.

American Stephen Hubbard has been freed from a Russian prison and is on his way home after United States President Donald Trump said his administration had secured his release.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, adding that the US was not required to give anything in return for the release of the 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan.

The deal came during a visit to Russia by a top US envoy, and just days after Trump took a series of actions seen as beneficial to Moscow.

Hubbard, whose family says had been living in Ukraine since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, was tried and convicted in a closed-door trial, with Russian prosecutors saying he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military and had fought alongside its forces before being captured. He was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2024.

The US had declared Hubbard a wrongfully detained American.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is in Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine war, told him that “our whole nation sends their thanks” and that Putin was a “humanitarian” for allowing Hubbard to walk free. Witkoff briefly met with Hubbard in St. Petersburg after his release, telling him, “from today is a new life for you”.

The release came at a dynamic moment in relations between the US, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship under strain at the same time that the Trump administration has pursued policies which Ukraine says have rewarded Putin.



Those include Trump’s decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that the US Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.

Named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in an effort to curb high gas prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

World.title: US congressional candidate Brad Lander freed after West Bank detention
World.content:
Lander says dozens remain in Israeli custody after being detained while helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives.

United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander says he has been released from Israeli military custody with a warning after being detained alongside dozens of volunteers helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.

But several dozen others, including rabbis and international volunteers, remain in detention, according to Lander, who called them to be released immediately.

“I’ve been released from IDF custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile,” Lander wrote on X. “I told them I wasn’t even a congressmember yet, just a nominee.”

Lander, a former New York City comptroller and mayoral candidate, was among approximately 80 volunteers detained by Israeli soldiers and police near the village of Nahalin, outside Bethlehem, according to the Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights.

The group, which included American, Israeli, Palestinian, British and Canadian volunteers, had been accompanying Palestinian farmers for about two hours when Israeli forces arrived and informed them that they were in a closed military zone.

The volunteers were then taken to a police station, according to Rabbis for Human Rights.

The Israeli government has not responded to a request for comment.

World.title: How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties
World.content:
Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia signed a deal on Wednesday to deepen their defence industry cooperation, reflecting a broader effort by countries in the region to widen their network of security partners amid the prolonged US-Israel war with Iran.

The four countries signed the memorandum of understanding in Doha, building on existing military projects through joint production, technology transfers and more closely integrated supply chains.

The initiative comes as the failure of the United States and Iran to reach a concrete peace agreement pushes countries in the region to diversify their defence partnerships and look beyond what experts described as an overreliance on Washington for their security. But they stress that closer cooperation does not mean abandoning long-standing alliances. Instead, the ambition is to gain greater control over their own security while strengthening pre-existing partnerships.

Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence industry analyst and managing director of Mergen Analytical Strategies, told Al Jazeera that the implications could extend well beyond the four participants.

“We may be witnessing the emergence of an interconnected network of defence and security arrangements extending from the Gulf to South and Southeast Asia, rather than a single formal alliance,” he said.

What would the agreement do?

In a statement, the Qatari Defence Ministry said the “Badr” Memorandum of Understanding “aims to foster cooperation in the field of defence manufacturing, enhance defence capabilities among the four countries, and promote collaboration in technical defence training, as well as in research and development areas, thereby contributing to the creation of solutions and industries worthy of the evolution of modern defences”.



Experts say that under the agreement, each country will bring its own resources or set of skills to the table. “Turkiye contributes technological expertise, systems integration and a mature defence industry; Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and sizeable domestic markets; and Qatar provides investment potential and demand,” said Mevlutoglu.

Together, the four nations could “establish integrated supply chains, allowing these countries to jointly develop, manufacture and sustain defence systems”, he told Al Jazeera.

Such arrangements could give buyers a larger role in producing and supporting their own equipment, while providing manufacturers with longer-term orders and investment. Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that Pakistan and Indonesia were both willing to purchase Turkish weapons and locate part of their production at home.

This could bring down costs for Turkish companies and bring jobs to Pakistan and Indonesia, while Qatar brings “financial depth”, he said.

Building on existing partnerships

Turkiye, home to one of the world’s most advanced defence sectors, already has military manufacturing ties with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia separately. Qatar and Turkiye, for instance, signed a bilateral defence industry memorandum in October 2025.

But Vidal says that the new agreement, bringing together all four nations, points to a strategic calculation alongside an industrial one. Closer relationships could give more countries a stake in each other’s security. He pointed to Qatar’s investment in the Turkish defence industry over more than a decade and Ankara’s deployment of forces to Doha during the 2017 diplomatic crisis.

Pakistan’s existing naval manufacturing project with Turkiye, meanwhile, shows how weapons purchases can support domestic manufacturing. Of the four ships announced under the project, two are to be built in Istanbul and two at Karachi Shipyard.

Indonesia and Turkiye, meanwhile, are jointly building a tank.

“The rationale is to streamline these distinct defence export and joint production agreements under a more structured and resilient networked hub, rather than reinvent the wheel with each new defence agreement,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera.

Less dependence on Washington?

The US-Israeli war with Iran and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have heightened regional security concerns, analysts say, while reported US weapons shortages may be adding urgency to efforts to strengthen pre-existing partners and bolster domestic arms-building capacity.



“Diversification is a major driver, particularly as recent conflicts have exposed vulnerabilities associated with dependence on foreign suppliers, technology restrictions and supply chain disruptions,” Mevlutoglu said.

But he cautioned against interpreting the memorandum as a break with Washington. “Qatar is unlikely to abandon its strategic relationship with Washington, while Turkiye seeks greater technological independence within NATO, not autonomy from it,” he said.

According to Bader Mousa Al-Saif, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme and an assistant professor at Kuwait University, the initiative reflects Gulf countries increasingly looking towards the Global South and fellow Muslim countries.

It also complements a separate effort to formalise military cooperation across the region, analysts say. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, establishing a mutual defence commitment. Ankara submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification on Wednesday, although deploying Turkish troops abroad would require separate parliamentary approval.

The Doha memorandum concerns industrial cooperation rather than a mutual defence pledge, but Mevlutoglu sees a connection between the two initiatives. “While Mecca focuses on collective deterrence and military cooperation, Doha could provide the industrial and technological foundations for such partnerships,” he said.

World.title: How war in Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD
World.content:
Experts warn that war takes a heavy toll on neurodivergent people, who often rely on routine.

Share How war in Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD on social media

Beirut, Lebanon – After her husband died from COVID-19 in 2020, Lena Kouyoumjian moved back to her parents’ house in Mazraat Yachouh, a village 20 minutes’ drive from Beirut. For Lena, energetic and outgoing, the move was difficult, but she accepted that she needed help to care for her 20-year-old daughter, Vana, who is autistic and non-verbal.

Lena first noticed her daughter’s symptoms when she was two years old. Vana is still unable to communicate verbally how she feels, but her mother does her best to understand her.

Like many autistic individuals – and neurodivergent people in general – Vana needs a supportive and stable environment, alongside a structured routine, to feel well.

Lebanon has been engulfed in war since October 2023, with bombings across the country and an economic crisis continuing to impact all Lebanese, particularly neurodivergent people.

When Israel escalated its attacks on southern Lebanon in March, as a trainer for children with disabilities, Lena understood that this could impact her autistic daughter.

“Any sudden change in routine, loud noises, fear, or uncertainty can increase their anxiety and make them feel unsafe,” Lena told Al Jazeera.

“I can see this in my daughter. Since the situation became more difficult, she has become more anxious and sensitive to the changes happening around her.”

Challenging a social stigma

The symptoms of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) vary depending on the person and condition, but they frequently include sensory issues and emotional dysregulation. ADHD and autism often occur together, combining to make AuDHD, where traits from both conditions can be seen.



People with these neurodevelopmental conditions are often stigmatised by societies that do not fully understand them, including in Lebanon.

While the pressures caused by Israel’s war on Lebanon and mass displacement have led to psychological issues for many, neurodivergent people are more vulnerable due to their need for consistent support and routine.

“Being a parent of an autistic child isn’t something every parent can handle. A challenge I often face is deciding the amount of time and energy I should allocate to my child,” said Lena.

Lebanon’s Autism Awareness Association (AAA) has provided support for both mother and child. Vana has attended classes at AAA, a nonprofit based in Antelias, outside Beirut, for the past six years, which serves as an alternative school for young autistic people.

But rising costs in Lebanon during the war have prevented Vana from attending classes regularly. “Even transportation to her centre became very difficult, especially with the increasing financial challenges. At times, it became impossible for her to go, so she had to stay home,” Lena said.

Ghada Hayek Makhoul, who co-founded AAA with other parents of autistic children in 2015, said the group has made constant efforts to increase awareness about the condition in Lebanon.

“Many people don’t know what autism really is. They don’t know the spectrum; how it can vary from mild to moderate to severe,” Ghada told Al Jazeera.

Sensory overload

Ghada’s son, Anthony, is a calm 27-year-old autistic, non-verbal man who relies heavily on helpers. Although he is unable to speak, his mother said it is clear when he is distressed, putting his hands over his ears when he is in pain due to sensory discomfort.

Autistic people can be more sensitive to noises than neurotypical people. During the war, people in Lebanon have been subjected to a harrowing range of sounds, from Israeli bombs exploding on the ground to the sonic booms of warplanes flying overhead.

“So, imagine the drones all the time [for autistic people], the bombs, and the vibration of the bombs … all of this that we were hearing, so of course it affected him a lot,” Ghada said.

“My son can’t listen to the TV any more due to the news. He switches it off and removes the remote control. It’s too triggering for him.”

Anthony’s mother said he senses tension and anxiety, even if his understanding of what is being said or happening is limited.



“[It affects] all the senses, everything. He doesn’t want to go into a pool any more. He used to love the water. And now, he doesn’t want to go into the pool any more,” Ghada said.

“I don’t know what changed. Because it’s outside? Because of the sound? I don’t know.”

Mental health support as a luxury

Israel’s war on Lebanon has had a direct economic impact on the AAA and other organisations providing neurodivergent or psychological support.

Lebanon’s economic crisis, with inflation potentially reaching 17 percent this year, has also led to a brain drain of professionals who could support neurodivergent people.

AAA is a crucial support base for families with autistic children. But it comes at a significant cost of $700 per month for children attending five days a week. With 80 percent of the population living in poverty, few can afford such services.

“We need more trained staff, and we also need to keep the staff that are leaving the country. So, we need to have better salaries, but we cannot afford it, because we will have to increase the load on the parents,” said Ghada. “Things are in crisis mode for everybody during the war.”

The same thing is being seen with other mental health services. While many nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) provide free therapy, private consultations can cost more than $100 for a single 50-minute session.

Nour Toukan, a public health researcher at Enmaeya, a media platform focused on sustainable development, told Al Jazeera that care for people with autism or even for ADHD is “very much an out-of-pocket expense.”

While the government did launch a National Disability Allowance in 2023, with funding from the European Union and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the allowance of $40 per month is not enough to cover even the basics in Lebanon. People with autism can get a personal disability card, issued by the Ministry of Social Affairs, making them eligible for support, but those with ADHD cannot.

Lebanon’s National Mental Health Programme, established in 2014 by the Ministry of Public Health, is trying to bridge gaps in support caused by economic and geographic variables.

Dr Rabih El Chammay, the founder and director of the programme, told Al Jazeera a national mental health strategy for children and teenagers is being finalised.

“National studies addressing autism and ADHD have also been conducted, providing evidence to inform this work. We are meeting with several organisations, particularly organisations representing families of persons with autism, to understand priorities and build momentum for further coordinated action,” Dr Rabih said. “War makes this work more difficult because it can increase support needs while disrupting the services people depend on.”

Developmental regression

Displaced people have been the most impacted, but all of those in Lebanon whose schooling and routines have been disrupted are affected.



Adham Faraj, a 23-year-old psychology student at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, who was diagnosed with ADHD in 2024, said that when his classes moved online due to the war, he found himself staying at home more and more.

“It’s less engaging, especially if you struggle with attention. You’re less motivated to go out, so you just attend classes from bed,” Adham said.

Adham said the intensity of Israeli air strikes in Lebanon unsettled him, along with concerns about the rising price of medicine.

“There’s always a cheaper alternative, but it depends on people’s social class. Maybe an $11 box of medication is affordable for some, but not for everyone,” he said.

Rim Ajjour, a psychologist and psychotherapist in Beirut, whose work focuses on young people with autism, has seen that many of the skills neurodivergent people learned before the war are now being lost.

“With the limited resources available in Lebanon and the shift in people’s priorities, there has been more limited access to therapy,” she said.

Rim said that her clinic and others are doing their utmost to keep therapy accessible by freezing consultation fees, even when their own expenses are increasing.

With Israeli attacks continuing in southern Lebanon, which remains occupied by Israeli forces, in violation of a US-brokered June ceasefire, many fear the impact on their work in case of a return to full-scale war.

“I don’t know how we’ll be able to take it again,” Rim said.

World.title: Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
World.content:
The European states say their support for Riyadh is ‘defensive’, but analysts warn Houthi reaction may complicate that.

Share Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict? on social media

France and the United Kingdom have both moved to deploy military assets to Saudi Arabia, deepening their defence ties with the kingdom as its conflict with the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), in Yemen escalates.

Paris last week said it had begun sending assets to Saudi Arabia as part of a previously announced agreement, after President Emmanuel Macron committed to deploying troops and air defence systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis.

The UK, for its part, on Tuesday announced plans to deploy fighter jets to help shield Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks.

Both countries stressed that their support would be defensive.

Analysts say the European moves serve several geopolitical purposes: protecting Saudi oil exports that are important to European energy markets, shoring up their strategic alliance in the Gulf amid US reluctance to offer direct military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and strengthening deterrence against future Houthi attacks.

But the deployments also carry significant risks, many analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states more directly into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

“If insufficiently deterred, the Houthis may decide that the moment is ripe to test the resolve and resilience of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture, and attempt to draw Saudi Arabia’s allies even further into the Yemen-Saudi confrontation,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.



‘Support during crisis’

The British and French military support measures come as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign against it, including targeting energy and transport infrastructure.

Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha this month have killed 19 people and injured more than 300 others, according to the Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki.

Addressing the UK’s stepped-up military support for Saudi Arabia, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia “absolutely despicable”, specifically condemning the group’s targeting of Riyadh airport.

The UK Ministry of Defence said it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to fly “defensive counter air missions” in Saudi Arabia, send UK military advisers to work with Saudi staff officers and provide an A400M transport aircraft to help move defence material within the kingdom.

French support for Saudi Arabia would include soldiers, radars and defence systems, Macron has said, without detailing the scale of the support.

Urban Coningham, a research fellow at RUSI, noted differences in the British and French roles, with the French mainly limited to protecting Saudi export infrastructure. The British, by contrast, will conduct “defensive patrols where they would shoot down incoming missiles or drones” in Saudi Arabia, as well as provide air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi bombers and jets heading into Yemeni airspace, he said.

Camille Lons, policy fellow and deputy head of the Paris office at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France is limited in what it can provide to Saudi Arabia, particularly given the demands on European defences amid the war in Ukraine. Still, Paris sees its assistance as a way to “show support [for Saudi Arabia] in times of crisis, and a way to deepen the defence partnership”, Lons told Al Jazeera.

‘Freeing up’ Saudi aircraft

Saudi Arabia will welcome the European deployments, as it has struggled to translate some of its security partnerships into high-level military support.

In September, US President Donald Trump rejected multiple Saudi requests to participate in strikes on the Houthis, agreeing only to provide intelligence and targeting support, the news agency Reuters cited informed sources saying.

Turkiye and Pakistan have committed to “collective deterrence measures”, including potential troop deployments, under the newly signed Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, but the agreement has yet to be ratified in Turkiye.



Egypt’s parliament has also postponed a vote that would authorise its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia.

Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at King’s College War Studies Department, called the UK and French deployments “militarily valuable and politically significant”, saying they could help shield the kingdom’s sprawling territory from persistent Houthi air attacks while giving Riyadh more room to focus its own assets on offensive operations.

“The British Typhoons can reinforce Saudi air defences and, crucially, free up Saudi Eurofighters for offensive operations,” Obaid told Al Jazeera. “France’s contribution is particularly important for protecting Yanbu.”

Saudi Arabia “does not need foreign assistance to conduct air strikes”, Obaid added, noting that the kingdom has its own powerful combat aircraft fleet. “What it needs is additional defensive coverage across its enormous territory, particularly for critical energy infrastructure.”

Ozcelik said the recent British move was “not insignificant”, but its deterrent impact was not immediately clear.

“The question remains whether the UK air missions will move the dial in deterring sustained Houthi attacks while Saudi air defences and interceptor stockpiles are stretched,” said Ozcelik. “The difference between deterrence and interdiction is an important one.”

‘Dragged into protracted conflict’

What also remains to be seen is whether the UK and France will maintain a purely defensive posture – and whether the Houthis will recognise that distinction at all.

Coningham said the Houthis could interpret European military involvement, especially the UK’s air-to-air support for Saudi bombers and jets, as “offensive” rather than defensive, leading the group to view those countries as belligerents and their forces as targets.

As a result, Coningham said, the Houthis could strike at British forces stationed in the region – whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, such as Cyprus – or reverse their position on allowing free transit to non-Saudi vessels, including European ships, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait – a key maritime route in the world.

Another potential flashpoint would be a Houthi attack in Saudi Arabia that kills British or French personnel, analysts noted.

“Whether it’s a direct attack planned by the Houthis or collateral damage, if the British or French have any casualties … then there becomes a pointed debate in those countries as to whether they should then retaliate,” said Coningham.

Ozcelik said the UK could face pressure to play a more offensive role in the event of a “mass civilian casualty event” caused by the Houthis or “debilitating attacks on Saudi’s energy infrastructure”, although London would likely view such a scenario as a “last resort”.

“Neither the Mecca signatories nor the UK are inclined to get dragged into deeper and likely protracted conflict inside Yemen,” said Ozcelik.

World.title: US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
World.content:
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.

Some other releases of detained Americans from Russia have been obtained through prisoner swaps.

Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".

The US state department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and the US president had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.

"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused â on âHubbard".

CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

Witkoff praised Putin for releasing Hubbard: "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian - you are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you."

Hubbard was later seen thanking Witkoff as they met separately. Putin's financial adviser Kirill Dmitriev was also present.

Witkoff, who had attended talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo the previous day, also asked Putin to consider a number of proposals agreed in the Norwegian capital, including renewing trilateral peace talks with Ukraine to try to end the war.

Putin has not publicly commented on whether any of the proposals would be acceptable for Moscow.

The Russian leader has so far rejected all proposals from Ukraine and its European allies to freeze the vast front line as it is and start peace talks.

World.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.

Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.

Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".

It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.

Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.

Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.

Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.

The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.

Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

World.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
World.content:
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.

Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".

The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.

Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.

"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.

"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.

Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.

He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.

World.title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
World.content:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.

While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (Â£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.

That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.

US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.

Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.

The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.

World.title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
World.content:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (Â£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

World.title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
World.content:
On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.

It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".

Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.

He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.

Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.

In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.

A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.

There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.

Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.

A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

World.title: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology
World.content:
The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.

Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.

Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.

There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.

The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament).

Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.

Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.

World.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
World.content:
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.

It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.

Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms.

In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.

He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria.

The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.

The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment.

"The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said.

Nigeria's health minister confirmed the woman had had no symptoms when she arrived in Nigeria, but he said the patient had not confirmed travel to DR Congo.

"We presume that it was likely picked in Uganda," Pate told the national broadcaster Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) on Tuesday evening.

Her travel documents will be used to trace contacts and the authorities have urged the public to co-operate with health officials carrying out contact tracing.

The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.

On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.

Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.

The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.

It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.

In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

World.title: Nigeria’s cocoa exports to US surge to $142m in 2025
World.content:
Nigeria’s cocoa bean exports to the United States increased more than sixfold in 2025, rising from $21.7 million in 2024 to $142 million, the US mission in Nigeria has said.

The figure represents an increase of about 554.4 per cent within one year, highlighting the growing value of Nigeria’s cocoa trade with the US.

“U.S. demand for Nigerian cocoa is booming. Cocoa bean exports to the United States jumped from $21.7 million in 2024 to $142 million in 2025,” the US mission said in a post on its official Facebook page on Tuesday.

The mission said the trade relationship also benefits Nigeria through US agricultural exports, noting that wheat accounts for 67 per cent of US agricultural exports to the country.

The trade, it said, represents “fair, two-way trade that works for farmers, businesses, and families on both sides of the Atlantic.”

The increase comes amid efforts to revive Nigeria’s cocoa industry, improve productivity and expand local processing to capture more value from the commodity.

Challenges facing Nigeria’s cocoa industry

Nigeria’s cocoa industry has struggled with declining productivity, ageing plantations and growing pressure from urbanisation and population growth, which continue to reduce available farmland in major producing states.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Many cocoa trees are between 20 and 40 years old, while the average cocoa farmer is about 60 years old. The ageing plantations and farming population have contributed to declining yields and limited youth participation in the sector.

Smallholder farmers also face high borrowing costs, inadequate access to fertilisers and pesticides, poor-quality or counterfeit seedlings, and limited access to affordable financing.

Meanwhile, international regulations, including the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), are increasing pressure on producers and exporters to demonstrate traceability and ensure that their supply chains are not linked to deforestation.

Nigeria’s limited domestic processing capacity is another major challenge. Historically, more than 80 per cent of the country’s cocoa has been exported in raw form, limiting opportunities for local value addition, industrial development, and job creation.

However, indigenous companies, including Johnvents, which operates in Ondo State, are seeking to expand domestic processing and the production of chocolate and other cocoa-derived products.

In a related development, EIB Global, the international development arm of the European Investment Bank Group, and First City Monument Bank (FCMB) announced €85 million in financing to support private-sector businesses across Nigeria’s agricultural value chains.

At least 70 per cent of the financing is expected to target the cocoa and dairy value chains.

Stakeholders and policymakers are also advocating the establishment of a National Cocoa Management Board to restore quality control, standardisation, and input distribution functions lost after the former board’s dissolution in 1986.

These proposals form part of broader efforts to improve the sector’s performance under Nigeria’s National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy (NATIP) 2022–2027, which seeks to increase agricultural output and strengthen the sector’s productivity and competitiveness.

Cocoa drives agricultural export earnings

According to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Nigeria’s agricultural exports have grown significantly, with cocoa beans accounting for a substantial share of export earnings.

In the first quarter of 2026, Nigeria exported agricultural products worth ₦1.17 trillion. Cocoa beans accounted for ₦596.90 billion, alongside other major export commodities, including sesame seeds and cashew nuts.

Cocoa and its derivatives also accounted for 41.11 per cent of Nigeria’s non-oil export value in the first half of 2025.

Despite the recent increase in export value to the US, the country remains a relatively modest destination for Nigerian cocoa. In the first quarter of 2025, the US was the fourth-largest destination for Nigeria’s cocoa exports, accounting for about 6.1 per cent, behind countries including the Netherlands.

The increase in cocoa exports also comes against the backdrop of changing trade conditions between Nigeria and the US.

Nigeria’s overall exports to the US declined by 20.5 per cent in the first nine months of 2025, while the US tariff rate applicable to Nigerian goods increased from 14 to 15 per cent in August.

The US subsequently exempted certain commodities that it does not produce domestically, including cocoa, from its 10 per cent reciprocal tariff.

Global cocoa prices also declined sharply during 2025. Prices began the year at about $10,950 per tonne before falling to approximately $5,400 by November.

Nigeria’s cocoa production was also projected to decline by 11 per cent in the 2025/2026 season, raising concerns about the sustainability of export growth.

Higher exports do not necessarily mean higher farmer incomes

Although rising export values could strengthen Nigeria’s foreign exchange earnings and non-oil revenue, the benefits do not automatically translate into higher incomes for farmers.

Export earnings are influenced by international prices, demand and trading arrangements, while farmers’ incomes depend on farm-gate prices, bean quality and productivity.

Consequently, falling global prices and lower projected output could reduce farmers’ earnings even when export values rise.

Speaking to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Agbo Bassey, the National Secretary of the Cocoa Farmers Association of Nigeria, urged the government to organise farmers into cooperatives so they can sell in bulk and negotiate better prices with buyers.

He also called for investments in fermentation and drying centres to improve bean quality and ensure that farmers receive better prices for higher-quality produce.

“Pay on quality: fermentation and drying centres, with premiums for good beans,” he said.

Mr Bassey also urged the government to provide farmers with reliable price information to help them understand international market trends before selling their produce.

He called for replacing ageing cocoa trees with improved seedlings, better farming practices, and affordable credit and inputs that farmers could repay on reasonable terms.

The association’s national secretary further stressed the need for transparent traceability records to help Nigerian farmers meet international buyers’ requirements and access premium markets.

“Process more cocoa in Nigeria, so more of the value stays here,” he said.

He also advised the government to diversify Nigeria’s cocoa export destinations instead of relying heavily on a few markets.

“The tariff changes show how quickly conditions can shift, so Nigeria should sell to several countries,” he said.

Nigeria’s shrinking cocoa production

Cocoa was one of Nigeria’s leading agricultural exports and a major source of foreign exchange in the 1950s and 1960s, before crude oil displaced agriculture as the economy’s main driver.

Nigeria was once the world’s second-largest cocoa producer. Between 1960 and 1969, agriculture accounted for an average of 57 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product and generated about 64.5 per cent of export earnings.

During that period, cocoa revenue helped finance major development projects in the former Western Region, including Cocoa House, a 26-storey building in Ibadan; Western Nigeria Television (WNTV), the first television station in sub-Saharan Africa; and the University of Ife, now Obafemi Awolowo University.

However, from the 1970s through the late 2000s, agriculture’s contribution to the economy and export earnings declined as government attention shifted increasingly towards petroleum exploration and production.

Urbanisation and population growth have further reduced the land available for cocoa cultivation across the country’s major producing states.

Data from the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations show that Nigeria’s average annual cocoa production declined from about 420,000 tonnes in the 1960s to 170,000 tonnes in 1999.

Production subsequently recovered to about 399,200 tonnes between 2000 and 2010 before falling to 302,066 tonnes in 2015 and 298,029 tonnes in 2016. The decline also affected Nigeria’s position in the global cocoa market, with the country falling to fourth place among the world’s largest producers during that period.

Production later improved, averaging about 333,000 tonnes in 2017 and 2018, reaching 348,448 tonnes in 2019, then declining slightly to 340,163 tonnes in 2020.

Nigeria continues to lag behind its West African neighbours, Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, which produce approximately 1.2 million tonnes and two million tonnes of cocoa annually, respectively.

Available estimates put Nigeria’s cocoa production at about 290,000 tonnes in 2021, 280,000 tonnes in 2022, 284,232 tonnes in 2023 and 350,000 tonnes in 2024 and 2025

Reversing the long-term decline will require renewed investment in plantations, improved access to finance and agricultural inputs, stronger quality assurance, and expanded domestic processing.

While the surge in exports to the US offers an opportunity to strengthen Nigeria’s non-oil earnings, sustained growth will depend on whether the country can increase production, improve farmers’ incomes and retain more of the cocoa value chain within its borders.

World.title: Otti flags off reconstruction of two key Aba roads after years of neglect
World.content:
Abia State Governor Alex Otti is set to flag off the reconstruction of Uratta Road and Old Express Road in Aba, two major routes whose poor condition has disrupted transportation, commercial activities and access to residential communities for years.

According to a statement issued on Wednesday by the governor’s media aide, Ferdinand Ekeoma, work on the roads had begun ahead of the day’s scheduled formal flag-off.

Roads abandoned for more than two decades

The two roads are considered important to Aba’s commercial and industrial activities, with Uratta Road connecting several adjoining streets to Port Harcourt Road and Old Express Road. At the same time, Old Express Road serves as a key route within the city’s industrial layout.

Mr Ekeoma said the roads had suffered neglect for more than 24 years, leaving some sections impassable and forcing residents and businesses to contend with difficult transportation conditions.

According to the statement, Uratta Road provides access to more than 100 adjoining streets. Its poor condition has affected residents, traders and small-scale manufacturers who depend on the road to transport goods and access their businesses.

The statement said the road had become waterlogged and overgrown with weeds, discouraging commercial motorcycle and tricycle operators from using it.

Similarly, the deterioration of Old Express Road forced heavy-duty truck operators, fabric merchants, spare-parts dealers and small businesses to use longer routes, increasing transportation costs and affecting productivity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Government targets economic recovery

The Abia State Government said the road reconstruction was part of its broader effort to restore Aba’s infrastructure and strengthen the city’s commercial base.

Aba, one of southeastern Nigeria’s major commercial centres, hosts manufacturing clusters, markets, and small and medium-sized enterprises that depend heavily on functional roads to move raw materials and finished products.

The government said the reconstruction would improve market access, reduce transportation costs, facilitate the movement of goods, and support businesses operating along the affected corridors.

Mr Ekeoma cited the reconstruction of Port Harcourt Road as an example of the administration’s infrastructure programme, claiming that improved road access had encouraged shops to reopen, attracted manufacturing activities and increased property rents along the corridor. However, the statement did not provide independent data to substantiate the claims.

The government also said the new projects would complement other road interventions in Aba, including work on Ohanku and Obohia roads, as part of efforts to improve connectivity within the commercial city.

Projects to include drainage, streetlights

Beyond road construction, the administration said its projects included drainage systems, solar-powered streetlights, and pedestrian walkways, which it described as necessary to improve safety, accessibility, and flood resilience.

READ ALSO: Otti pledges accelerated work on Abia industrial park project

Mr Ekeoma said Governor Otti viewed infrastructure development as an economic strategy rather than merely a construction programme, arguing that better roads would help businesses operate more efficiently and create employment opportunities.

He also quoted the governor as saying at an earlier church event that his administration was shifting attention from basic infrastructure improvements to healthcare, education, technology and industrialisation.

Otti remains in Labour Party amid defections

The governor, a former banker, was elected in 2023 on the Labour Party platform, defeating candidates from the major established parties in a state historically dominated by the Peoples Democratic Party.

Mr Otti has remained in the Labour Party despite the defection of its 2023 presidential candidate, Peter Obi.

His administration has made rehabilitating Aba’s roads and public infrastructure central to its governance agenda, presenting the city’s recovery as essential to reviving economic activity across Abia State.

World.title: Wike’s ‘Rainbow Coalition’, threat to democracy – PDP faction
World.content:
A faction of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), led by former Minister of Special Duties and Inter-Governmental Affairs, Kabiru Turaki, has urged party members to disregard the Rainbow Coalition being promoted by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, to campaign for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election.

The faction said opposition parties should offer Nigerians an alternative to the incumbent government rather than praise it.

It described the coalition as a major threat to electoral democracy, warning that it could push Nigeria towards an electoral monarchy.

The faction’s spokesperson, Ini Ememobong, stated this in a statement on Tuesday.

“The paramount duty of the opposition is to provide an alternative to the incumbent, not to massage their ego. If opposition parties are to ally, they will do so among themselves, not with the governing party.

“This political anomaly, styled and championed as a ‘rainbow coalition,’ is the greatest threat to electoral democracy and the fastest way of railroading the country into an electoral monarchy,” he said.

Mr Ememobong also criticised Mr Wike for urging PDP members to collapse their political structures in support of Mr Tinubu’s re-election, describing the move as shameful.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The news attributed to Minister Nyesom Wike that PDP candidates should collapse their structures and support the re-election of President Bola Tinubu is nothing new, except for the fact that his message is not directed at real PDP members. The message is meant for people who, like him, pretend to be in the opposition but work for the governing party.

“The true and principled members of the Peoples Democratic Party are not part of the shameless, self-serving support for the APC-led federal government and its destructive policies,” he added.

The faction’s spokesperson urged party members to remain loyal to the PDP as the group awaits a Court of Appeal judgment in its bid to take over the party’s leadership.

“We urge all true and faithful members of the Peoples Democratic Party to remain steadfast as we await the judiciary’s decision, hopeful that it will return our party to its true owners. Our case at the Court of Appeal has been heard, and we await judgement. We know that the entire judiciary is conscious that justice delayed is justice denied,” he said.

Mr Ememobong also cautioned Nigerians against those pretending to be party members.

“Nigerians should be wary of elite accommodation and state capture masquerading as broad-based political collaboration. The election next year provides a great opportunity to vote out these insensitive and irresponsible political actors,” he added.

Wike’s coalition

Mr Wike, a chieftain of the opposition PDP serving in the APC-led federal government, has been at odds with APC governors over his Rainbow Coalition, which he says is aimed at mobilising support for President Tinubu’s re-election.

The coalition, which initially emerged in Rivers State, where Mr Wike served as governor from 2015 to 2023, has since expanded to other parts of the country.

The Abdulrahman Mohammed-led PDP loyal to the FCT Minister had supported his continued mobilisation for President Tinubu’s re-election despite the party’s decision to field Sandy Onor as its presidential candidate in the 16 January 2027 election

But the APC governors opposed the coalition, describing it as a political arrangement that could undermine the party and its candidates ahead of the 2027 elections.

The governors and other APC leaders also alleged that Mr Wike was using the coalition to support politicians who lost the ruling party’s primaries and are now contesting elections on the PDP platform.

The APC Governors Forum, chaired by Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, said it would not support any political arrangement that could undermine the party and its candidates in the 2027 elections.

Mr Wike, on the other hand, accused the governors of opposing the coalition because they feared losing their elections. He also criticised their performance in their respective states.

The FCT minister specifically named Governors Uzodimma, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State and Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State as opponents of the coalition, accusing them of acting for “selfish reasons”.

The APC South-East caucus and other mobilisation groups within the party also rejected the coalition. They asked Mr Wike to apologise to the party’s governors for his comments about their political capacity and their opposition to his Rainbow Coalition.

World.title: Ebola: Nigerian lawmakers reject visit to country’s entry points, urge FG to release emergency funds
World.content:
The Senate on Wednesday rejected a proposal for its members to visit the entry points through which a woman infected with Ebola entered the country before she was isolated at a private hospital in Abuja, the nation’s capital.

The upper chamber instead urged the federal government to immediately release emergency funds from the Service Wide Vote to prevent the spread of the Ebola virus.

Lawmakers passed the resolutions during plenary while debating a motion to enforce mandatory health screening at all international airports and other entry points to prevent the spread of Ebola and other epidemic-prone diseases.

The motion was sponsored by Francis Faduyile (APC, Ondo South).

Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case on Tuesday. The patient, a woman who recently arrived in the country on an international flight from Uganda, is currently in isolation and receiving medical care at a private hospital in the Federal Capital Territory.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, said 44 people had been identified as the patient’s contacts and that the government was tracking them for isolation.

The motion

Mr Faduyile, a professor of medicine, expressed concern about Nigerians’ safety, noting that the strain responsible for the outbreak has no approved vaccine.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The senator said Nigeria needed to strengthen surveillance at its entry points in line with the International Health Regulations, without imposing travel bans or engaging in discrimination.

He urged the Senate to encourage the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the Port Health Services to make health screening compulsory for all international arrivals at airports, seaports and designated land borders.

Mr Faduyile said the screening should include health declaration forms, temperature checks and symptom assessments. He also called for enhanced screening of passengers who had been in or transited through affected areas within the preceding 21 days, regardless of their nationality or country of departure.

The senator further recommended exit screening for departing passengers during any declared public health emergency.

He urged the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria and the Nigeria Immigration Service to ensure all entry points are adequately staffed and equipped with trained port health officers, thermal scanners, protective equipment, and isolation rooms.

The lawmaker also called for functional isolation and treatment centres in all 36 states and the FCT.

Mr Faduyile recommended reviewing the Quarantine Act of 1926 to align it with modern public health legislation and the International Health Regulations.

He further urged the Senate committees on Health, Primary Healthcare, Development and Disease Control, Aviation, Interior, and Appropriations to work with relevant agencies, visit major entry points and submit a report within four weeks to guide further legislative action.

Debate

Most senators who contributed to the debate supported the motion and its proposed measures.

However, the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, while commending Mr Faduyile for sponsoring the motion, objected to the proposal for lawmakers to visit the country’s major entry points.

Mr Akpabio argued the visit was unnecessary, suggesting senators could risk exposure to the virus. He put the proposal to a vote, and most lawmakers opposed the planned visit.

Ekong Sampson, the senator for Akwa Ibom South Senatorial District, said Nigeria needed a stronger health system to protect its citizens from epidemic-prone diseases.

Sadiq Umar, who represents Kwara North Senatorial District, urged the government to deploy appropriate technology to strengthen contact tracing and prevent further transmission of the virus across the country.

Adamu Aliero (APC, Kebbi Central) described the matter as urgently important to the nation. He called on the federal government to immediately release emergency funds from the Service Wide Vote to contain the outbreak, rather than wait for funds previously approved in the budget to be released.

Tahir Monguno (APC, Borno North) also called for an amendment to the Quarantine Act.

World.title: Ebola: Nigerian lawmakers demand release of outstanding funds for health agencies to strengthen response
World.content:
The House of Representatives has urged the executive to urgently release all outstanding funds appropriated for health agencies to strengthen Nigeria’s response to Ebola following the confirmation of a case in Abuja.

The resolution comes a day after the government confirmed that a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria from Uganda had tested positive for Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory.

The patient is currently receiving treatment in isolation at a private hospital in Abuja. At the same time, health authorities have identified 44 close contacts, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, for monitoring as part of the contact-tracing exercise.

The House therefore called for the immediate mobilisation of federal and state health agencies, private healthcare providers, and other relevant institutions to step up surveillance and prevent further transmission of the disease.

The resolutions followed the adoption of a motion of urgent national importance on Wednesday titled, ‘Urgent need to strengthen preventive and emergency medical measures against the spread of Ebola virus disease in Nigeria,’ and sponsored by Amobi Ogah (LP, Abia).

Leading the debate on Wednesday, Mr Ogah described Ebola as a severe and potentially fatal viral disease that requires early detection, isolation of infected people, effective infection prevention and control measures, contact tracing and coordinated public health intervention.

He said confirming the Abuja case required an immediate, coordinated response to prevent the infection from spreading.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said delays in identifying suspected cases, conducting laboratory investigations, isolating confirmed cases, tracing contacts, and providing medical care could increase transmission risk and put additional pressure on the healthcare system.

“Any delay in identifying suspected cases, conducting appropriate laboratory investigations, isolating confirmed cases, tracing contacts, or providing timely medical care could increase the risk of transmission and place additional pressure on the country’s healthcare system,” he said.

Mr Ogah noted that public health authorities had already begun tracing the 44 contacts linked to the confirmed case. Still, he stressed that surveillance and contact tracing must be sustained to ensure that other potentially exposed people are identified and monitored.

He also raised concerns about inadequate public awareness, shortages of infection prevention and control supplies, gaps in healthcare workers’ preparedness and limited emergency response capacity.

The lawmaker asked the House to express concern that “inadequate public awareness, insufficient infection prevention and control supplies, gaps in healthcare workers’ preparedness, and limited emergency response capacity could undermine efforts to prevent and contain the Ebola outbreak.”

In adopting the motion, the House urged the federal government, through the Ministry of Finance, to immediately release outstanding appropriated funds to the relevant health agencies to strengthen their preparedness and response measures.

It also asked the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to assess the additional resources needed to respond effectively, taking into account current epidemiological evidence and public health guidance.

The lower chamber further called for the involvement of the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, state ministries of health, port health authorities, and other relevant agencies to strengthen surveillance and epidemic preparedness.

It urged the government to work closely with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other regional and international public health institutions to ensure Nigeria’s response is based on current scientific evidence and international health regulations.

The House consequently mandated its Committee on Infectious Diseases to engage relevant ministries, departments, agencies and public health institutions to obtain updates on the Ebola situation and the country’s preparedness and response measures.

The committee is expected to report its findings to the House for further legislative action.

READ ALSO: WHO pledges support as Nigeria records first imported Ebola case

What Ebola is

Ebola is a rare but severe illness caused by viruses in the orthopoxvirus group. It is mainly transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or someone who has died from the disease, as well as contaminated materials.

The disease can cause symptoms including fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, and in some cases internal or external bleeding. The incubation period is generally 2 to 21 days.

Previous outbreak of the disease in Nigeria

Nigeria has previous experience of containing Ebola. The country recorded an outbreak in 2014 after an infected traveller from Liberia arrived in Lagos. Nigeria was declared free of Ebola transmission on 20 October 2014 after 42 days without a new case.

WHO records show the 2014 outbreak recorded 19 confirmed cases and one probable case, with eight deaths. The response involved rapid case detection, isolation and extensive contact tracing.

The latest case comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and recent cases linked to the wider regional spread of the disease. Nigeria had already increased surveillance following developments in the region, including the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

World.title: Police rescue three-year-old boy, arrest four suspects over abductions
World.content:
The police in Katsina State have rescued a three-year-old boy and arrested four suspects in two child-abduction cases involving ransom demands.

The police said the suspects were linked to a group allegedly targeting children under five years old and using Point-of-Sale (POS) accounts to receive ransom-related payments.

The command’s spokesperson, Abubakar Aliyu, disclosed this in a statement issued on Tuesday, 20 October.

According to the statement, the investigation began on 5 October when Abubakar Ahmed Rufa’i reported to the police Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU) in Katsina that his four-and-a-half-year-old son had been abducted on 30 September.

The kidnappers initially demanded ₦5 million but later agreed to collect ₦20,000 as feeding money before releasing the child, the police said.

The payment was made through POS accounts, leading investigators to arrest two operators, identified as Abubakar Muntari and Aminu Idris, who allegedly received and withdrew the money.

Three days later, on 8 October, another resident, Abdulrahaman Bello, reported that his three-year-old son was missing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Bello told the police that the abductors had contacted him by telephone, demanding a ransom and an additional ₦100,000 for the child’s feeding.

Investigators subsequently linked the two incidents through what the command described as technical analysis.

At about 10:15 p.m. on 8 October, detectives arrested a 16-year-old suspect while he was allegedly attempting to collect money at a POS terminal.

The police said the two previously arrested operators identified the teenager as the person who collected the ₦20,000 payment in the first case.

According to the command, the teenager admitted involvement in the abductions and led detectives to a hideout where they rescued the three-year-old boy unharmed.

Police arrested another suspect, Aminu Musa, 20, during the operation.

The police alleged that Mr Musa had guarded the abducted child and participated in ransom negotiations.

A SIM card allegedly used to communicate with the victims’ families was also recovered.

During interrogation, the suspects reportedly identified two other alleged accomplices, named only as Ibrahim and Mohammed, also known as Malam.

The police said both men remain at large, and efforts are underway to arrest them and identify other suspected members of the group.

The Commissioner of Police in Katsina State, Ali Fage, urged POS operators and other financial service agents to verify customers’ identities and report suspicious transactions to the police.

He also pledged that the command would continue its operations against people involved in child abductions.

World.title: FSGRN warns against reintroduction of Federal Lottery Regulation through the back door
World.content:
OFFICIAL POSITION OF THE FEDERATION OF STATE GAMING REGULATORS OF NIGERIA (FSGRN)

FCCPC SALES PROMOTION REGULATIONS 2026: AN AFFRONT TO THE SUPREME COURT, STATE REGULATORY POWERS AND THE PRINCIPLES OF TRUE FEDERALISM

FSGRN Warns Against the Reintroduction of Federal Lottery Regulation Through the Back Door

The Federation of State Gaming Regulators of Nigeria (FSGRN) expresses its unequivocal opposition to the provisions of the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) Sales Promotion Regulations, 2026, insofar as they seek to confer regulatory, licensing, approval and supervisory powers over lotteries, promotional lotteries, games of chance and related gaming activities on a federal agency.

The Federation considers these provisions a direct affront to the constitutional powers of the States, the binding judgment of the Supreme Court of Nigeria delivered on 22 November 2024, and the principles of true federalism championed by the administration of His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR.

At a time when Nigeria should be consolidating the gains of constitutional federalism, strengthening regulatory certainty and eliminating overlapping governmental mandates, it is deeply troubling that a federal institution would introduce regulations that appear to revive powers already declared unconstitutional by the nation’s highest court.

The issue before us is not whether consumers deserve protection. They unquestionably do. The issue is whether consumer protection can become a convenient instrument for a federal agency to assume regulatory authority over activities constitutionally reserved for the States.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The answer, in our considered view, is an emphatic no.

The Constitution Is Clear: Gaming Regulation Belongs to the States

Nigeria operates a federal system of government founded on the constitutional distribution of legislative powers between the Federation and its constituent States.

Section 4(7) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended), establishes the legislative competence of State Houses of Assembly over matters falling within their constitutional jurisdiction, including residual matters not assigned to the Federation.

Lotteries, betting, gaming and games of chance fall within this residual legislative competence, subject to the constitutional position regarding the Federal Capital Territory.

This constitutional arrangement is neither an administrative concession from the Federal Government nor a privilege that can be withdrawn through subsidiary legislation. It is a fundamental feature of Nigeria’s constitutional architecture.

Accordingly, promotional activities that constitute lotteries, prize draws or other games of chance fall within the regulatory jurisdiction of the relevant State gaming authorities.

Whether a lottery is presented as a standalone commercial venture, a consumer reward programme, a promotional raffle, a digital competition or a marketing campaign does not, by itself, alter the constitutional character of the underlying activity.

A lottery does not cease to be a lottery merely because it is described as a sales promotion.

The legal substance of an activity, rather than the commercial terminology attached to it, must determine the competent regulatory authority.

The Supreme Court Has Spoken: Declaration No. 9 Must Be Respected

On 22 November 2024, the Supreme Court of Nigeria delivered its landmark judgment in Attorney-General of Lagos State & Ors v. Attorney-General of the Federation & Ors, Suit No. SC/1/2008.

The judgment settled a longstanding constitutional dispute over the authority to legislate and regulate lotteries and games of chance in Nigeria.

In affirming the legislative competence of the States, the Supreme Court invalidated the National Lottery Act, 2005, insofar as it purported to regulate lotteries within the States of the Federation.

Of particular significance to the present controversy is Relief/Declaration No. 9, under which the Supreme Court granted a perpetual injunction restraining the Federal Government and its agencies from continuing to exercise the impugned lottery regulatory powers within the States.

The significance of this injunction cannot be overstated.

A perpetual injunction issued by the Supreme Court is not an advisory opinion, a policy recommendation or an invitation to administrative negotiation. It is a binding judicial order that must be obeyed by the parties against whom it operates and by those legally bound through them.

The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission is an agency of the Federal Government. It cannot, merely by invoking its general consumer protection mandate, acquire authority that the Supreme Court has restrained the Federal Government and its agencies from exercising.

The FSGRN therefore maintains that any attempt by the FCCPC to license, approve, supervise or otherwise exercise core gaming regulatory powers over lotteries and games of chance within the States raises a direct question of compliance with the Supreme Court’s judgment and, particularly, its perpetual injunction.

What the Federal Government has been restrained from doing directly cannot lawfully be accomplished indirectly through another federal agency, a different regulatory instrument or a change in administrative terminology.

To permit otherwise would undermine the authority of the Supreme Court and create a dangerous precedent in which constitutional judgments could be circumvented through subsidiary regulations.

The Federation insists that the judgment of 22 November 2024 must be implemented in substance, not merely acknowledged in principle.

FCCPC Regulations 2026: A Troubling Attempt to Reassert Federal Control
