Use the generated complaint information to contact the relevant organization through available official channels. You can also review the site's reporting options.

PACspam can prepare complaint information and help document unwanted political messages, but it doesn't automatically send those complaints on your behalf. It also cannot guarantee that your number will disappear from political texting lists. I also asked George an important privacy question. What happens to the information people submit? "We're not collecting your number. I just want that message," he said. According to Weiner, you don't need an account to use PACspam. Whole Whale also says uploaded screenshots are processed and discarded, while personal messages aren't displayed publicly. Those are the service's stated privacy practices, so I still recommend removing identifying details before submitting anything.

Are unsolicited political text messages legal?

Here's where things get frustrating. The Federal Communications Commission treats political texts differently depending on how they're sent. Political messages sent through an automatic telephone dialing system generally require prior express consent before reaching your cellphone. However, messages sent manually through peer-to-peer texting systems can fall outside those restrictions. That helps explain why so many campaign texts can reach people who never specifically requested them.

The National Do Not Call Registry generally doesn't cover political outreach either. So, registering your number may reduce some telemarketing calls without stopping political fundraising appeals. The FCC also says political campaigns should honor opt-out requests when recipients reply STOP. For robotexts covered by federal consent rules, revocation requests must generally be honored within 10 business days. However, an opt-out from one sender won't necessarily remove your number from other political organizations' databases.

5 ways to block political text messages and protect yourself

You may not be able to eliminate every political text, but several steps can reduce the interruptions and help protect your information.

1. Reply STOP when you recognize the sender

If you receive a message from a legitimate political campaign or organization, replying STOP can unsubscribe you from that sender's messages. However, be selective. If the text looks suspicious or contains an unfamiliar fundraising link, avoid responding. Scammers sometimes impersonate political organizations, and engaging with suspicious messages may confirm that your number is active.

2. Turn on spam filtering on your phone

Your smartphone already has tools that can help move unwanted messages out of your main inbox. Here's where to find them.

On iPhone running iOS 27:

Open the Messages app.

app. Tap the Filters button.

button. Select Manage Filtering .

. Turn on Screen Unknown Senders .

. Make sure Filter Spam is enabled.

Unknown senders can move into a separate folder, reducing interruptions. If needed, tap Allow Notifications to choose which categories of unknown messages can still alert you. Availability varies by region.

On Google Pixel or Samsung Galaxy using Google Messages:

Open Google Messages .

. Tap your profile picture or icon .

. Select Messages settings .

. Tap Protection & safety .

. Select Spam protection .

. Turn on Enable spam protection, if available.

Google Messages can flag suspicious texts and move some of them into the Spam & blocked folder. Menu options may vary by device and app version. Remember to review your filtered messages occasionally so important texts don't get overlooked.

FCC ROBOCALL CRACKDOWN COULD CHANGE PHONE PRIVACY

3. Block and report repeat senders

Blocking individual numbers can reduce messages from persistent senders, even though other numbers may still get through.

On an iPhone, open the unwanted conversation, tap the sender's icon, select Info and choose Block Contact. On an iPhone, reporting a message as spam doesn't automatically block the sender. You need to block the contact separately if you want messages from that number stopped.

On Google Messages, touch and hold the unwanted conversation, then tap Block. You can also select Report spam before confirming.

For additional guidance, see our guide to blocking phone numbers and texts.

4. Report unwanted texts to your carrier and the FCC

You can forward unwanted political texts to 7726, which spells SPAM on a telephone keypad. This alerts your wireless carrier and can help its spam detection efforts. For suspected violations of federal calling or texting rules, you can also submit a complaint through the FCC Consumer Complaint Center. If the text appears to be a scam, report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Keep a screenshot of the suspicious message if you may need it for your report.

5. Donate directly and limit your personal data exposure

One of George's strongest recommendations involves political donations. If you want to support a candidate, find that candidate's official website yourself rather than following a link in an unsolicited text. During our interview, George warned that donating through unfamiliar political fundraising texts can encourage additional solicitations. He described how a successful donation might lead organizations to think, "We got one, let's send twice as many messages." His recommendation was straightforward: Give through the candidate's official website instead of an unsolicited fundraising link. That helps you verify who is receiving your money. However, even donating directly can lead to additional campaign messages, so review the site's privacy disclosures and contact preferences.

Additionally, consider limiting how widely your phone number appears online. Data brokers can collect and resell personal information, and removing your details from covered sites may reduce future exposure. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Keep in mind that commercial data removal services cannot erase legally required public campaign finance records. They also can't guarantee removal from every political organization's contact database.

Kurt's key takeaways

What struck me most about my conversation with George is how much money is being made from messages that so many of us desperately want to stop. We block numbers and ask to be removed, yet the texts keep coming. And the organizations making money from this system have little incentive to change it. I appreciate that George decided to do something about it. His PACspam tool offers a way to investigate who's behind these messages and push back through official complaint channels. I'd love to see political organizations become more accountable for how they use our personal information. After all, supporting a candidate shouldn't mean giving every fundraising operation unlimited access to your phone. Want to hear exactly how George is fighting back? Listen to my full interview with George Weiner on The CyberGuy Report podcast. We dig deeper into the political texting business, the companies behind it and what you can do when blocking numbers fails. And if you're ready to reduce even more unwanted messages, head to CyberGuyLive.com for my free Sick of Spam? class replay. You'll get practical advice for reducing robocalls, unwanted texts and junk email, along with a free spam-stopping checklist.

Should political campaigns have to get your permission before sending fundraising texts, and should the companies profiting from those messages face consequences when you repeatedly ask them to stop? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Thune makes bold prediction about Republicans' Senate chances as GOP pulls millions from key races
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FREMONT, Neb. — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is predicting Republicans will outperform the polls and retain their narrow Senate majority, even as GOP-aligned groups pull millions of dollars from struggling candidates and redirect resources to races that have suddenly become more competitive.

Thune has been crisscrossing the country campaigning for vulnerable Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 election. He’s confident that they can hold onto their slim, 53-to-47-seat majority in the Senate but acknowledges that the GOP as a whole faces headwinds.

And as Election Day inches closer and closer, several contests across the country have tightened, like in Kansas, while others may be slipping away from Republicans, like in North Carolina or Georgia.

DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT

Thune, in an interview with Fox News Digital on the trail supporting Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., was still optimistic about the GOP’s chances.

"I think there are a lot of races right now just looking at the polling that are up for grabs," Thune said. "I mean you could call them jump balls, however you want to say it. They're margin of error races, and there are some that are maybe a little out of the margin. But I do think the polling right now, like it has been in past elections, under-reflects the Republican vote."

"And I think you'll see some of that. So we're not giving up on any of them," he continued.

Republicans are hoping to defend six toss-up races this cycle, according to Cook Political Report. And several that earlier appeared as safe bets, like Mississippi and South Carolina, have recently shifted more favorably towards Democrats.

12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK

The flow of campaign cash has been staggering during this midterm cycle, with Republican political action committees (PACs) and outside groups dumping hundreds of millions of dollars in key races across the country.

But where the money is being shifted could be more telling.

Earlier this month, the Senate Leadership Fund, a PAC closely aligned with Thune, moved money from Georgia to Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., is locked in one of the more unexpected toss-up contests of the cycle.

The Senate Leadership Fund had initially pledged $44 million to bolster Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., in his quest to topple Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. But the incumbent first-term senator has been raking in campaign donations and consistently led Collins in polling.

DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS

And in North Carolina, where former Republican National Committee (RNC) co-chair Michael Whatley is running to keep retiring Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat red against former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, outside funding has begun to dissipate.

The Senate Leadership Fund similarly pulled back nearly all of its spending in the state earlier this month, a sign that confidence in Whatley’s ability to best Cooper was waning. Even President Donald Trump, who held a rally for Whatley on Tuesday, is worried about the race.

"I think he’s a great man, and I am worried about him," Trump told reporters earlier this month. "I hope he wins. He was a great leader for the whole Republican Party when I won, and he’d be a great senator."

Meanwhile, Thune was still bullish that Republicans could hold on, but ultimately, it would come down to getting the "low propensity, particularly Trump, voters out, and then you've got to work on winning the middle of the electorate."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Turnout's going to be a big part of whether or not we're successful or not. And in every state I've been in, that is a clear-eyed focus of our candidates," Thune said.

"That's where resources are being invested. And I think that could be the difference for us come Election Day on whether or not we win a lot of these close races or not," he continued. "And I think that we're gonna outperform the polls for sure come Election Day."

World.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy open to freezing front lines in ceasefire with Russia
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday that he is open to freezing the front lines of the Ukraine-Russia war in an effort to bring the long-running conflict to an end.

Zelenskyy made the remark after being asked by Brian Kilmeade if he would "accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country, regardless of how it started."

"Yes, right now, we have to freeze," Zelenskyy responded. "And I think this is [a] real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire or ‘stop killing’ like President Trump called it.

"Freeze and stop. And, of course, this is the minimum of what we need from Russia today. Then, of course, we will go to [the] president and to Europeans, and we'll ask security guarantees," he continued.

RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN

"This is the most important … not to be afraid," Zelenskyy also said. "We need 9.5 million people [who have] lost their houses, which are abroad, everywhere. We need them to come back to Ukraine just to live and to build their country."

Russia has often rejected ceasefire deals with Ukraine, saying they would give Kyiv time to rearm themselves.

VIDEO: TRUMP SUGGESTS ZELENSKYY DOES NOT WANT TO END WAR WITH RUSSIA

"There will be no ceasefire to bring him back to his senses and pump him full of weapons," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week, according to the Interfax news agency.

Zelenskyy said on X Wednesday that "Russia strikes our country virtually every hour."

"Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people. Because of the Russian attacks, we're losing people and time. It's such a pity, because our children don't have a real life and childhood. Not only children, but all people," he wrote in another post.

"That's why we need to end this war as quickly as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us. God bless, our strong soldiers stay strong on the battlefield. It helps me stay strong during any kind of negotiations," Zelenskyy added.

The remarks come as President Donald Trump on Wednesday secured the release of Stephen Hubbard from Russia, a retired U.S. teacher who was locked up on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin also agreed Wednesday "in principle" to resume trilateral negotiations with the U.S. and Ukraine after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said, according to The Associated Press.

Fox News Digital's Alex Nitzberg contributed to this post.

World.title: Critical vulnerabilities in commonly used web code spark rush to update systems
World.content:
Crucial vulnerabilities in a programming language that underpins much of the internet are so severe that European and British authorities have recommended websites temporarily go offline until they can be fixed.

The flaws are in PHP, a little-known but crucial programming language which powers how web servers process code. The security team that maintains PHP released patches to fix the problem around 10 a.m. ET.

But several websites were temporarily down as of Wednesday morning, citing fear that hackers could take them over. They included Pinboard, a bookmarking site and some parts of Wikipedia.

Two massive but largely unmoderated forum sites, 4Chan and Something Awful, both went offline to wait for a patch.

Japanese websites were also voluntarily offline, including systems for daycare centers and video games, the Japanese tech news site ITmedia reported.

PHP is used in 69% of all websites, according to W3Techs, which surveys the software behind how the internet works.

OpenAI said that it helped discover the vulnerability and brought it to PHP’s attention before hackers exploited it more severely.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” the company wrote in a blog post Wednesday.

“It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The vulnerability was discovered through OpenAI’s program to give cybersecurity companies access to ChatGPT models that are adept at finding software flaws, the company said.

As websites around the world patched the flaws Wednesday, it was unclear how severely hackers were already exploiting it. Patchstack, a cybersecurity platform, said it had received “reports of active exploitation.”

The chief technical officer of Cloudflare, one of the internet’s largest website hosting companies, wrote on X, “We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up.”

Government agencies around the world, including the U.S. National Security Agency, have warned of the flaws and recommended potentially taking sites offline until they’re fixed.

CERT-EU, the European Union’s technical cybersecurity advisory body, said, “Organisations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available.”

The United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre recommended, “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

The primary U.S. cybersecurity agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said in an advisory late Wednesday morning that it recommended patching the software flaws, but that it had “not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication.”

World.title: New York congressional candidate Brad Lander says he was detained by IDF in the occupied West Bank
World.content:
Congressional candidate Brad Lander said Wednesday in a post on X that he was detained in the occupied West Bank by the Israel Defense Forces while participating in an olive harvest.

“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis & volunteers,” Lander said in the post, sharing a picture of himself on a bus.

“We were simply harvesting olives in a grove” in the West Bank, he continued. “The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

NBC News has reached out to Lander and his campaign for further information and comment. The IDF did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lander, a former New York City comptroller, is running for Congress in New York’s 10th Congressional District, a deep blue Democratic stronghold. He previously posted that he was visiting the occupied West Bank with the “Protect the Harvest” coalition, which he said was “bringing people together from around the world to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the face of state-sanctioned settler terrorism.”

“Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest — and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he said in a post to X on Monday.

Last week saw two high-profile Israeli settler attacks, including one in which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was injured, and another that targeted European diplomats. Earlier this week, Israeli police said they arrested 10 people suspected of participating in the violence against Palestinians and others.

More than 900 Palestinians were injured in settler attacks since the start of the year, according to a United Nations report from July. The same report said that 76 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank were killed by Israeli forces or settlers or died from their injuries since the start of the year.

Lander ousted incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman in the 10th district primary, which was was dominated by the candidates’ views toward Israel. Both men are Jewish, and Lander has been more critical of Israel’s government and the war in Gaza, which he has said was a “genocide.”

World.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
World.content:
A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses.

The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants.

“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”

Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago.

The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation.

“These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.”

“The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization.

Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university.

Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit.

She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.”

“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.”

She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.”

The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says.

The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances.

“I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News.

The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says.

After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her.

Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on.

She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night.

The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report.

Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report.

Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit.

A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case.

Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs.

Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university.

The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case.

“At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.”

World.title: Secret Service study explores how to prevent workplace violence
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Secret Service, best known for protecting presidents and dignitaries, is leveraging its vast intelligence gathering, research capabilities and other tools to help prevent workplace violence.

A new report seen by NBC News from the Secret Service’s National Threat Assessment Center analyzed 50 cases of workplace violence over the past decade to seek common motivations, tactics and warning signs, including the shooting at the Capital Gazette in 2018 in Annapolis, Maryland, in which a gunman killed five employees. In the incidents under review, 119 were killed and 128 were injured. The report was born of the center’s examination of mass attacks, which found most of the targeted locations were businesses.

“Which is why we launched this initiative,” said Lina Alathari, who leads the threat assessment center. “To look at how can we prevent targeted workplace violence. What is the thinking, behavior and circumstances of workplace attackers?”

The threat assessment center was developed to study how other kinds of attacks could be prevented. Officials use that knowledge and apply it in other situations, such as school shootings, mass attacks and now workplace violence.

The report, expected to be released Wednesday, is intended to provide guidance to businesses, human resources officials, local law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals who mitigate workplace risks.

Alathari said there are almost always warning signs before someone attacks. While the reviewed cases do not suggest that attackers belong to any specific demographic group, they do share similar patterns.

“Grievances are always the No. 1 motive that might sort of trigger someone to carry out an attack,” Alathari said.

Retail and service businesses are the most frequently attacked, because the public often has easy access, followed by manufacturing and healthcare facilities.

The connection between a targeted business and a perpetrator is typically direct and personal; 16 of the attackers were actively employed at the sites they targeted. Others are tied through current or estranged romantic partners, she said.

According to the Secret Service’s research, more than 40% of the suspects in cases of such violence had histories of domestic violence, but they were not always charged with crimes related to that violence, the report found.

Given the prevalence of violence against intimate partners, the study urges workplaces to recognize signs and support employees.

“That includes empowering those who may be experiencing stalking, harassing, threats from romantic partners or other relatives to feel connected enough to come forward and ask for help,” Alathari said.

Most of the attackers used firearms, but others used knives, explosives or vehicles. Nearly 25% of the attacks involved more than one weapon. The resolutions of the incidents varied; in more than 75% of them, attackers stopped causing harm on their own and were arrested at the scene. Nearly half died by suicide. In 14% of the studied cases, law enforcement ended the violence by killing the suspect.

The National Threat Assessment Center Team described one case in which the suspect had been fired but the employee’s badge access remained active and allowed the attacker to return and gain access. It advised people to look for common warning signs: changes in behavior, depression, increased absenteeism, discussion of weapons, expression of violent thoughts or any kind of threats against co-workers.

Last year, the Secret Service led 400 training sessions on preventing mass violence for roughly 50,000 participants nationwide.

“There are always opportunities for intervention, and what I can tell you is that the cost of inaction can be deadly,” Alathari said.

World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

World.title: Witkoff says he hopes Ukraine included in U.S., Russia talks
World.content:
Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.

If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.

During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S.

State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026. Sputnik/Kristina Solovyova/Pool via Reuters

Video of the meeting as it opened Wednesday showed Witkoff saying he hoped to discuss the resumption of trilateral talks between Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine. The Kremlin did not initially indicate any new willingness to engage, and Russian officials said before the gathering in St. Petersburg that Moscow's position and demands had not changed.

After the meeting, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov was quoted by TASS as saying the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was "generally ready" to resume trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine in early November, and that the two men had "specifically discussed a potential framework for resuming trilateral negotiations."

But Ushakov also said, according to a Kremlin transcript of his remarks, that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us."

Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."

After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."

Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine, but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and Masud Gharahkhani, the president of Norway's Parliament, speak to journalists on Oct. 21, 2026, in Oslo. Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB/AFP via Getty Images

Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.

"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."

The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.

Mr. Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.

The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."

Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

World.title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
World.content:
A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.

A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal. No injuries have been reported.

Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius was ordered to shelter in place, due to a hazardous materials release.

The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday.

Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.

MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.

According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.

Who is in the evacuation zone?

According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:

Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.

Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.

City of Toledo

The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported.

Toledo public schools were closed on Wednesday.

World.title: George W. Bush's brother says he voted for Talarico in Senate race
World.content:
Neil Bush, the brother of former President George W. Bush and son of former President George H.W. Bush, said Tuesday that he voted for Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race while criticizing President Trump and "those who have enabled him" for causing "enormous damage to the Republican Party."

"My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico," Bush wrote in a Facebook post.

Talarico is currently facing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the country's most closely contested Senate races. Early voting started Monday.

The Bush name is nearly synonymous with the rise of the Republican Party in Texas. Democrats dominated Texas politics for much of the 20th century, and George W. Bush's defeat of Democratic Gov. Ann Richards in 1994 helped cement the GOP's takeover. Within a decade, Republicans swept every statewide office, redrew the U.S. House map to enhance their advantage and took the majority in both houses of the state Legislature.

Neil Bush and Presidents George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush at Reliant Stadium on Nov. 17, 2013, in Houston, Texas. Bob Levey / Getty Images

George P. Bush, the son of Jeb Bush and nephew of Neil and George W. Bush, unsuccessfully challenged Paxton in a primary for attorney general in 2022.

In his post, Neil Bush wrote that he is "deeply troubled by Paxton's conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power."

Most members of the Bush family have generally avoided criticizing the sitting president since George W. Bush left office in 2009.

Neil Bush noted that he has been a "Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles."

"But character matters more than party affiliation," he wrote. "Our democracy depends on leaders who respect our institutions, tell the truth, accept accountability, and seek to unite rather than divide."

One of the more controversial candidates on the ballot this cycle, Paxton was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015, which were later settled as part of a diversion agreement. He was impeached in 2023 by the GOP-controlled Texas House on separate accusations of bribery and abuse of office. He was acquitted in the state Senate trial.

Paxton toppled incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a bitter GOP primary earlier this year after receiving Mr. Trump's endorsement. The president has continued to vigorously back Paxton throughout the general election, making several trips to Texas to campaign for him.

Although Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, Democrats are hopeful their fortunes will change this year. Talarico has had a narrow lead in most polls, including a recent CBS News poll. CBS News' Battleground Tracker rates the race as a toss-up.

Neil Bush said in his post that his "vote today was about much more than opposition to Ken Paxton."

"I've never met James Talarico, but I have been enormously impressed by the way he approaches complicated and controversial issues," Bush wrote. "He speaks with respect, seeks common ground, and seems genuinely interested in bringing people together rather than driving them apart."

Bush praised Talarico, who is a seminarian, for his faith, and added that he sees "in him the qualities I admire most in public servants: integrity, civility, humility, and a willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees."

World.title: Witkoff blasted for calling Putin a "humanitarian"
World.content:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff is facing immediate backlash for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained.

"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."

Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter.

Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked immediate backlash from Republicans who have openly criticized the president and his administration.

"WTF, Steve?" said North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a 'humanitarian.'"

WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of “humanitarian.” What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a “humanitarian.” https://t.co/SMQiTy46cc pic.twitter.com/Nbu0wKPmby — Senator Thom Tillis (@SenThomTillis) October 21, 2026

Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas responded to a video of Witkoff's comments: "No. Putin is a stone cold killer," he wrote on X.

"Another embarrassment," said Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the Trump administration's handling of Russia and Ukraine.

Witkoff's praise of Putin also comes as Mr. Trump made the surprise move last week to waive new U.S. sanctions on Russia two days before they were supposed to go into effect, defying Congress and his late friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. The waivers came one week after Mr. Trump had eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.

Mr. Trump has expressed increasing frustration with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and on Tuesday, said "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."

World.title: Trump weighs moving White House press corps out of building
World.content:
President Trump has discussed the possibility of moving the White House press corps to another building, according to two people close to the president — a move that could escalate Mr. Trump's clashes with news organizations over coverage and access.

Outside allies of the president have pushed the idea in recent weeks, including former Trump strategist Steve Bannon, one source told CBS News.

No final decisions have been made, according to both sources.

The discussions were first reported by The New York Times.

White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement: "America is rightly distrustful of the fake news media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information. … All options remain on the table, and we will make an announcement when appropriate."

Reporters have had dedicated workspaces in the White House building for more than a century. The current press briefing room was constructed during the Nixon administration, replacing a swimming pool that dated back to Franklin D. Roosevelt's presidency.

But late last month, Mr. Trump posted a before-and-after image to Truth Social that suggested the briefing room could be turned back into a swimming pool.

Ahead of Mr. Trump's first term, administration officials floated the idea of moving the press corps out of the building, framing it as a bid to broaden access by using a roomier part of the White House complex rather than the small, cramped spaces in the West Wing. Incoming chief of staff Reince Priebus told NBC News the administration had discussed holding news conferences in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which is adjacent to the West Wing.

Mr. Trump ultimately did not follow through with the plans, telling Fox News two days before his 2017 inauguration: "The press went crazy, so I said, 'Let's not move it.'"

The idea has appeared to reemerge after more than a year of disputes between the Trump administration and journalists over access to the White House.

Last month, Mr. Trump attempted to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House complex, accusing them of unfair coverage. Journalists from all three outlets were briefly unable to access the building, but a federal judge reinstated their press credentials, finding the ban likely violated the First Amendment and the news outlets' right to due process.

The Trump administration has continued to periodically block CNN from participating in the television press pool, a group of five networks that cover the president's travel and events on a rotating basis and provide video to other news organizations.

(CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.)

More than a year ago, the White House prevented the Associated Press from accessing the Oval Office and some other spaces because the wire service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump's preferred term, the Gulf of America.

The Pentagon has also clamped down on press access. Last year, the military required reporters to sign onto a set of restrictions — including a promise not to "solicit" sensitive information — in order to maintain daily access to the Pentagon. Most news organizations declined to sign the new rules and vacated the building.

After a judge struck down the Pentagon's press restrictions earlier this year, the military announced it would stop allowing reporters to enter the building unescorted altogether.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said a "new and improved press workspace will be established in an annex facility outside the Pentagon, but still on Pentagon grounds."

World.title: Should you trust personal AI agents? What security experts say.
World.content:
Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information.

"It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do."

While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent.

"I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts."

Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse.

For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.

Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.

Should you let an AI agent shop for you?

Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them.

When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money.

"If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said.

One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25."

Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.

If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended.

"We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."

Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends.

"If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."

Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained.

"Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done.

His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy."

"Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.

How much data are you sharing?

New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services.

"We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."

To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity.

He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco.

Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions.

It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all.

"In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said.

He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks.

"The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster."

Ask how it works

Matt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds.

"The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."

Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.

He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks.

"If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said.

Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said.

Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent.

"If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said.

She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though.

"What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."
