World.title: Millions are struck off India's voter rolls in largest disenfranchisement in history
World.content:
Millions are struck off India's voter rolls in largest disenfranchisement in history

toggle caption i Elke Scholiers for NPR

NEW DELHI — Like many Indians, Kanchan has one name and lives in hardscrabble quarters. Her home is built of tin and a tarp, constructed under a flyover in the capital New Delhi. And like many on the margins, Kanchan was proud of her right to vote — a rare equalizer in unequal India.

"It's important, because it shows we are citizens," Kanchan said on a recent October day, sitting on a plastic chair as vehicles trundled overhead.

But a few weeks ago, Kanchan said about 500 adults were deleted from their voter roll in this community, which resides around a bridge. They found out through another resident who is allowed to examine the voter rolls as a representative of a political party.

Sponsor Message

They were among an estimated 130 million names that were deleted during a revision of voter rolls that began last year in June.

The number is an estimate by Yogendra Yadav, an elections specialist and prominent critic of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Nevertheless, the BJP has cited the figure as authoritative in its defense of the voter roll revision. The rolls once had listed 980 million names.

"The government is choosing the people that support them," Kanchan told NPR, accusing the BJP of engineering voter rolls to disenfranchise communities opposed to the party. That is a widespread belief among critics of the voter revision process, including a former chief election commissioner of India, SY Quraishi. "Normally voters choose the government, here the government was choosing the voters," said Quraishi, who served in that role from 2010 to 2012.

India's election commission, which is overseeing the voter revision, is ostensibly independent. But critics accuse chief commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of being partisan to Prime Minister Modi's party. And it is the party, not the commission, that has mounted a defense of the revision. In a video issued on the BJP's YouTube channel in early October, it said those approximately 130 million deleted names were of people who had died, had duplicate entries, had moved residences or were otherwise absent.

Sponsor Message

Kanchan said in her community, people were deleted on the basis they had relocated, even though an election official came to visit and she "made me sign and hand over the form to her."

And activists helping Indians get back on the voter roll say many others were deleted because they could not provide information that had never been demanded of voters before, like demonstrating that their parents or grandparents voted in elections more than two decades ago. Others were told to prove who they were after discrepancies appeared between how their names were spelled on voter rolls and how they were spelled on enumeration forms that were distributed to some, but not all, voters.

One notice was handed to Nasir Malik, a community activist in a New Delhi quarter called Mustafabad, who waved it around on a recent day. "This makes no sense," he told NPR. "If this was a problem, how did I vote in elections before this?"

Name spelling discrepancies are so common in India that experts said they were not regarded as a problem in previous voter roll revisions, as long as the local election official believed they were dealing with the same person.

In a downtown New Delhi café, a lawyer who has filed multiple petitions against the voter revision process said his country once took pride in ensuring that every eligible adult could vote. Now, the burden of proof was flipped onto citizens to prove who they were, triggering "the largest disenfranchisement exercise in human history," said the lawyer, Kaustubh Chaturvedi. "It's an unconscionable process. What you've really done is you've purged the right to the vote from almost all of those who need it most."

It is the largest disenfranchisement by numbers. By ratio, the Jim Crow laws led to higher percentages of people being disenfranchised in the United States, according to historian Carole Anderson, who has written extensively about voter suppression of Black communities.

Sponsor Message

For 27-year-old Kanchan, in the New Delhi community around the bridge, her right to vote wasn't just about voting.

toggle caption i Elke Scholiers for NPR

She's raising her 6-year-old son alone after her husband, a food delivery driver, was killed in a road accident four years ago. She supplements her teaching income with a monthly government stipend equivalent to $25, and free monthly food staples of rice, wheat and sugar. She feared authorities would deny her those services by calling into question her citizenship, because she was struck off voter rolls. "They'll cut us off from everything slowly," she fretted.

Those fears were particularly triggered after government officials in some states ruled by the BJP vowed to strike people off assistance programs if they'd been deleted off voter rolls.

After an outcry over voter deletions in September, the election commission said it worked with "complete integrity." It said officers would help those deleted from voter rolls to be reinstated. Sunil Kumar, a senior election official in Kanchan's constituency of Chandi Chowk told NPR that his department was working to get Kanchan's community back onto voter lists.

Any help now has come too late for some disenfranchised Indians, like Malika, who only has one name.

In the working-class quarter of Mustafabad, Malika worried she'd now be accused of being an illegal migrant, because she was struck off voter rolls. Her concern stems from the claim by the powerful interior minister, Amit Shah, who first said the voter revision would be aimed at detecting, deleting and deporting infiltrators. And while authorities tried to quell protests against the voter revision deletions in October, Shah described those opposing the voter revision as protecting infiltrators. That is often a dog whistle in India for Muslims from neighboring Bangladesh.

Malika, who is Muslim, says her voter ID was one of the few ways she could prove who she was. She was born without a birth certificate, says she never went to school and that her parents died when she was young. "I had no elders," she said. "I pretty much raised myself."

Sponsor Message

She said she was struck off her old voter roll in Mustafabad after she moved two hours away — she couldn't afford the rent after her husband was killed in communal violence here six years ago. More than 40 people were killed, mostly Muslims, by Hindu mobs. Malika now commutes to Mustafabad each day where she works as a cleaner, making $80 a month, which she said barely feeds her three children.

She said no election officer ever visited her in her new digs to take down her details, which they were supposed to do so she could get back on the voter roll. Malika said she'd visited her local officer on a recent Friday, but she lost a day's work without resolving anything.

toggle caption i Elke Scholiers for NPR

"These people, the government officials — they like to sit in their air-conditioned offices and they make certain rules," she said, referring to the voter revision process. "But they really need to come to the ground and see how it is," she said, "to work in the hot sun, to be poor like we are."

For now, she signals her identity through the plastic bangles on her arms, colored orange, white and green — the colors of the Indian flag. She smiled as she jangled them. "This is my India too," she said.

World.title: Bank of Canada increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Bank of Canada has not raised interest rates since July 2023.

And while an eighth-consecutive hold is widely predicted next week, a growing number of economists and traders are now expecting the central bank to hike its trend-setting rate to tamp down stubborn inflation.

The policy rate has stood still at 2.25 per cent since a quarter-point cut in October 2025.

But Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem recently warned it may need to raise borrowing costs if energy prices remain elevated, saying on Saturday there is "no resolution in sight for the conflict in the Middle East" that has roiled global energy markets for the past several months.

On Monday, the latest inflation data from Statistics Canada put a spotlight on soaring energy costs. The report showed rising fuel prices have yet to meaningfully spill into other sectors of the economy. However, the Bank of Canada's latest survey, also released on Monday, found businesses are bracing for higher prices.

The consensus in a recent Bloomberg survey still points to a hold, but so far this week, the Bank of Montreal, RBC Dominion Securities and Desjardins Group have flipped their predictions for Oct. 28 from a hold to a hike.

According to Bloomberg data, traders in the overnight swap market now put the odds of a 25-basis point rate hike from the Bank of Canada next week at 87 per cent, up from 70 per cent earlier this week. Swap market data measures the gap between today's interest rate and the future rate traders are betting on.

WATCH | How AI is changing the real estate business: That perfect Ontario real estate listing might be staged by AI. Here's what to watch for | Duration closed caption 3:08 If you've been looking to buy a home in Ontario, you may have seen a few listings where the furniture doesn't look quite right. That's because many of them are being staged virtually, using AI. Experts say there are benefits and drawbacks. CBC's Talia Ricci breaks down what you need to know.

Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, is among those calling for a rate hike.

"It's not a slam dunk call, but there is probably enough supporting evidence for a hike," he wrote in a research note on Monday .

Macquarie Group economist David Doyle agrees. He predicts the Bank of Canada will raise its policy rate by 125 basis points by the end of 2027.

"Our baseline case remains for a rate hike at this month's meeting," he wrote in a note to clients on Monday. "We continue to see a steady rate hike cycle ahead."

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and an expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, agrees.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

WATCH | U.S. tariffs take toll: Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll | Duration closed caption 2:00 Canada's economy has shown resilience in the face of punishing U.S. tariffs, but new import bans on a range of Canadian products are creating further drag. Accounting firm Deloitte has lowered its growth forecast for next year by 20 per cent.

'Massive' impact on real estate

Higher rates would have significant impacts on the county's sagging real estate market , according to mortgage and debt experts. Payments on variable-rate mortgages would rise immediately, along with rates for new fixed mortgages. The pool of eligible buyers would shrink, shifting power from sellers to those who can qualify for the financing needed to make a purchase. Home prices could dip lower.

"The housing market is kind of on its knees right now, and rising rates is like tossing a drowning guy an anchor," said Scott Terrio, manager of consumer insolvency at Ontario-based Hoyes Michalos & Associates.

He said a hike "would reverberate massively."

The volume of home sales across the country is currently at a 25-year low, says Ben Rabidoux of Ontario-based Edge Realty Analytics.

He describes confidence among buyers today as "unbelievably weak," owing to a slew of economic uncertainties ranging from the Canada-U.S. trade war to the impact of AI on jobs.

"The reality is that when we look at per capita home sales, we're already back to 1990s levels, which [was] a really terrible recessionary environment," he said.

If interest rates start rising, Rabidoux says a gradual drop on home prices "over the next three or six months is very plausible."

Last week, the Canadian Real Estate Association downgraded its forecast for 2026 home sales activity for a third straight quarter.

The industry group referenced a "notably more hawkish tone from the Bank of Canada," as it called for 444,530 homes to be sold by year-end, a 5.2 per cent drop from 2025.

Home prices dropped recently in the notoriously expensive Toronto area which Zlatkin, the mortgage broker, cites as a sign that now is a "good time to buy."

"There's a possibility [that] housing prices are going to continue falling, but the reality is, if you'll qualify for the property today, then you'll qualify again later on if rates rise."

World.title: Alberta separatists lost the vote. They'll continue their fight inside Danielle Smith's party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith has long expressed a desire to put the separatist issue to rest after the referendum. United Conservative Party activists stand in the way of her wish.

Now that the broad Alberta public has decisively rejected the separatist idea, the debate is returning to where it began: within Smith’s own political coalition.

The more energy she must expend on taming UCP turbulence and any challenges to her leadership, the less time she can spend on actual government priorities. And could the disappearance of the UCP’s lead in the polls and the NDP’s recent byelection victory in what used to be a cabinet minister’s safe seat be a sign that Albertans have noticed her focus appears to be more on her base than on everyone else?

In a videotaped speech Smith released Tuesday evening, she asserted her government has a “clear mandate” to support a united Canada, and begin the “next chapter.” And the country’s current state, with pro-pipeline Mark Carney as prime minister, is one the premier believes could soothe the disillusionment that created the recent push for independence.

“So tonight I want to invite every Albertan who may still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again,” she said.

“Because although our country isn’t perfect and there is still much work to be done, I believe that Canada is on the rise again.”

That’s a video message aimed at separatists and many of her own partisans, who appear to have become synonymous.

Surveys suggest that Alberta independence is a phenomenon almost solely contained inside the United Conservative voter base and party membership.

And the referendum results appear to bear that out: the province’s major cities wanted to stay in Canada, and so did almost all rural ridings, as UCP-friendly as they are.

Independence supporters watch for voting results in the referendum on separation. Their side only mustered one-quarter of the votes. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

The western Canadian unity question will no longer preoccupy international media, and no longer pose the threat to business and investor certainty that chamber of commerce types have discussed.

But certainty for the premier’s future and her party’s direction? That’s not as clear — not after so many thousand United Conservatives pursued independence, as their party leader promoted Canadian unity alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“Our own government is working against a large percentage of its base,” said Mitch Sylvestre the day after Albertans voted “remain” by a three-to-one margin. He’s not only the leader of the separatist group Alberta Prosperity Project, he’s also a prominent organizer within the UCP.

“They've made a decision, and, you know, they're going to have to live with the consequences.”

He and APP fellow traveller Jeff Rath have mused about trying to push Smith out of the party leadership.

On Tuesday, he also spoke of taking his separatist cadre out of the UCP if it can’t transform the party into a pro-separatist vehicle.

Throughout his lengthy campaign for a pro-independence citizen’s petition and then to have a true “leave” referendum, Sylvestre said he didn’t want to split the party “because I didn't want to split up the vote.”

“But at some point, you know, at some point you have to decide that if that's not working, then you have to go another direction.”

Smith will have to fight to keep the separatists and federalists within the same tent, and there are early indications that a pro-Smith, anti-separatist movement will line up behind her in that fight.

Moderates and old Progressive Conservatives from that side of the Wildrose/PC unity party may show up in force at late November’s annual UCP convention to rival what their more hardened conservative counterparts used to term “the freedom movement.”

Smith has reported that 6,900 party members have already registered to attend the Calgary gathering — more than showed up at last year’s gathering or at 2024’s, when she campaigned for and secured a 91.5 per cent support vote in a leadership review .

Mitch Sylvestre was an influential figure at the 2024 UCP convention, and intends to be the same again this November. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

Discontent after the referendum defeat may push more UCP riding associations to demand another leadership review, following on the lead of the Highwood and Calgary-Buffalo constituencies. But there have been several more pulling in a pro-Smith direction, passing resolutions in support of Smith’s continuing leadership and against a leadership review.

Two factions showing up in force, each trying to overwhelm the other? That could be a recipe for even more friction than has been on display at past gatherings, especially now that the fault line isn't PC and Wildrose — it's federalist and separatist .

But while APP’s Sylvestre and Rath may be more resolved to break up the UCP if that’s what it takes, they don’t stand for all separatists in a movement that’s wide-ranging and leaderless (and as of Monday, officially defeated and perhaps somewhat demoralized).

Sylvestre attended Saturday’s rally at the legislature, but wasn’t asked to speak alongside other top organizers and an Ultimate Fighting Championship mixed martial artist.

Chris Scott, frontman of Let’s Talk Alberta, believes Sylvestre has his own political ambitions and ideas that others don’t share.

“He thinks that if somehow the UCP has a hard-core, independence-minded, Alberta sovereigntist as premier, that they will get a better outcome on a referendum,” Scott said.

He believes that won’t happen, at least not quickly after a 25 per cent vote for Option 2.

Scott said it might be more of a long march now toward the independence he believes is inevitable. He’s applied to run for a spot on the UCP’s board of directors at the convention, in hopes he can help push the party along that road.

Scott agreed that Smith’s internal support is in trouble, but said she could shore it up by more firmly supporting the “sovereign Alberta within a United Canada” that she’s long spoken of — beyond the immigration or judicial selection powers she’s proposed with some of her other nine referendum questions.

By that, the Let’s Talk Alberta activist means starting Alberta’s own tax collection and pension agencies.

Smith already floated those ideas through the Alberta Next panel last year, and found them unpopular. They probably couldn’t marshal popular support any more than Alberta independence.

WATCH | Alberta premier's message to Option 2 voters: Danielle Smith has a message for pro-independence voters | Duration closed caption 1:51 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is asking those who voted for a referendum on separation to believe in Canada again.

And at the same time as Smith works toward survival beyond her party’s convention, there are other dates to eyeball.

Now that Oct. 19 is behind Smith, United Conservatives (and their rivals) will pivot toward Oct. 18. The one on next year’s calendar: the fixed date for the 2027 Alberta election.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi repeated Tuesday his accusations that Smith’s referendum machinations are just for her own self-preservation, and that the decline of public faith in Smith has buoyed his own party’s prospects for victory.

“Every time Danielle Smith is offered the choice to do what’s right for Alberta or do what’s right for Danielle Smith, she’ll pick Danielle Smith every single time,” Nenshi told reporters.

This may be a rare case on which Alberta separatists and the NDP leader agree: that they don’t reckon Alberta’s premier can put the big national unity question behind her.

World.title: Meta's AI agent Muse set up Marketplace sale without telling him — and gave out his address
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Matt Robb started using Muse, Meta’s AI agent, to handle Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got more than he bargained for. One expert advises people to really look at what they’re letting Muse access.

He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back

Matt Robb started using Meta's new AI agent Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace transactions.

But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got a bit more than he bargained for.

"I was like, ‘Oh God, OK... This isn't good," he said of the moment he realized Muse had set up a sale and given his home address to a stranger on Marketplace without his knowledge.

"Muse doesn't check with me, it doesn't tell me this guy has messaged and then it gives the guy my address, agrees to his price and literally tells him to come right now, that's the crazy part," Robb said.

When the buyer showed up, Muse even told him, "Yep I'm here!" on Robb's behalf, when he wasn't home.

A screenshot of the interaction between Robb's Muse agent and the buyer on Facebook Marketplace. (Submitted by Matt Robb)

'Your data is not secure': cybersecurity expert

Muse is an artificial intelligence agent run by Meta — Facebook and Instagram's parent company.

It acts as a virtual personal assistant, promising to stay on top of your emails, buy your kids' school supplies and even rebook an upcoming flight, all in exchange for access to your most sensitive data.

But behind the cuddly face, experts say, there is danger.

"All these big companies, they're in it for your data," said Éric Parent, a cybersecurity expert. "The answer is no, your data is not secure."

Meta’s Muse is an AI agent which acts as a virtual personal assistant. (Meta)

Parent says not only is your data at risk, but also the data of those who communicate with you.

"A person who wrote you an e-mail or sent you a text message is expecting that message to go to your eyes," Parent said.

"Now, overnight, you can be emailing somebody and they've actually granted access to a major corporation to actually sift through your emails. That's going to be an uncomfortable thing down the road."

Parent advises you to really look at what you're giving Muse access to and ask yourself what the impact can be if it takes an action on your behalf.

"You have to put it to the worst case scenario," Parent said.

Pay attention to permissions

Meta says the data and credentials Muse collects is securely stored, adding Muse will always check with you first for sensitive actions like purchases or sending an email.

When asked how a situation like Robb's could have happened, a spokesperson for Meta pointed CBC to a social media post by Robb, who shared his ordeal on X.

Robb explained he had clicked on "Allow always" instead of "Allow one time" when asking Muse to handle his Marketplace transactions, and by doing so, he says it granted the AI permission to send messages on his behalf going forward, using a template it put together with information it asked from him.

"Which also included the pick-up address that I did give to Muse," Robb wrote in his post, adding he didn't think it would send his address out "to everyone that gave me an offer."

"I mentioned to the Meta team it could be easily overlooked as it was with me and they said they will be making this more clear moving forward."

In a tweet replying to Robb's post, David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta Superintelligence Labs wrote: "Glad that we were able to confirm together that there was no breach of privacy controls."

In an email to CBC, Meta said Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else's agent can reach it.

"That is where Muse lives and where the data and credentials for any service a person connects are securely stored," a Meta spokesperson wrote.

But Meta has a history of mishandling its users' personal information , even facing fines totalling hundreds of millions of euros in Europe.

Another concern is that Meta is subject to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which gives the American government the authority to access data maintained in a server owned by a U.S. company.

Lawyer Jean-François Latreille says it's a privacy concern.

"That would mean that technically, the American government could have access to privacy information that is being stored on these systems," he said.

Quebecers protected by strict data privacy legislation

But Latreille says Quebecers are protected by Law 25, Canada's strictest data privacy legislation.

Under Law 25, if a company fails to keep personal information safe, it can be fined up to $25 million or the amount corresponding to four per cent of its global revenue.

Latreille says Quebecers who believe their rights are violated can file a complaint any time directly with Meta's privacy officer or by addressing the Quebec Access to Information Commission .

The commission told CBC in an email it urges individuals to always exercise caution when sharing their personal information.

"Today's practices and mechanisms for collecting and exchanging information mean that large amounts of personal information are held and circulate widely, posing growing risks to individuals' privacy," wrote a spokesperson.

A screenshot of Robb and Muse's interaction after Robb found out about the Marketplace transaction. (Submitted by Matt Robb)

As for Robb and his keyboard, he told the buyer what happened and they rescheduled another meeting — one he was privy to.

Robb also says Muse admitted to giving out his address without his explicit authorization.

Now, he's warning others not to share too much personal information to avoid a stranger showing up at their door unannounced.

"It could happen to someone more vulnerable, right?" he said.

World.title: More than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips leaked, CBC exclusive finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Andrew Rivard spotted a Crime Stoppers ad offering a $2,000 reward for tips in the winter of 2025, he decided to report what he knew about illegal cigarette sales in his neighbourhood.

Rivard’s original tip shows he disclosed his full name. He says he trusted the organization’s long-standing promise to protect the identities of all tipsters.

"I was told nothing would come of it; no one would come to me with, you know, I guess, resentment," Rivard said. "I just was hoping it would be that exactly — anonymous."

But the Manitoba man's report — along with information from more than 1.5 million other tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years — was exposed in a massive data breach , an exclusive CBC investigation has found.

The personal information captured in some compromised tips was detailed enough for CBC to contact more than a dozen tipsters — including Rivard — who reacted with shock and fear for their safety.

"It’s very scary, to be honest," said Rivard, who now worries his home address and phone number may be used by criminals for retaliation.

Rivard’s original tip as it appeared in the leaked data, including his full name. CBC retroactively redacted other personally identifiable information. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel — the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips — that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure."

A copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists, including CBC, by Distributed Denial of Secrets , a U.S. non-profit that archives and publishes hacked and leaked documents it deems to be in the public interest.

CBC took extensive precautions to protect this sensitive data throughout its investigation. Our security measures included, but were not limited to, encryption and working in a self-contained, offline environment. The sensitive information was only accessible to a small number of CBC journalists working on the project. Ultimately, CBC intends to destroy its copy of the dataset.

Beyond confirming they were hacked over six months ago, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters have not spoken about the extent of the breach, only saying they await a detailed report from Navigate360, the company that owns the P3 platform.

This is the first time precise figures on how many Canadian tipsters were compromised in the breach — and the severity of the information exposed — have been made public.

Our interviews and analysis of Canadian content in the leaked data suggest that Crime Stoppers, along with the company it contracted to manage its database, failed to protect tipsters' identities, left personal information unredacted and improperly retained decades of sensitive records.

"For a system that has been designed to promise anonymity to the users, that has failed categorically," said Prof. Ali Dehghantanha, the Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence at the University of Guelph.

He’s one of two experts who were shown our methodology and limited samples of the data from a secure CBC laptop.

After seeing CBC’s main findings, the RCMP shared concerns that the breach could “jeopardize public safety, including the safety of tipsters, individuals identified in tips and police officers," it said in a statement, adding it was originally told the leak did not include Canadian data or personal information.

CBC also shared the same information with the CCSA, which declined an interview.

In a written statement, the organization’s president, David J. Forster, said they “recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created, particularly for people who trust Crime Stoppers with sensitive information.”

There are currently 68 Crime Stoppers chapters registered as non-profits in Canada, according to data from the Canada Revenue Agency .

Professor Ali Dehghantanha is one of two cybersecurity experts who examined samples of the data. (Li Yanjun/CBC)

Tips about high-profile Canadian investigations

Crime Stoppers is a network of civilian-run non-profits that collects anonymous tips on crime and suspicious activity. It operates independently of law enforcement, though it refers a portion of tips back to them to assist in investigations.

The organization often appeals to the public, in partnership with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them.

CBC’s analysis of Canadian tips found mentions of many high-profile cases that generated significant public attention — from Barry and Honey Sherman’s murders to Amber Tuccaro's disappearance , Montreal’s Luka Magnotta case and, more recently, the international manhunt for Ryan Wedding .

Many of the tips dealt with serious allegations, with some people explicitly saying they feared retribution for speaking out.

Citizens called with information about alleged murderers, terrorists and pedophiles or incriminating details about people they were close to, like family members on the run or breaching court orders.

In 2012, police asked for the public’s help in identifying the voice of a man with a connection to missing Indigenous woman Amber Tuccaro. CBC found hundreds of tips mentioning her disappearance in the leaked Crime Stoppers tips. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

A third of all tips talked about drugs and drug trafficking; hundreds reported suspicious activity in their neighbourhoods, often naming individuals and implicating organized crime, biker gangs or drug cartels — including the Hells Angels, Rock Machine and Outlaws, as well as B.C.’s Red Scorpions and Independent Soldiers.

Notes in the data from Crime Stoppers staff suggest some of those tips led to real-life consequences: Nearly 49,000 tips were linked to a case cleared by an arrest or criminal charges, while nearly 1,000 tipsters were approved for cash rewards.

"I am concerned. I am really worried," said Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade.

“I am really concerned about these records … being in the hands of the wrong people, while those people who have been impacted are not aware of that and do not have any support.”

WATCH | CBC finds Canadians' personal information in leaked Crime Stoppers tips: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 5:32 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

That's exactly the situation one Canadian woman is facing. CBC agreed to withhold her identity given her safety concerns.

She gave a tip about the murder of a loved one, which was unsolved at the time.

"I just feel all the anxiety and scared feeling come back," said the woman. Police have now charged an individual with murder.

"They were capable of hurting my loved one. They could come back and hurt one of us."

Tipsters self-identified in over 4,300 tips, data suggests

More than 850,000 tips — about half of all Canadian records identified by CBC — included personally identifiable information about tipsters, individuals named in allegations and even Crime Stoppers staff and police.

Street addresses and phone numbers appeared most frequently, alongside tens of thousands of personal emails, licence plates and hundreds of banking details related to cash rewards — information that could all be used to uncover an individual's identity.

We could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or those accused of a crime.

However, CBC found that in over 4,300 reports, tipsters introduced themselves with a full name, although Crime Stoppers explicitly tells the public to avoid including identifying details . Still, this represented a fraction of reports, at less than one per cent of all entries over 25 years. CBC wasn't able to verify whether all names were legitimate.

In 2021, police sought the public's help in identifying a suspect caught on video near the home of billionaire philanthropists Barry and Honey Sherman. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Despite hundreds of those tips containing clear staff warnings that a tipster had "self-identified" or had been "exposed," the information still appeared in the database unredacted.

Storing all these data points together is a gold mine for fraudsters, said Dehghantanha.

"Imagine I am calling you and talking about the tip that you have provided and asking for more information. Immediately, I build ... trust," he said.

A name or phone number on a list might not seem like much, but it’s enough to do serious damage, said Ben Coon, chief intelligence officer of U.S. cybersecurity firm Unit 221B, who was also shown limited samples of the data.

"From what I saw, there's so much low-hanging fruit here that we could ask questions," said Coon, who said the data could be used for crimes ranging from financial fraud and extortion to money laundering.

Beyond what was collected, experts say the decision to store decades of historical tips in a single place defies basic data retention standards.

"If a tip is closed, does that need to stay online?" said Coon. "The answer to that, to me, is no."

Both experts agree that even though Crime Stoppers uses a third party to manage its data, it is still responsible for auditing how well it is secured.

"You can always outsource the operation … [and] the work," said Dehghantanha. "But you cannot outsource the accountability. You are always accountable when you are collecting the data."

Hacker claims data not publicly available online

Both cybersecurity experts said they were surprised CBC had found the data as they couldn’t locate copies of it online, which they said was reassuring. But they added that once a dataset has been leaked, it’s generally available somewhere.

In an email exchange with CBC News in September, someone purporting to represent Internet Yiff Machine wrote, "I briefly attempted to sell it publicly; however, changed my mind and no copy has made it into the public yet."

They added that the security measures of P3, which was storing Crime Stoppers' tips, were "terrible" and that the platform is still vulnerable.

"I wouldn’t trust [the hackers] at all," said Dehghantanha. "Selling [data] on the underground market is not that difficult, right…. There is a demand."

Internet Yiff Machine’s manifesto includes lines critical of police departments and for-profit prisons. (Valérie Ouellet/CBC)

In a statement, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association said, "If there is information within the leaked records that could identify people who submitted tips, it is an extremely serious issue." It added that protecting people's safety and anonymity is its "highest priority."

It did not directly comment on the precise figures shared by CBC, but said that it has been communicating with the third-party platform "to assess what records may have been affected, what personal information may have been exposed and what measures were taken to enhance the security of the platform."

"With regard to notifying individuals identified in the records, CCSA has concerns about doing so without jeopardizing the anonymity and safety of tipsters," it said, adding that "the information available to us does not distinguish people who submitted tips from people identified in them."

"We will share further verified information as it becomes available, while ensuring that our communications do not create additional risks for individuals."

Navigate360, the U.S.-based company that owns the P3 platform, did not respond to CBC's requests for comment, which included questions about what security measures it had taken since the hack, whether it had shared reports with Crime Stoppers about the compromised data and whether it was still collecting tips.

The RCMP told CBC that at the time of the leak, it was “advised that Canadian data had not been affected based on the results of the preliminary personally identifiable information (PII) assessment."

"Then, in May 2026, the RCMP was informed by Crime Stoppers that the data breach did include Canadian data but would not contain PII of persons who have reported.”

The national police service added that it is now “engaged with the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association to determine the full scope of the incident."

It stated that it has not received reports of anyone being threatened as a result of the breach and advised anyone with concerns about their submitted information to contact the organization or their local chapter.

The Toronto Police Service, which uses tips from Toronto Crime Stoppers — the chapter with the most tips in the leak — told CBC that the group had notified it of a hack in March, but that it "has not received any information indicating the safety of officers, tipsters or members of the public has been compromised."

As for Rivard, the Manitoba man whose tip was exposed in the leak, he says Crime Stoppers should have been more transparent.

"It might have been embarrassing, but own up to it, just tell the public, let them know, and they might have your trust after, they might not: Let them decide."

World.title: Carney, Ford to announce funding for clean auto investments: source
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are expected to unveil new support for auto companies making clean investments during a time of uncertainty caused by the trade war with the U.S., CBC News has learned

A source with knowledge of the announcement that is expected later Wednesday said it includes addressing Canada's greenhouse gas standards after the Trump administration made changes on Monday.

Earlier this week, the U.S. finalized rolling back fuel economy standards for new vehicles, reversing policies meant to boost fuel efficiency and promote using electric vehicles.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on her way into a caucus meeting Wednesday that the government wants to continue to provide support to auto companies impacted by the Trump administration's reversal in regulations.

"A lot of our auto producers have been deeply impacted, not only by the American tariffs but indeed by the fact that the American administration has decided to reduce massively its different protection regarding GHG emissions," Joly said.

Carney and Ford are slated to roll out the support package on Parliament Hill on Wednesday afternoon and are expected to be joined by their industry and finance ministers.

'Trying to square the circle'

Joly said that along with providing support, the government also wants to be "pragmatic" and is working on its electrification strategy to get more battery-powered vehicles on the road.

That plan includes subsidies to try to get more Canadians to move to electric vehicles to reduce emisssions, she said.

"We're trying to square the circle."

In August, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to increase tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, 2027. That threat came after Carney announced he was retaliating with matching dollar-for-dollar tariffs on American goods.

The U.S. is already hitting finished vehicles and non-CUSMA-compliant auto parts imported to the U.S. with 25 per cent levies.

The Trump administration has also been hammering Canadian steel imports with tariffs ranging from 10 per cent to 50 per cent.

World.title: Problem gambling jumps, suicides triple in Ontario after expansion of online casinos
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

Anna, a 51-year-old single mother of two teens, says online slot machine games cost her nearly everything.

And even at that point, the Ontario resident says it was hard to stop.

"The amount of money that I spent and lost — it was astronomical," she told a recent meeting of Gamblers Anonymous in Toronto, which CBC News was invited to witness.

The peer support group has been a lifeline that helped her stop betting and break free from inducements and marketing she would receive from the betting apps, she says.

"If I had gone a little while without gambling, they would literally send me thousands of dollars to say 'free money' to keep you going," she recalled.

WATCH | 'Anna' kicked her betting habit with help from Gamblers Anonymous: Gamblers Anonymous helped 'Anna' kick her addiction | Duration closed caption 1:18 Anna says Gamblers Anonymous helped her find connection to recover from her addiction last year.

She’s not alone.

The number of problem gamblers in Ontario has spiked and gambling-related suicides have tripled since the expansion of private online casino games and sports betting in 2022, CBC News has learned.

Nearly 130,000 Ontarians now show signs of gambling problems, compared with roughly 43,000 in 2018, a tripling of the number of people who meet the criteria of gambling too frequently, losing money and struggling with addiction.

These estimates are based on new research from the Alberta Gambling Research Institute (AGRI), which found a 0.5 per cent jump in Ontario’s rates of problem gambling compared to 2018. Their analysis uses the "Problem Gambling Severity Index" and data from Statistics Canada’s 2025 Canadian Community Health Survey.

AGRI researcher Carrie Shaw says the research is "brand new" and significant, showing that six months after Ontario’s private casinos opened in 2022, the number of problem gamblers in the province climbed while dropping in the rest of Canada.

"In Ontario’s market, gambling is very much normalized through access and s," said Shaw, who presented her findings at an AGRI conference in May.

"It's true across Canada, but more so in Ontario, given the amount of exposure there is," she said.

Carrie Shaw of the Alberta Gambling Research Institute found rising rates of problem gambling in Ontario after the 2022 online expansion of online betting. (CBC)

In July, Alberta joined Ontario in legalizing online gambling run by private companies. Everywhere else in Canada, it is illegal.

"With online gambling ... the barriers to access are completely removed. You can access it anytime from your computer, your mobile phone, any time of day or night," Shaw said. "You can be sitting at your desk at work and still be engaging."

Gambling suicides rising

The Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario also reports a spike in gambling-related suicides in the years after Ontario began allowing online betting.

Before Ontario’s expansion, the province had an average of five gambling-related suicides each year from 2016 to 2021. That number tripled after 2022.

Matthew Young, chief research officer for non-profit gambling research network Greo Evidence Insights, says he called on government two years ago to do a better job of tracking online gambling activity for fear of increased addiction, bankruptcies and suicides.

"We warned that we might be seeing the harms that we're now seeing in the data," he said.

Those calls were ignored, he says.

A study published in the September 2026 American Journal of Preventive Medicine found a dramatic jump in the number of people with gambling disorders showing up at Ontario hospital emergency departments in distress.

A March 2026 study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) found a 95.5 per cent increase in men and boys making gambling-related calls to ConnexOntario, the province's 24-hour mental health and addictions help line, over the last decade.

Young calls it "unfathomable" that Canada changed the Criminal Code to allow online gambling and that provinces are opening their markets without proper study of the potential public health impacts.

WATCH | Gambling addiction needs better monitoring, says expert: Gambling researcher says Canada needs better addiction monitoring | Duration closed caption 0:48 Matthew Young, addictions researcher, says there was no harm analysis done before Canada opened the floodgates to online gambling.

Young says that amid lobbying to legalize online gambling in other provinces, he would like to see better monitoring and for a share of the billions in revenues to be dedicated to independent research into ways to curb addiction and gambling-related harms.

Greo Evidence Insights was formerly known as the Ontario Problem Gambling Research Centre.

Ontario defunded it in 2019.

Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

World.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said on Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.

Doctors amputated Haines's left leg after she was struck twice by a car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They worked for days to save her right leg but were ultimately unsuccessful, he told a news conference in Melbourne.

"The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said.

Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines's electorate, was charged with three offences: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official.

Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed.

Phil Haines, left, Haines's husband, speaks to reporters alongside Australia's Governor General Sam Mostyn in Melbourne. (William West/AFP/Getty Images)

The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested.

Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition.

Police are still investigating the motive for the rare attack on an elected official.

Appears in court

During a brief court appearance on Wednesday, the accused's lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.

There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until Feb. 4.

Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was "targeted," they say they believe it was an isolated incident.

There was no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.

"What I can say is we didn't have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon," she said.

Victoria state police said they could not find any direct past contact between Haines and the accused, with the motive still unknown.

"Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation," Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said.

Bush declined to comment on the man's mental health, saying the matter was before the court.

Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to Parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and 2025.

Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security.

However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising political polarization, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.

World.title: Ontario cancer patients speak out over disappointment with drug funding decision
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.

A rare form of cancer in the 31-year-old's knee had metastasized, spreading to her lungs. She has undergone radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgeries, though the synovial sarcoma couldn't be fully removed.

Apitz-Grossman's doctors are recommending a treatment approved in the United States but unavailable in Ontario. She needs it urgently but the Ontario Health Insurance Plan turned her down for out-of-country coverage. An appeal failed, as did an application under a Case-by-Case Review Program to get special permission for the treatment to be administered at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto.

She is still fighting.

"I so desperately would love to turn 32," she said.

Apitz-Grossman and other Ontarians with Stage 4 cancer told by their doctors that they are good candidates for treatments unavailable in the province were buoyed last month when 37-year-old Alex Shved, in a similar situation, won a court challenge against his OHIP out-of-country denial.

Alex Shved, a 37-year-old father of two young children, took the province to court after his out-of-country cancer treatment request for the Ontario Health Insurance Plan was rejected. (Alex Shved/The Canadian Press/Handout)

But their hopes were dashed when Health Minister Sylvia Jones responded to the court ruling by changing the rules.

Drug treatments will now only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed, a set of circumstances some patients see as impossibly narrow. The government said it clarified in regulation what was already long-standing policy.

"We’re protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas,” Jones wrote in a statement.

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2 billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year.”

Patient questions cost-saving at cost of saving lives

Framing the move as a cost-saving measure is not sitting right with Apitz-Grossman.

"Are we saying that we could save like 5,000 or more people's lives, and they're proud of themselves for not doing that?" she said. "Is this supposed to be good news that we're not going to save those people, so that we can instead buy a couple more private jets?"

Ontario Premier Doug Ford came under fire earlier this year for a government purchase of a $29-million private jet and quickly returned it.

The treatment Apitz-Grossman is seeking, Tecelra, is a personalized therapy made from a patient's own T-cells, a type of white blood cell. Nearly half of patients in Apitz-Grossman's situation respond to the treatment, and among those who respond, there is a 90 per cent chance of survival after a year and 70 per cent after two years, according to her oncologist.

WATCH | How often Ontario turns to international health care: This machine helps cancer patients. Why doesn’t Canada have one? | Duration closed caption 7:40 CBC News has obtained exclusive data showing how often Ontario turns to international healthcare, revealing proton beam therapy as one of the most commonly outsourced treatments. For The National, CBC’s Valérie Ouellet explores why this life-saving cancer therapy isn’t available in Canada and the toll it takes on families.

But the treatment is costly, at $727,000 US, Apitz-Grossman said. She feels terrible guilt for seeking such a pricey treatment, she said, but she wants to live.

"There has never been a moment where I have thought to myself, 'Gosh, I wish that patient who was in the ICU for weeks and who it cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to save, hadn't been saved,'" Apitz-Grossman said.

The origin of Jones' $5.2-billion figure was unclear in her news release, and a government official later explained that it would be the additional cost if the province entirely stopped negotiating prices with drug manufacturers for public coverage in Ontario.

OHIP's reason for denying Apitz-Grossman, Shved and others out-of-country drug treatment funding is that routinely paying for such requests while drugs are undergoing review for funding in Ontario would "undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada's drug review processes."

Some manufacturers have no plans to apply in Canada

Kevin Nash, 59, has metastatic melanoma and is seeking the same tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy as Shved. Nash's out-of-country application and subsequent appeal were also denied, and he does not believe the government's reasoning.

"These companies make billions of dollars a year, not a billion, billions of dollars a year," he said. "Do you think that they care one bit whether Kevin Nash goes to Buffalo for a treatment? That's so preposterous."

In Apitz-Grossman's case, the manufacturer of Tecelra has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada. That means there is no review process in this case to undermine, she noted.

Holly Wardlow, 61, is in a similar boat, with the government denying coverage through its Case-by-Case Review Program for a medication to treat her rare form of liver cancer because the drug was "expected to be reviewed for public funding in Ontario."

That's despite the manufacturer submitting two letters telling the province it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada.

"We just thought, 'Well, this doesn't make any sense,'" Wardlow said.

"We provided evidence that there is not going to be a population-based review. This drug is never going to be approved in Canada, let alone Ontario, because the manufacturer is not going to make an application, and they have evidence of that. And yet they provided the same reason for denying funding."

Wardlow and her husband have been paying $78,000 a month for her to receive infusions in Ontario every two weeks, and her tumour has been shrinking with almost no side-effects, she said.

Their savings have been depleted and they have now started a GoFundMe.

"I'm getting out there and trying to stay fit, partly because I can, and partly because the weather is beautiful, and partly because I'm thinking ahead that surgery may be possible in the future," Wardlow said.
