World.title: Witkoff to Putin: ‘You are a humanitarian … I salute that’
World.content:
The American envoy met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, and is expected to propose trilateral talks between the two leaders and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Russia’s strikes on Kyiv and Kharkiv continued overnight, killing three people, local mayors reported.

Putin’s assault on Ukraine killed 328 civilians in September alone, according to the United Nations, while Kremlin forces bombard energy infrastructure across the country heading into winter.

The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 over the forced transfer of children to Russia after the Kremlin’s invasion of Ukraine began.

World.title: Macron slams ‘stupid’ comments after Trump pins French riots on immigration
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump attends a bilateral meeting with France's President Emmanuel Macron on the sidelines of the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 15, 2026. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via AFP/Getty Images

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday hit out at the “unacceptable and stupid comments from many foreign leaders” in the aftermath of unrest which rocked several French cities over the weekend.

“Some people have claimed that we’ve been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron told reporters during a trip to Qatar. His comments were a clear swipe at U.S. President Donald Trump, who this week railed that France is “being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and Communists.”

While hundreds of thousands of protesters in France demonstrated peacefully over the cost of living and school conditions at the weekend, the mayhem — including public buildings being set on fire, stores being looted and clashes with riot police — sparked widespread condemnation in France and abroad, including in the U.S., where Trump is using the French unrest to rally voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.

World.title: Spanish left-wing leader accuses Trump of denying her travel visa to Puerto Rico
World.content:
In a bid to appeal the decision, Colau requested an appointment at the U.S. embassy in Madrid, during which consular officials asked her only about her role in the flotilla. She was among the activists intercepted by Israeli forces and detained for three days before being deported to Spain.

Colau said Wednesday it was “shameful” that “those of us who denounce genocide and defend human rights can’t enter the U.S. or other territories it has appropriated in a colonial manner.”

The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

In response to her visa denial, the former mayor also hit out at right-wing populist leaders of the U.S., Argentina and Israel and the Spain’s far-right Vox party. “Sooner rather than later, we will end this reactionary wave, kick out the Trumps, Mileis, Netanyahus and Abascals of the day,” she said.

Her remarks come just over a month ahead of Spain’s upcoming election. Campaigning against Trump, an unpopular figure in Spain, could help Colau rally support for the Broad Front. The coalition has been weakened by its failure to unite with Podemos, the country’s other major far-left force. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez needs parties to the left of his Socialists to perform well to have any chance of remaining in power.

World.title: Suspicious drones spotted flying over French military sites
World.content:
Members of the French navy stand on the deck of the Dixmude amphibious helicopter carrier in Toulon, France on Feb. 17, 2026. | Thibaud Moritz/AFP via Getty Images

An investigation was opened after drones were spotted above a naval base in Toulon.

PARIS — Suspicious drones flew over military facilities in southeastern France earlier this month, the French navy said on Wednesday.

During a large-scale armed forces exercise that lasted from Oct. 5 to Oct. 16, "unauthorized drones were detected in the no-fly zone, near and above military sites," the navy said in a press statement.

"In each instance, the planned security measures were activated by the deployment of anti-drone devices, in coordination with domestic security forces," it continued, adding that a judicial investigation was opened.

World.title: African health ministers to hold Ebola crisis talks as Nigeria confirms first case
World.content:
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for urgent action to contain the growing Ebola outbreak and is convening African health ministers to coordinate the response, as Nigeria becomes the latest country to confirm a case.

 

The outbreak began in Congo and has so far also spread to Kenya and Uganda; the latter said it has no cases at the moment. Such geographic spread across Central, Eastern and Western Africa demands urgent, coordinated action, Africa CDC said.

“Ebola is crossing borders. Our response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity and decisive political leadership,” said Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC in a press release.

“We have the expertise and the capacity on this continent. We must mobilise them together to stop this outbreak and save lives,” he added.

On Tuesday, Nigeria reported its first case, linked to a traveller from Uganda who arrived there earlier this month.

Uganda, which declared itself Ebola-free in July after recording 20 cases, has denied claims that Nigeria’s first case originated there.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement on X. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases."

Nigerian authorities said they were tracing 44 contacts.

The patient, who entered Nigeria on 5 October, was initially treated for malaria but failed to recover, arousing suspicion among the attending physicians, Odianosen Ehiakhamen, an assistant director at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control, local media reported. The patient is now in isolation and receiving medical care.

Ehiakhamen said the contacts are mostly healthcare workers, along with the patient’s spouse, a Swiss national.

Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or via contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May and 9,552 confirmed cases.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists, although trials are underway in Congo.

The risk of importation into Europe from the outbreak areas remains very low, according to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

“While sporadic importations cannot be excluded, the probability of multiple independent importations is very low, even in a pessimistic scenario whereby incidence continues to rise in the affected regions,” the Center wrote on its website.

World.title: EU should revive talks on broader China trade deal, top MEP says
World.content:
The European Union should seek a broad trade agreement with China, potentially including investment, rather than continue negotiating over individual sectors, a senior European Parliament lawmaker said on Wednesday.

 

Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Parliament's Trade Committee, made the call ahead of a visit to Beijing next week by 12 MEPs, as Brussels and China seek to ease mounting trade tensions.

The two sides reached a deal on hybrid cars on 9 October, but the EU views it as insufficient to address a trade imbalance that sees the bloc run a deficit of around €1 billion a day with China.

Brussels and Beijing previously negotiated a Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI), but the European Parliament froze its ratification in 2021 after China imposed retaliatory sanctions in response to EU measures over human rights abuses.

“It is necessary to have a more comprehensive agreement,” Lange told reporters. “I'm also in favour to have an agreement quite soon. Negotiation forever make no sense.”

Lange added that the discussion should include investments. Speaking of the CAI, he also said: “Perhaps it's useful to have a look at that, specifically regarding the investment part.”

Beyond cars, a wider threat to industry

Earlier this month, the European Commission announced a deal under which China agreed to halve its hybrid car exports to the EU over the next four years.

Under the agreement, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.

The deal was presented by the Commission as a "first phase" of the negotiation which will continue on a technical level until next political talks scheduled for March 2027.

But French liberal MEP Pascal Canfin, who will join Lange on the trip, warned that the EU needs to look beyond individual industries. He argued that the Commission's negotiations on behalf of the 27 member states should address broader unfair trade practices that threaten European manufacturers across multiple sectors.

“We are open for negotiation, sector per sector, but at the same time, we look at things that it is not a sectorial threat,” Canfin said. “It's the risk of horizontal unfair practices that would have a very detrimental impact on our industries.”

During their visit to China from 27 to 29 October, EU lawmakers will meet representatives of the Chinese Ministry of commerce and members of the National People’s Congress. They are also expected to hold meetings with high-tech business representatives in Hangzhou.

Lange highlighted other issues that should be covered by a future agreement with Beijing, including Chinese export restrictions — Beijing imposes strict licensing requirements on EU businesses seeking to export rare earths, essential to European industry — unfair subsidies in the chemicals and machinery sectors, and a 20% price surcharge on EU bids in public procurement.

The EU is walking a tightrope in its relations with Beijing, pushing for dialogue while simultaneously enforcing trade defence measures to protect its industry.

Last week, EU leaders gave the Commission a political mandate to introduce unilateral quotas to protect the chemicals and machinery sectors, given the urgency of the threats posed by Chinese competition.

However, some member states, such as Spain, favour a softer approach towards Beijing, keen to secure Chinese investment.

World.title: Poland’s abortion reforms would leave it among the EU’s most restrictive, even if signed into law
World.content:
On Tuesday, 20 October, the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, passed amendments to the Criminal Code that would ease some penalties for people helping women access abortion care and restore access to abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities.

 

The vote marks a tentative step towards fulfilling Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition pledge to restore reproductive rights, made nearly three years ago. But even if the legislation survives a likely presidential veto, it would fall well short of the coalition’s promise.

The changes would not introduce abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, a pledge made by Tusk’s Civic Coalition during the election campaign. Their passage into law is also uncertain: President Karol Nawrocki, who took office in 2025, has previously said that he would not support legislation easing abortion restrictions.

Under current law, anyone who terminates a pregnancy with a woman’s consent can face up to three years in prison. The same penalty applies to people who assist a woman in obtaining an abortion or encourage her to have one.

The proposed bill, backed by 217 parliamentarians, with 213 voting against and three abstaining, would exempt doctors, nurses and midwives from criminal liability when an abortion results from a medically necessary procedure intended to protect a pregnant woman’s health or life.

“It's time to end the punishment of all those who love, worry, and respect our choices,” Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s equality commissioner and a lawmaker from the Left, said on X.

Another bill, passed with 233 votes in favour, 203 against and one abstention, would again permit abortion in cases of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life.

It would overturn the effect of a 2020 ruling by Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, which found abortion on the grounds of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities unconstitutional.

‘Incremental step forward’

Seeing these changes become law remains a challenge. Even if it passes the Senate, it will need Nawrocki’s signature. The president is aligned with the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, which oversaw a tightening of abortion restrictions five years ago.

Overriding a presidential veto would require a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, a threshold Tusk’s coalition does not have.

Despite that, such an “incremental step forward” shouldn't be understated “as it's the first time in many years now that there's been movement in the Polish Parliament,” Leah Hoctor, Senior Regional Director for Europe at the Center for Reproductive Rights, told Euronews. A similar attempt was unsuccessful in July 2024, after failing to secure the required majority.

However, even if the amendments become law, Poland would remain one of only two EU countries, alongside Malta, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is not legal.

“The legal changes that these bills represent are so narrow in scope that for most women who need abortion care, that care will remain illegal,” Hoctor said, adding that women would still be forced to travel to access care.

That would leave Poland out of step with much of Europe, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is legal in most countries and several governments have moved to reduce barriers to care and remove criminal penalties.

“Poland is an outlier in the European context,” she said. "Globally, Poland and the US are two of only four countries in the last 30 years to have removed a ground for legal abortion from their laws," she added.

Abortion in Poland is allowed when pregnancy threatens a woman's health or life or results from a criminal act, including rape or incest. Such a near-total abortion ban has been criticised by international human rights bodies.

The European Court of Human Rights has ruled against the country in several cases involving barriers to abortion access, while in 2024, following a three-year inquiry, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women found that Poland’s abortion laws had resulted in grave and systematic violations of women’s rights and called for comprehensive legal reform.

World.title: Roaming roots: Artist Gulnur Mukazhanova explores her nomadic heritage at Frieze London
World.content:
What can a piece of fabric tell us about where we come from, where we have been and where we are going?

 

At this year's Frieze London, considered one of the world's most influential contemporary art fairs, Kazakh-born, Berlin-based artist Gulnur Mukazhanova explored these questions through a series of textile artworks that brought together centuries of cultural history.

Presented in collaboration with Turkish Airlines, Bosağa: Journeys Across Cultures and Time features a triptych from her ongoing Bosağa series which she began in 2021. The title comes from a word shared by Kazakh and other Turkic languages, meaning “threshold” - a point of passage between places, cultures or even different states of being.

Journeys across time: Gulnar Mukazhanova's triptych are from her ongoing series '‘Bosağa’ – a word in Kazakh and Turkic languages meaning ‘threshold’, 14 October 2026 Credit: Matt Stills and Frieze

At the heart of the works is felt - a material deeply rooted in the nomadic traditions of Central Asia. Traditionally used to construct yurts, felt provided shelter for generations of the artist's ancestors as they travelled across vast landscapes.

Mukazhanova combines handmade felt with fragments of vibrant fabric collected during her travels across Asia. Rather than sewing or gluing these pieces together, she pins them into place, creating a feeling of fragility and reflecting the idea that things don’t have to be permanent.

Her work also draws inspiration from the tuskiiz, a traditional Kazakh embroidered wall hanging often rich in symbolism and associated with protection. Her research into 14th-century Italian art also informed the series, particularly the richly decorated carpets that travelled from Asia to Europe along the Silk Road.

World.title: Brussels goes back to the drawing board on Europe-wide taxes
World.content:
European Council President António Costa is scrambling to find new EU-wide taxes to fund the bloc's next long-term budget after last week's inconclusive summit left leaders deadlocked over how much they are willing to pay.

 

With national governments reluctant to increase their contributions, Costa is exploring ways to raise money directly for Brussels, from taxes on large companies and digital services to levies on tobacco, carbon emissions and online gambling.

And with negotiations entering a critical phase, no option appears to be off the table.

“To reach an agreement, we need to keep national contributions at a reasonable level, while preserving our ambition and the means to deliver on our common priorities. For this to be possible, it is fundamental to consolidate the work on the new own resources,” Costa said at a press conference following last week's European Council summit.

Throughout his tour of the capitals, Costa returned again and again to the same point: EU-wide taxes are essential to square the circle between strained national budgets and the bloc’s emerging priorities.

EU leaders failed to bridge their differences over the budget last week, leaving Costa to steer the next stage of negotiations.

During his tour of European capitals, he repeatedly stressed that new EU revenue sources – known in Brussels as own resources – are essential to reconcile strained national finances with the bloc's growing spending ambitions.

“We had three tests for new own resources. One, that they command unanimity. Two, that they can deliver substantial funds. And three, that they’d be ready, by the 1st of January, 2028,” Thomas Byrne, Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs, said when presenting when presenting the country's budget compromise.

The Irish proposal nonetheless drew criticism from all sides, including the European Parliament, whose ideas for new taxes on digital services, online gambling and crypto assets could raise up to €25bn a year.

“It is clear that the presidency refused to take any decision on the revenue side, proposing only minor adjustments. We are especially very disappointed that none of Parliament’s proposals were taken on board, despite having received positive feedback from many member states,” said MEP Danuše Nerudová (Czechia/EPP).

Indeed, the Irish compromise kept the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), one of the most contested proposals among member states, which argue that taxing companies runs counter to the EU’s competitiveness agenda.

The Commission has defended the proposal, stressing that CORE would only hit large companies with a net annual turnover above €100m, and that the contribution would normally be lower than the bonuses paid to their senior executives.

But the Commission is now examining whether CORE could be combined with a digital levy, another controversial proposal that risks provoking Washington because most of the world's biggest technology companies are American.

Under the emerging idea, the tax would no longer target a specific sector. Instead, the threshold would be set high enough to ensure that it fell mainly on large foreign companies, whether American or Asian.

Such a compromise could become increasingly important as other potential revenue sources run into opposition.

One proposal would divert 30% of revenues from the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS), which charges major polluters for their carbon emissions, into the EU budget.

Poland has been particularly vocal against sending ETS revenues to Brussels. The issue has become so politically charged at home that Warsaw may struggle to accept it as it heads towards elections next year.

The Irish compromise also kept the Tobacco Excise Duty Own Resource (TEDOR), which would see member states pay the EU a 15% call rate on the excise duty on tobacco products. Governments fear it could fuel the black market and lead to a drop in quality.

Luxembourg is particularly opposed. Though small, the Grand Duchy is a net contributor that seldom objects to the Commission’s budget proposals, so it may have significant political capital to spend against TEDOR.

Other proposals have attracted broader support. The least controversial is a revenue source linked to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon price on certain imports, including steel and cement, to ensure foreign producers face costs comparable to their EU competitors.

A tax based on the amount of electronic waste each EU country produces is also largely uncontroversial, with most open issues technical in nature.

Parliament’s proposed tax on online gambling, however, has met strong opposition from Malta, home to most of the EU’s betting websites.

Another parliamentary proposal, a tax on capital gains from crypto assets, is widely seen as extremely difficult to implement, with highly uncertain yields given the market’s volatility.

Greece has also proposed coordinating national 6G spectrum auctions to finance the EU budget. But member states have long resisted harmonising spectrum allocation, which has traditionally brought in significant national revenue.

“Now is the moment to evaluate the situation and assess the best way forward. We do not exclude taking on board any proposals,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

“We will need to modulate the own resources to better distribute their impact on the member states,” the official added.

World.title: UN warns El Nino could be strongest on record as it urges world to prepare
World.content:
The current El Nino could reach a strength never seen in modern records, United Nations officials warned on Wednesday, calling on governments to act now to limit the damage.

 

"The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), told reporters in Geneva.

"El Nino will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that," she added.

According to the WMO's latest global seasonal climate updates, sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, where the phenomenon originates, could climb as high as 3.8C above average between November and January. That would be far beyond what is normally seen during an El Nino.

"This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world," Saulo said.

The agency expects the event to push up temperatures across much of the globe, adding to the warming already driven by human-caused climate change.

A call for early action

Saulo appeared alongside Tom Fletcher, the UN's under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs.

"Today, we are issuing a joint call for urgent and coordinated anticipatory action... We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences," she said.

Fletcher described the coming El Nino as a "wrecking ball" of extreme heat, drought and flooding, warning it would bring "massive humanitarian consequences".

"The damage will not stay in the countries in the immediate path of this El Nino," he said. "It will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration.

"I am sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system... cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale." He urged governments, development banks and international financial institutions to release funding "before that damage is done, not afterwards".

"The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster or we can invest in resilience. We cannot prevent El Nino but we can be serious about the challenges ahead."

Fletcher said he had already released $50 million to support 11 of the most exposed countries, among them Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.

What is El Nino?

El Nino is a naturally occurring climate pattern in which surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm. This shifts winds, air pressure and rainfall around the world. It usually returns every two to seven years and lasts between nine and 12 months.

The climate swings between El Nino and its cooler counterpart, La Nina, with neutral periods in between.

World.title: EU prosecutors raid far-right group's offices in €4 million funds scandal
World.content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) raided the offices of the far-right Patriots for Europe (PfE) group in Brussels and Strasbourg on Wednesday as part of an investigation into the alleged misuse of millions of euros in EU funds.

 

The searches at the European Parliament’s two main seats are linked to an investigation into the former Identity and Democracy (ID) group, the Parliament confirmed to Euronews.

PfE, which includes France’s National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen; Italy’s Lega, led by Matteo Salvini; and Hungary’s Fidesz, led by Viktor Orbán, could be ordered to repay more than €4 million allegedly misspent by its predecessor.

“It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy group, which dissolved in 2024,” the PfE group said in a statement, insisting that it has no “legal continuity” with ID and is therefore “not involved in the ongoing investigation”.

Neither the EPPO nor the Parliament has released further details about the searches.

The Parliament “cooperates with relevant authorities” and “does not have any additional comment,” its press service said.

Jean-Paul Garraud, an MEP who leads the National Rally delegation in the Parliament, wrote on X that the searches targeted “the offices of former ID staff members”.

The anti-graft body has been investigating since last July the alleged misappropriation of EU funds by ID between 2019 and 2024. The group brought together MEPs from far-right parties such as France’s National Rally, Italy’s Lega and the Alternative for Germany (AfD).

ID dissolved after the 2024 European elections, and many of its parties went on to form PfE, which also includes newcomers Spain’s Vox and Hungary's Fidesz.

An opinion approved by the Parliament’s Committee on Budgetary Control (CONT) last September argued that EU funds wrongly spent by ID during the previous term should be repaid by PfE once the investigation is closed.

Under the Parliament’s rules, a political group is treated as “the successor” of a dissolved one, and therefore liable for any remaining debt, if certain conditions are met.

These include “a decisive share of the former group’s members moved together into the new formation”, “premises, IT systems, bank accounts or other assets passed to the new structure”, and “the new name and public messaging presenting the entity as the direct heir of the dissolved group, or following so closely in time that the rebranding appears designed mainly to shed liabilities.”

World.title: Eurozone government debt climbs to 88.8% of GDP as Italy closes in on Greece
World.content:
Public debt across the 21 countries of the eurozone reached 88.8% of their combined economic output between April and June, up from 87.3% a year earlier, the EU's statistics office, Eurostat, said on Wednesday.

 

Italy's debt ratio is now less than one percentage point below Greece's, while France's has climbed to 119.1% as its borrowing costs rose above 5%.

The debt-to-GDP ratio compares what governments owe with the size of their economies. Under EU rules, debt should not exceed 60% of GDP, and annual budget deficits should not exceed 3%.

Across the wider EU, government debt rose to 82.9% of GDP in the second quarter, from 81.4% a year earlier. In cash terms, eurozone governments owed some €14.4 trillion.

Full-year figures, also published on Wednesday, show EU debt rose to 81.5% of GDP in 2025 from 80.3% in 2024, while the bloc's budget deficit held at 3.1%, just above the EU's 3% limit.

EU debt has stayed above 80% of GDP since the COVID-19 pandemic, when it peaked at 89.5% in 2020.

For the eurozone, Eurostat's headline full-year figures still cover the 20 countries that used the euro last year, as Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026. Their debt rose to 87.7% of GDP from 86.6%.

Eurostat also expressed a reservation about the quality of Bulgaria’s 2025 data on how it records spending by its road infrastructure agency.

Germany, the bloc's largest economy, saw its debt ratio rise to 62.8% from 61.4% as its deficit widened to 2.9%.

Deficits are also increasing again this year. Adjusted for seasonal swings, the combined deficit of eurozone governments edged up to 3.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 3.2% in the first, while the figure for EU governments rose to 3.5% from 3.1%.

Last year, 12 member states had debt above the EU’s 60% ceiling, and 11 ran deficits of 3% or more.

Italy closes in on Greece while France's debt and yields climb

Greece remained the most indebted EU country at 140.8% of GDP in the second quarter, but Italy was just behind at 139.9%.

Greece's ratio has fallen by 11.2 percentage points in a year as the country runs budget surpluses, while Italy's rose by 1.3 percentage points in the second quarter alone.

In 2022, Greece's debt stood at 177.8% of GDP, against 138.4% for Italy.

France has the third-highest debt-to-GDP ratio, at 119.1%, up 3.7 percentage points in a year, one of the steepest rises in the bloc. Debt also remained above 100% of GDP in Belgium and Spain, at 110.2% and 101.4%, respectively.

Estonia had the lowest ratio, at 26.1%, followed by Denmark and Luxembourg, while Poland recorded the sharpest increase in its debt ratio, up 6.7 percentage points from a year earlier.

The figures landed on the same day the yield on France's 10-year government bond rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors demanded more to hold French debt.

France's deficit was 5.1% of GDP last year, the fourth-largest in the EU after Romania, Poland and Belgium.

A divided French parliament is debating the 2027 budget, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lacks a majority to pass his spending cuts.

Ratings agency Moody’s is due to review France’s credit rating on Friday, with most economists expecting a downgrade that could push its borrowing costs higher still.

World.title: Russia arrests German man, calls him a Ukraine 'mercenary'
World.content:
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national and accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine's military. They claim he deserted over unpaid wages and say he was a sniper who once served in the Bundeswehr.

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) domestic intelligence agency said on Wednesday that it had arrested a German national on allegations of mercenary activity, calling him an "active member of the Ukrainian armed forces."

The news came on the same day that Russia released a retired teacher from the US, Stephen Hubbard, after years in detention on similar mercenary charges, which he denied.

Russia has detained a number of foreign nationals since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, accusing them of assisting Kyiv in some way or another.

There was no immediate comment from Germany's government, besides acknowledging that it had seen the reports and was pursuing them.

What did the FSB say about the arrest?

The FSB said in a statement carried widely by Russian media that the man was a former Bundeswehr soldier and trained sniper. It did not issue his name but published a short video in which he could be heard speaking German.

The FSB also published footage that it said showed the man holding a sniper rifle with Ukrainian Armed Forces Image: Russian Federal Security Service/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

According to the FSB, the man was a Bundeswehr soldier from 1996 to 2010, who served in Afghanistan and Somalia between 2004 and 2010.

They alleged that he later operated as a mercenary fighter in Syria's civil war.

From 2016 to 2018, according to the Russian spy agency, he fought in Ukraine against the Russian-backed rebels in eastern states, prior to Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The FSB claimed that he returned to Ukraine as a "mercenary" in 2025 and was fighting in the contested region of Donetsk, but then deserted over non-payment of wages.

They did not comment on why or how the man, whom they said was born in 1976, had come to be in Russia. Nor did they say where or under what circumstances they arrested him.

How did German authorities respond?

A spokesperson at the German Foreign Ministry only initially responded by saying that Berlin was aware of the reports from Russia.

The spokesperson said the ministry would not comment on the individual case or specifics for the time being.

German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Similar Swedish arrest last week, US prisoner freed

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals on charges like espionage, sabotage and treason amid its invasion of neighboring Ukraine. The charges can carry lengthy prison sentences.

A smaller number have also been accused of mercenary activity.

The FSB last week arrested a Swedish national, again accusing him of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

In his case, they said he was operating as the commander of a drone unit and that he was detained attempting to illegally cross the border in the western Pskov region.

A Japanese journalist was also arrested last week, accused of espionage, prompting sharp criticism from Tokyo.

Also on Wednesday, Russia released a retired US teacher, Stephen Hubbard, who had been arrested in 2024 on comparable allegations.

This took place as US negotiator Steve Witkoff was visiting St. Petersburg and after a series of recent concessions to Russia and criticisms of Ukraine from US President Donald Trump.

Trump claimed there was no quid pro quo involved in the release, but later said Hubbard would not be free if he had not eased sanctions on Russian diesel shipments.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks
World.content:
During talks between Vladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff, Putin announced that jailed American Stephen Hubbard had been released. The Kremlin also said Russia was "in principle" ready to resume trilateral talks next month.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.

Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."

US President Donald Trump later said he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.

"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

Putin and Witkoff met in St. Petersburg for their ninth in-person talks Image: Kristina Solovyova/TASS/picture alliance

However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.

"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.

Russia agrees to trilateral talks with Ukraine, US

The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administration as the two sides discuss a deal for peace between Russia and Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.

After the talks, the Kremlin said Witkoff's proposals "lacked substance" and would not be of real use for a potential peace settlement.

However, Putin agreed "in principle" to resume peace talks with Russian, Ukrainian and US delegates after November 10.

Such talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends," Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said.

Putin also proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow.

Meanwhile, Putin appeared open to a potential trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

"A possible first-ever meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the United States... is being prepared," Ushakov said.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin — came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.



How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European leaders hope for productive negotiations

Zelenskyy on Wednesday called for freezing the front line as a first step toward ceasefire talks.

"Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," Zelenskyy said in an interview with "Fox & Friends."

The European Union, which was represented by delegates from several member states at the Oslo talks on Tuesday, said it expected to be debriefed by Washington after Wednesday's talks.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also said on Wednesday that Berlin was supporting Ukraine to end the war as quickly as possible, adding that any capitulation by Ukraine would be "a capitulation by all of us."

Witkoff to return to Oslo

The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.

"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: Germany news: Nvidia CEO optimistic about EU's AI economy
World.content:
A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.

The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).

Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.

"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.

Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.

There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.

Huang demonstrated robots that he said had been trained by AI Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.

Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

World.title: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
World.content:
As Pakistan's influence in Afghanistan comes under strain, India is rebuilding ties with the Taliban in Kabul. Can New Delhi turn this diplomatic opening into lasting strategic gains?

Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.

The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.

At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.

Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Where does India come into play?

As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.

"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.

However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.

"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.

India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."

Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.

"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.

"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.

For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.

The cost of closer ties

Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.

He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.

"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.

Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."

'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trade cannot overcome geography

India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.

Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.

On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.

But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.

New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.

D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.

Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.

"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.

"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.

Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.

Islamabad's security fears

Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.

"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.

The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.

Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.

India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.

"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.

Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."

"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.

India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.

World.title: UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
World.content:
Drilling is set to begin in the controversial North Sea plot as the government seeks to tackle high energy costs. Environmental groups have criticized the move and called for more clean energy.

The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.

The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.

The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.

What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."

"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.

"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.

Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.

What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?

Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.

"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.

However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."

"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.

Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.

Protesters had called on Burnham to block approval for the Jackdaw gas field Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP

In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.

The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.

It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
World.content:
As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Iran expands regional rail links

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

China-Iran rail traffic expands

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

Ships wanting to transit the Strait of Hormuz have faced recurring and serious disruptions since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year Image: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/AP Photo/picture alliance

Delivery date cannot be guaranteed

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Rail works best for critical inputs

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

When delays become a cash problem

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Sanctions push trade toward other corridors

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack as suspect appears in court
World.content:
Doctors have amputated both of Helen Haines legs after the Australian lawmaker was hit in an apparent deliberate attack. The suspected driver involved in the attack has appeared in court.

Helen Haines, an Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday, has lost both of her legs, her husband said on Wednesday.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

A 43-year-old suspect, Brendan N. from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Haines loses both legs after apparent attack

The independent MP underwent surgery on Monday night after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that her left leg had been amputated.

Doctors then proceeded to amputate her right leg on Wednesday after having tried to save it.

"The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines told reporters in Melbourne.

"We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape," he said.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. Later reports from witnesses said that after first pinning Haines against her own car, the driver reversed and rammed into her a second time.

The driver was arrested shortly after, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

The suspect's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told Magistrate Allison Vaughan on Wednesday that his client suffers from a rare neurological condition, as well as an undiagnosed mental health condition. He also said the defendant was suffering from a concussion.

Local barber ran to assist

Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.

Barber Ricky Jefferies has been called a hero for restraining the driver Image: Seven Network/REUTERS

Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.

"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't ​pull it ‌out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.

Jefferies said he then held the man down until ‌police arrived.

"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and ‌he was ​no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.

Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."

"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.

Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese

Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident' Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

Edited by: Karl Sexton and Louis Oelofse
