World.title: Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon. Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border. Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU. This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace. What appears to be a drone exploded… — Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026 On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object. President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”. Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace. “I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT. However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”. Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country. In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”. Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”. We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia. We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have… — Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026 Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian. “We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.” The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was. Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming. On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself. It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place. Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank. It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”. World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.

She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: How Prague Helped Write the Chemistry of Peptides
World.content:
Prague has a quiet but real place in the history of peptide chemistry.

From the 1950s, chemists at what is now the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry (IOCB) worked out how to build and redesign pituitary peptides, the city hosted the first European Peptide Symposium in 1958, and one of the institute’s analogues was licensed abroad and produced industrially. The same research base now underpins Prague’s new biotech cluster.

A field that started with nine amino acids

In 1953 Vincent du Vigneaud’s group in New York published a short paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society reporting that they had made oxytocin in the laboratory. Oxytocin is a peptide, a chain of just nine amino acids, but nobody had synthesised a peptide hormone before, and two years later the work brought du Vigneaud the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Making even a chain that short was slow and fiddly. Amino acids have more than one reactive group, so a chemist had to block all the groups that should stay out of the reaction, join two units, unblock exactly one end and repeat the whole cycle for the next amino acid. Every step lost some material. What du Vigneaud’s paper showed was that it could be done, and that a peptide whose sequence was known could be rebuilt and, in principle, rebuilt differently.

That same year, Prague got its own institute for the job. The Institute of Organic Chemistry, renamed the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry in 1960, was formally founded in 1953 under František Šorm, who ran it until 1970. Šorm listed peptides and proteins among the handful of subjects the institute would build its research around.

The Prague school of peptide analogues

By 1958 the Prague group was established enough to host the first European Peptide Symposium. It took place in September of that year, and the IOCB chemist Josef Rudinger edited the proceedings, which the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences published in 1960. The symposium has been held regularly since and is now run by the European Peptide Society.

The institute’s peptide chemists spent the next three decades on what is called structure–activity work. The idea is simple to describe and laborious to carry out: take a natural peptide, change one feature, measure how its biological activity shifts and let that result decide the next change. Their material was the family of hormones from the posterior pituitary, the group that oxytocin belongs to, along with its close relative vasopressin. In 1960 they synthesised lysine-vasopressin, a natural form of the hormone found in pigs, and later derived terlipressin from it.

The best-known result came from Milan Zaoral’s team in the early 1960s. Working from vasopressin, they replaced the arginine at position 8 with D-arginine, its mirror-image form, and removed the amino group at the very beginning of the chain. Drawn on paper, the new molecule looks almost identical to the old one. Biologically it behaved very differently: of the two main activities the natural hormone has, the analogue kept one at full strength and lost most of the other. They named it desmopressin.

In the late 1960s the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences licensed desmopressin to the Swedish company Ferring AB, and by the early 1970s it was being made on an industrial scale in both Czechoslovakia and Sweden. For a structure–activity programme, it was about as clear a demonstration as one could ask for that two small, deliberate edits can change what a peptide does.

How synthesis stopped being the bottleneck

While Zaoral’s group was redesigning vasopressin, Bruce Merrifield at the Rockefeller Institute in New York changed the way peptides were made. His 1963 paper described fixing the first amino acid of a chain to a small resin bead. The chain then grew while attached to the bead, and instead of purifying the product after every coupling, the chemist simply washed the excess reagents away.

Solid-phase synthesis, as it became known, was repetitive enough to automate, and Merrifield received the 1984 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. It is still the standard method for producing peptides for research, which is why a sequence that once took a team months can now be ordered from a catalogue.

That availability turned peptides into ordinary laboratory tools. Immunologists use short synthetic sequences to pinpoint which part of a protein an antibody recognises. Biochemists use them as substrates when they measure enzyme activity, receptor researchers use them to study binding, and analytical chemists rely on them as reference materials when they develop methods such as mass spectrometry.

The weak point is the material itself. A coupling step that does not quite finish leaves chains one amino acid short, a protecting group can survive to the end, and some of these by-products are hard to tell apart from the intended peptide. Researchers at Ghent University found this out directly when they tested a set of synthetic peptides bought for their own research with a requested purity of at least 95%. Only about 44% met that figure under their analysis, and in one sample the main compound was not the structure that had been ordered.

Problems like that contribute to a wider issue in experimental science. In a 2016 Nature survey of 1,576 researchers, more than 70% said they had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist’s experiment.

Labs that buy research peptides for this kind of work therefore tend to judge a supplier by its documentation as much as by its catalogue:

Peptides supplied on this basis are laboratory materials, made and documented for experiments, and not intended for use in people or animals.

Prague’s research base today

In September 2023 IOCB Prague, its technology-transfer company i&i Prague, the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institutes of Biotechnology, Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, and the University of Chemistry and Technology, Prague, announced a joint biotechnology cluster called Prague.bio. Its purpose is to bring academic research and business closer together, and in May 2024 Zentiva joined as its first industry partner. The peptide work of the 1950s and 1960s is part of the scientific inheritance the cluster now builds on.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prosecutors seek to arrest former Hungarian central bank chief Matolcsy
World.content:
Prosecutors have requested the pre-trial detention of former National Bank of Hungary governor György Matolcsy following a lengthy interrogation over suspected economic fraud. A judge is expected to decide on Friday whether he will be remanded in custody.

Matolcsy did not make a statement during questioning

György Matolcsy’s questioning as a suspect ended shortly before 3.30 PM on Wednesday, 21 October, according to reports by Hungarian news outlets Telex and Index. His lawyer, Pál Bátki, said his client had not made a statement about the allegations during the several-hour interrogation, speaking only about his personal circumstances.

Bátki added that the investigating prosecutors had outlined the circumstances on which they based the suspicion against the former central bank governor and had requested his pre-trial detention.

“It was very difficult to process this five-page document containing a great deal of information. Until we see what evidence forms the basis of it, we cannot respond to it,” the lawyer said.

Matolcsy is suspected of economic fraud causing significant financial damage and the misdemeanour of using a forged private document.

Judge to decide on pre-trial detention

After the interrogation, Matolcsy was transferred from the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office to a police detention facility, where he is expected to remain until the hearing on the prosecution’s request. A judge is expected to rule on Friday whether to order his pre-trial detention. The court could also decide on a less restrictive measure, such as criminal supervision, instead of keeping him in custody.

Under Hungarian procedure, detention following arrest can last for up to 72 hours before a decision on further measures must be made.

Bátki had previously said that the defence had lodged a complaint against Matolcsy’s detention. He also argued that pre-trial detention would be unjustified, citing his client’s age, stable living conditions and close family ties.

If you missed it: BREAKING: Former Hungarian central bank governor Matolcsy detained

Prosecutors outline alleged scheme involving foundation assets

In a more detailed statement released on Wednesday afternoon, the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office outlined the specific transaction at the centre of this strand of the National Bank case. Prosecutors allege that Matolcsy and his associates used a sham securities-lending agreement signed on 28 February 2025 — one of the former central bank governor’s final working days — in an attempt to transfer control over the assets of the PADME Foundation to people who would remain under his influence after he left office.

The foundation originated from the Pallas Athéné foundations established by the central bank under Matolcsy’s leadership in 2014. According to prosecutors, these foundations received more than HUF 266 billion (approximately EUR 700 million) from the central bank’s exchange-rate gains. They merged in 2019 under the name PADME, with their assets managed by Optima Befektetési Zrt.

The alleged transaction involved Optima and the Central European III Private Equity Fund, represented by Quartz Befektetési Alapkezelő Zrt. Prosecutors claim the agreement was not a genuine securities-lending arrangement, but a means of transferring control over the foundation’s assets to a circle of people whom Matolcsy could continue to influence after his term as governor ended.

According to the prosecution, the alleged purpose was to enable Matolcsy and his son, Ádám, to make investments serving their own interests and to generate personal gains. The transaction transferred the shares of Optima Befektetési Alapkezelő Zrt. to the private equity fund, shifting ownership control over an asset manager overseeing assets with a market value of nearly HUF 200 billion (around EUR 547 million).

Prosecutors said the precise financial damage has not yet been established, but that it substantially exceeded the HUF 500 million threshold for particularly significant financial damage under Hungarian law.

Alongside Matolcsy, two other people were detained, while prosecutors also sought international arrest warrants for two further individuals. Searches were conducted at several locations and evidence was seized.

Investigation into the National Bank case continues

Investigating prosecutors detained Matolcsy early on Wednesday morning as part of the ongoing case involving the National Bank of Hungary (MNB). Investigative measures were also carried out at several locations.

According to Telex, other people were also detained in connection with the case, including the regular lawyer for companies belonging to Matolcsy’s son, Ádám, and a senior official at a company linked to Ádám Matolcsy and István Száraz.

World.title: Paks nuclear power plant hit by turbine failure: only one unit runs at full capacity
World.content:
A turbine-generator failure has forced Unit 1 of Hungary’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant to operate at half capacity. With another unit undergoing maintenance and a third out of service for an overhaul, only one of the plant’s four units is currently running at full power.

The incident occurred at 8:02 AM on Wednesday, when one of Unit 1’s turbine-generator units shut down following the activation of generator protection, MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant announced.

As a result, the unit’s output fell by more than 100 megawatts and it is now operating at 50% capacity

Three of four units operating at reduced capacity or offline

Unit 1 is not the only part of the facility affected by reduced output. According to reports, Unit 2 was also scaled back to 50% capacity from Wednesday because of maintenance ahead of a major overhaul. Unit 4 has been undergoing a major overhaul since 18 September and is not generating electricity. This leaves Unit 3 as the only unit currently operating at full capacity.

Data from Hungary’s National Atomic Energy Authority showed that the plant was already generating around 1,274 megawatts on Tuesday, compared with its nominal capacity of just over 2,000 megawatts. The latest incident has further reduced the plant’s available output, although the operator has not announced how long Unit 1 will remain at half capacity.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Is the Danube’s low water level to blame?

The turbine failure was attributed to the activation of generator protection, not to the Danube’s low water level. The operator has not reported any connection between the two issues.

Nevertheless, low river levels have posed significant challenges for the plant in recent months, as the Danube supplies the cooling water needed for its operation.

On 13 October, Paks recorded the lowest water level ever measured there, according to Index. A submerged sill constructed over the summer raised the water level by around 61 centimetres, helping the plant avoid further production restrictions.

During the summer, seven of the plant’s eight turbines had to be shut down at one point because insufficient water was reaching their cooling systems. The military transported 38,000 tonnes of rock to the area to help construct the submerged sill between Paks and Dunapataj.

If you missed it: Átlátszó: Hungarian government building Paks bottom sill without environmental permit

The plant has already faced a historic shutdown

Drought conditions and exceptionally low Danube water levels forced the plant to gradually reduce output during the summer. On 2 August, it was shut down completely for the first time in its history. Paks returned to full output on 26 August, following improvements in water conditions and the measures taken to maintain water levels near the cooling-water intake.

World.title: “Prepare for your death” – Another 27 schools in Hungary receives bomb threats, message leaked
World.content:
A new wave of bomb threats has targeted 27 schools in Hungary’s Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County, with a further threat reported at a school in Budapest. Police are inspecting the affected buildings, and no explosives have been found at sites searched so far, authorities said.

Another 27 bomb threats two days after the previous messages

Hungary’s National Bureau of Investigation (Nemzeti Nyomozóiroda, NNI) is examining whether the latest threats are connected to previous incidents involving educational institutions. Dávid Janiczak, the mayor of Ózd, confirmed on social media that 27 schools in Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County had been named in the latest threat and published a copy of the message.

The bomb threats were reported on Wednesday, 21 October. According to the authorities, a threatening email listing several schools in Northern Hungary was sent to the functional email address of a news website. A Budapest school received a separate message directly in its own inbox.

What does the message say?

The perpetrators in the email first mention the settlements, then list the institutions involved, while claiming they “have come for the young”. In the paragraph second to last, they claim the primary attack means detonating the explosive devices placed in the listed schools, and “if it does not seem effective enough”, their armed members “will continue to hold the targets accountable at the scene”. In the closing, they warn everybody to “prepare for death”, and they signed it as “your honorable fellow compatriots”.

Police inspect affected schools

Police are visiting the institutions concerned and coordinating their response with school management, following the procedures established during earlier incidents. In a statement, the National Bureau of Investigation said officers had found no explosives or devices suitable for detonation in buildings already searched. Inspections were continuing at the remaining locations.

The Pestújhelyi Primary School in Budapest’s 15th district was also targeted. District mayor Angéla Cserdiné Németh said the school had received another threatening message that morning and that police had begun inspecting the affected buildings. She added that children had been moved to safety at the Pestújhely Community Centre.

The school had also received a bomb threat the previous week. The National Bureau of Investigation has opened proceedings over threats to commit a terrorist act. Investigators are examining possible links between the latest messages and threats reported on 15 October and in other recent cases.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Series of threats raises concern

The latest incidents follow a series of bomb threats affecting schools across Hungary. On Monday, 19 October, more than 70 educational institutions reportedly received messages threatening that explosive devices had been planted on their premises. Police searched the affected buildings but found no explosives.

Further threats were reported on Tuesday, including at several practice schools and kindergartens associated with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), as well as the Miklós Radnóti Practice School in Budapest’s Zugló district, where an extraordinary school closure was ordered.

Threats were also reported in Serbia on Monday, affecting schools in several cities, including Subotica, Novi Sad and Belgrade. Authorities have not established whether the incidents in Hungary and Serbia are connected. Hungarian investigators continue to examine the messages and their possible links to earlier threats as police work to ensure the safety of pupils and staff.

World.title: Péter Magyar to AP News: public funds, similiarities with Viktor Orbán, chasing corruption
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has pledged to hold former officials accountable for alleged corruption under Viktor Orbán while maintaining Hungary’s strict immigration policies, in his first interview with a global news organisation since taking office.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar gave an exclusive interview

Speaking exclusively to The Associated Press (AP) on Tuesday, the prime minister said his government was working to recover public assets allegedly misused during Orbán’s 16 years in power. However, he stressed that investigations must respect the rule of law.

“The Hungarian people obviously want to see results in holding those responsible accountable, punishing them and recovering stolen property,” Péter Magyar said. His centre-right, pro-European Tisza party defeated Orbán’s Fidesz in April, ending more than a decade and a half of government marked by disputes with the European Union (EU) over corruption, democratic standards and migration.

New push to recover public funds

Magyar’s government has established a National Asset Recovery and Protection Office with investigative and prosecutorial powers. He described it as a “superauthority” capable of coordinating with police, prosecutors and tax officials to speed up complex corruption investigations. Hungary has also applied to join the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates crimes involving EU funds — a significant departure from Orbán’s refusal to join.

Although some former officials have already been detained on suspicion of corruption-related offences, Péter Magyar acknowledged public frustration over the pace of progress. He insisted, however, that building a democratic state governed by law would take time. Reforms have helped pave the way for the EU to announce the release of EUR 16.4 billion in funding for Hungary that had been frozen under the previous government.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Migration remains a sticking point

Despite improved relations with Brussels, the 45-year-old politician said Hungary would retain strict border controls, including razor-wire fencing and the practice of escorting irregular migrants back across the southern border into Serbia. Hungary was fined EUR 200 million by the EU’s Court of Justice in 2024, plus EUR 1 million for every subsequent day of non-compliance with an earlier asylum ruling.

Magyar said Hungary had already lost EUR 1 billion through the penalties and expected an agreement to end the dispute by the end of the year. He also linked the issue to negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget, arguing that a common budget would be difficult to approve while the dispute remained unresolved.

Ukraine ties improve, but differences remain

Prime minister Péter Magyar has sought to repair relations with Ukraine, which deteriorated under Orbán. He welcomed new legislation expanding minority-language education rights, calling it an opportunity to open a new chapter in bilateral relations. However, he opposes fast-tracking Ukraine’s EU membership, arguing that accession should be merit-based and that a country at war should not join the bloc.

Stay up-to-date: PM Péter Magyar reveals how Hungary will fund minimum wage tax cuts in 2027

Wealth tax to fund social measures

Domestically, Péter Magyar’s proposed 2027 budget includes a 1% annual tax on net wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion (more than EUR 2.7 million), rising to 1.5% on wealth above HUF 100 billion (EUR 273.5 million). The government estimates the measure could affect around 15,000 people and raise HUF 200 billion (almost EUR 547 million) annually.

The revenue would help fund tax cuts for lower earners, doubled child benefits and an increase in the minimum monthly pension from HUF 28,500 to HUF 120,000 (from EUR 77.95 to EUR 328.23). Magyar defended the measures as a matter of fairness, saying that supporting poorer households does not make him a socialist or a left-wing politician, but reflected “humanity” and “social justice”.
