World.title: MOL signs deal to buy Russian stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company – UPDATE: MOL reaction
World.content:
Hungarian oil and gas group MOL has signed an agreement to acquire the Russian-owned stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company, Serbian Finance Minister Siniša Mali has announced. The deal still requires regulatory approval, including clearance from US authorities.

The Russian shareholders and MOL have agreed on the sale, while the Serbian state has signed a separate shareholder agreement with the Hungarian company, Mali told Bloomberg Adria television, according to Hungarian news agency MTI.

The minister expects applications for regulatory approval to be submitted shortly to the competition authorities in Serbia and, as far as he knows, Bosnia and Herzegovina. The ownership change could then be completed within a relatively short period.

UPDATE: MOL says no relevant change has occurred

Several hours after Mali’s announcement, MOL issued a statement on the Budapest Stock Exchange website responding to the news reports.

The Hungarian oil and gas company said there had been no change in the ongoing NIS transaction that would require it to inform capital market participants.

MOL added that it would provide information promptly in accordance with applicable regulations if any new, relevant developments occurred.

The statement did not directly explain the discrepancy between the Serbian minister’s announcement that the sale agreement had been signed and MOL’s position. Therefore, it’s unclear precisely what has been agreed between the parties and whether the transaction has reached a new stage.

Serbia to increase its stake in NIS

Under the agreement, the Serbian state would increase its ownership in NIS from around 30% to 35%. Mali said a written agreement had already been reached, as Belgrade wanted its stake to exceed one-third.

However, the minister did not disclose the purchase price or the exact shareholding MOL would acquire.

The announcement is a significant step forward in negotiations that have dragged on for months. In early October, Serbian Forbes reported that talks had effectively collapsed because the Russian owners were unwilling to sell. MOL did not confirm that report at the time, saying the process was ongoing and the transaction would require several regulatory approvals.

MOL’s Százhalombatta refinery. Photo: MOL Group

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

US sanctions make the deal urgent

On 19 January, MOL signed a binding letter of intent with Russian oil company Gazprom Neft to acquire the Russian shareholders’ combined 56.15% stake in NIS.

In June, MOL also reached an agreement with the Serbian government on the company’s future management and the possibility of the state acquiring an additional five percentage points. The agreement also envisages MOL maintaining operations at the Pančevo refinery for at least ten years, at a capacity comparable to its pre-sanctions level.

The transaction is driven in part by US sanctions imposed on NIS in October 2025 because of its Russian majority ownership. The company has since received several temporary exemptions allowing it to continue operating.

The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) most recently authorised NIS to continue operating, including importing crude oil and refining it, until 30 October. MOL was also given permission to continue negotiations over the purchase until that date.

US approval is therefore another key hurdle before the transaction can be completed.

Why NIS matters to Serbia

NIS is one of Serbia’s most important energy companies and operates the country’s only oil refinery, in Pančevo. It is also involved in crude oil production and fuel retailing.

Gazprom Neft currently holds a 44.9% stake in the company, while its parent company, Gazprom, owns a further 11.3%. The Serbian state holds approximately 29.87%, with the remaining shares owned by minority shareholders.

World.title: BREAKING: Former Hungarian central bank governor Matolcsy detained
World.content:
György Matolcsy, the former governor of Hungary’s central bank, has been detained on suspicion of economic fraud causing significant financial damage and using a forged private document, his lawyer has confirmed.

Matolcsy was taken to the Central Chief Prosecution Office of Investigation early on Wednesday morning, according to Telex. Several other people have also reportedly been detained, including a lawyer and a businessman linked to the renovation of a villa on the Greek island of Mykonos associated with Matolcsy’s son, Ádám.

What charges does Matolcsy face?

Pál Bátki, Matolcsy’s legal representative, told Telex that his client was suspected of economic fraud causing significant financial damage and the misdemeanour of using a forged private document. The suspect’s formal questioning had not yet begun, but was expected to take place later on Wednesday morning.

Meanwhile, the Central Chief Prosecution Office of Investigation confirmed that coordinated investigative operations were under way at several locations as part of an ongoing investigation into suspected misappropriation of funds causing particularly significant financial damage. Further details were expected later in the day.

Investigation into central bank foundations

The detention marks a huge development in the long-running scandal surrounding the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) and its foundations, which managed hundreds of billions of forints in public assets during Matolcsy’s tenure as governor.

In March 2025, Hungary’s State Audit Office published reports identifying serious problems in the management of assets linked to the central bank’s foundations. One report raised concerns about the management of the Pallas Athéné Domus Meriti Foundation (PADME), with findings pointing to substantial losses.

The audit office concluded that assets worth hundreds of billions of forints had disappeared from the foundation during Matolcsy’s leadership. Earlier investigations by independent media had also raised questions about the foundations’ finances and their property investments.

If you missed it: Hungary’s central bank probe summons former and current governors

New developments in the MNB case

In September 2026, the central bank’s current leadership filed a criminal complaint over the depreciation of five properties it owned, citing suspected misappropriation, negligent mismanagement, fraud and abuse of office.

Governor Mihály Varga subsequently announced that a further 30,000 pages of documents relating to the MNB’s previous operations had been handed over to a parliamentary investigative committee.

The committee has been examining the case and seeking to identify those responsible. In early October, it questioned former Fidesz MPs Lajos Kósa and Erik Bánki about their knowledge of the central bank foundations and their operations.

World.title: Fidesz co-founder and former house speaker has surprising claims on party’s mistakes
World.content:
László Kövér, former Speaker of Hungary’s National Assembly and a co-founder of Fidesz, has admitted that the party failed to address several important issues during its 16 years in government, singling out the country’s education system as an area that has deteriorated.

Co-founder of Fidesz used their own mistakes as examples

“Our education system is in a worse state in this respect than it was 16 years ago,” Kövér said in an interview on the KözBeszéd programme, broadcast on Tuesday. He is stepping away from parliamentary politics following Fidesz’s election defeat.

However, he argued that the previous government should not bear all the responsibility for the problems in education. He said schools had also been forced to cope with wider social pressures arising from the breakdown of families.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Election defeat came as a shock

Reflecting on the election result, Kövér said Fidesz had expected a close contest based on opinion polls and still believed victory was possible on election day. Although he acknowledged that losing power after 16 years in government had always been a possibility, the scale of the defeat surprised him. “We knew in advance that it would not be a triumphant march, but we never expected such a heavy defeat,” he said. “It was a staggering surprise for us, at least for me.”

Kövér also conceded that Fidesz had made mistakes in several areas. One particular failure, in his view, was the party’s relationship with younger voters. He said it should have done more to build dialogue with young people well before the election campaign. His comments amount to an unusually direct acknowledgement of shortcomings from a senior figure who helped establish the governing party and remained influential throughout its years in power.

Stay up-to-date: Orbán speaks out on political comeback and Fidesz’s future in opposition

Kövér cautious about Orbán’s future

The former Speaker also addressed the future role of Viktor Orbán, Fidesz’s long-time leader, in shaping Hungary’s political right. Kövér urged caution over speculation about Orbán becoming prime ministerial candidate again in 2030. He argued that Orbán’s intention to remain influential on the right did not necessarily mean he planned to seek the premiership.

“I do not think he himself believes he has put himself forward as a candidate for prime minister,” Kövér said, adding that the question remained a long way off. Orbán’s future political options have also become a subject of debate following changes to Hungary’s constitution, according to the reports.

Kövér’s remarks come as Fidesz faces the challenge of assessing why it lost power after more than a decade and a half in office. His criticism of education and the party’s engagement with younger voters suggests that at least some prominent figures within its ranks recognise the need to examine its record. The interview with László Kövér can be watched below:

Read also: Former Budapest mayor makes striking claims about Orbán and corruption

World.title: Ryanair boss warns of record airfare increases in 2027 – Tickets could cost 20% more
World.content:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary expects airfares to rise by as much as 20% next year as soaring fuel costs put pressure on airlines. The warning comes amid continuing conflict in the Middle East and growing concerns about the future of European air travel.

Passengers could face the biggest increase in airfares in European history over the next 12 months, according to Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary. Speaking at a press conference in Brussels on Tuesday, he warned that ticket prices could climb by up to 20% in 2027 as airlines struggle with rising fuel costs.

The budget airline boss attributed the expected increase partly to the ongoing war in the Middle East, which has pushed oil prices higher and increased pressure on carriers to pass additional costs on to customers.

“I think you’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares in European history over the next 12 months,” O’Leary said, according to Bloomberg. He added that even such substantial price rises might not be enough to cover dramatically higher fuel costs.

Have you heard? Ryanair announced 29 new summer 2027 routes, including Budapest connection to UK

Why could flights become more expensive?

Fuel is one of the airline industry’s biggest operating expenses, making carriers particularly vulnerable to sharp oil price increases. According to O’Leary, Ryanair has secured part of its fuel supply for 2026 at around USD 67 per barrel, providing some protection against market fluctuations.

However, that protection is expected to weaken as existing agreements expire. O’Leary warned that fuel costs could potentially double in 2027, putting further pressure on airlines’ finances. Ryanair does not plan to introduce a separate fuel surcharge, he said, but passengers could still pay significantly more for tickets as higher operating costs feed through into fares.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Ryanair has already warned of airline failures

Europe’s largest low-cost airline warned in September that airfares could rise sharply in 2027 if oil prices remained elevated. It also cautioned that some airlines could go bankrupt under sustained cost pressure. Ryanair has already lowered its passenger traffic target for the financial year ending in March, reflecting concerns about the challenging operating environment.

European aviation faces further pressure

O’Leary has also criticised EU environmental taxes and regulations, arguing that they put European airlines at a disadvantage compared with competitors in the United States and Asia.

In Belgium, Ryanair announced plans to discontinue 20 routes during the winter season and reduce the number of available seats on flights departing the country by one million. The airline cited the Belgian government’s decision to increase its air travel tax by EUR 2 to EUR 7 per ticket.

O’Leary said Ryanair would move aircraft to markets offering more competitive operating conditions, describing Belgium and France as uncompetitive and Germany as particularly challenging.

World.title: Albania’s Students Demand the Fall of Rama and an End to Corruption
World.content:
In a meeting with the heads of educational institutions on Tuesday, Prime Minister Edi Rama said that the ongoing student protests that began as an expression of public discontent, had turned into an organised attempt to destabilise the country and hinder the EU integration process. He warned that he will respond to the protests with a new package of penal and administrative sanctions.

After the meeting, he published a video on Facebook that showed him placing a sign with the word “Dialogue” and 12 red chairs at the entrance to the Prime Minister's Office, indicating an offer to talk.

Jesmina Senga, a student involved in the protests, responded with the comment: “In your dreams.”

According to Senga, "Rama never meant his request to engage in dialogue. His invitation is not sincere. He is responding to the pressure of the international community to ask the protesters for dialogue and to present himself as willing to change.”

World.title: Leader of Kosovo Opposition Party PDK Steps Down
World.content:
PDK leader Bedri Hamza. Photo: BIRN.

The head of the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) Bedri Hamza, announced on Wednesday he is stepping down from the role he took less than a year ago.

Hamza said that the decision to step down opens the way for an internal election process in which party members should decide about the future leadership. He suggested a greater role for youth in the process.

“Every leader must know when it is time to pave the way for a new phase. I just finished the presidency meeting and today I have irrevocably resigned from the position of leader of the Democratic Party of Kosovo,” he said. PDK is the largest opposition party in Kosovo currently.

“I am not leaving the PDK. I am only leaving the position of chairman, but not from the belief in our political values. As long as I live, I will be a loyal PDK voter and a member of this great political family,” he said.

Hamza’s resignation comes five weeks after a Hague-based war crimes court convicted Hashim Thaci and Kadri Veseli, two previous PDK leaders, of war crimes and sentenced them to 25 and 18 years of imprisonment, respectively.

The PDK emerged from the senior ranks of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) following the end of the 1998-1999 war in Kosovo. For years it was led by Hashim Thaci, the KLA’s wartime political director.

It first took power in 2007 and oversaw Kosovo’s declaration of independence from Serbia the following year.

When Thaci became president of Kosovo in 2016, the leadership of the party passed to Kadri Veseli, who previously led the shadowy Kosovo Intelligence Service (SHIK).

After 12 years in power, the PDK slipped into third place in terms of parliamentary seats in elections in 2019. In the June elections this year, it won 22 out of 120 seats in the assembly, far behind the ruling party Vetevendosje of Prime Minister Albin Kurti, which won 53 seats.

World.title: Kosovo Court Sentences Serb for War Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Milorad Djokovic at the Pristina Basic Court, October 21, 2026. Photo: BIRN

On Wednesday, the Pristina Basic Court found Kosovo Serb Milorad Djokovic guilty of war crimes during the war in Kosovo. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

Djokovic was found guilty of having been involved in murders, raids, beatings, arrests, torture and inhumane and cruel treatment of ethnic Albanian civilians in the village of Ozdrim in the western municipality of Peja/Pec, during the 1998-1999 war in Kosovo.

According to the prosecution, Djokovic was part of the Serbian armed forces that surrounded and attacked Ozdrim in May 1999.

“The village was surrounded and then attacked from three directions by Serb military and police forces. Six Albanian civilians were killed and three others were wounded during these actions,” the indictment said. The remains of five of the people who were killed have not been found.

“Those three wounded people were sent to Peja/Pec hospital and then executed and buried in the village of Lutogllave,” the indictment said.

According to the indictment, the armed group that included Djokovic arrested around 40 civilians. Twelve of them were released after three days “deprived of food and water and suffering torture”, while 28 others were sent to Peja/Pec prison and then transferred to Leskovac prison in Serbia after the war.

They were released after the intervention of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the indictment said.

After the verdict, Halit Gashi, one of the damaged parties in this case told media that “no sentence can bring back the lives of those who were unjustly taken”.

“I don’t know what kind of sentence this is. It’s ridiculous,” Gashi added.

Djokovic had pleaded not guilty in July 2023.

His arrest in 2022 sparked angry reactions from the Serbian government, which claimed that it was an example of the intimidation of Serbs in Kosovo.

World.title: Serbians Abroad Organize to Vote Amid Obstacles
World.content:
With polling stations few and far between, Serbians abroad are joining solidarity networks to arrange rides and accommodation, while some face voting in the middle of the night.

“Everything is done on a voluntary basis. People who have often never met before are now opening their homes to one another, picking people up at airports and helping them get to the polling station,” Duska Vujovic from Toronto told BIRN.

Canada has only two polling stations, in Toronto and Ottawa, forcing some voters to travel thousands of kilometres.

“Those travelling the furthest are coming from Vancouver and Victoria, covering approximately 4,000 kilometres each way. The journey also involves crossing several time zones,” Vujovic said.

Despite Serbian diplomatic and consular missions in western Canada, no stations were opened in Vancouver or Calgary, although more than 800 people had registered in Vancouver. Toronto-based volunteers are providing accommodation and transport.

In Italy and Spain, voters are using Facebook groups to organise shared journeys and accommodation. Many are also turning to VoteBnB, a platform whose creators reported 1,343 accommodation offers and 742 people offering rides.

The creators told BIRN the idea emerged after Serbs abroad learned they could not vote locally. A prototype was online by 3am, and hundreds signed up within days. More than 30 cities now have local organisers coordinating transport and accommodation, they said, describing the initiative as part of efforts to reverse Serbia’s democratic backsliding under Aleksandar Vucic.

Serbia’s authorities approved just 93 polling stations abroad, amid criticism that the network is inadequate for the number of registered voters. Sunday’s election pits Vucic’s ruling Serbian Progressive Party against opposition forces led by students, whose movement has become a major challenge to its long-standing dominance.

In Australia, voters from Brisbane are preparing to travel about 900 kilometres to Sydney by minibus, car or plane after the Serbian Electoral Commission (RIK) declined to open stations in several cities.

Nemanja Djurovic, a Serb living on the Gold Coast, said 130 people registered in Brisbane had contacted his group and expressed support for the student movement.

“People are furious, and everyone who could possibly take a day off work decided they didn’t care how much the ticket would cost,” he told BIRN. “We specifically want to travel by bus to send a message. We can’t exactly cycle or walk like the students have been doing, but through this journey, we want to join their fight.”

In France, voters from Toulouse, where 107 people registered but no station was opened, have arranged a minibus and shared cars to Paris. Another group from Montpellier has hired a minibus, while some travellers will collect students from Bordeaux en route.

Milena Mihajlovic, a member of an informal citizens’ group in Toulouse, told BIRN that organisers in Paris had arranged free accommodation for those needing it. Although not everyone who registered can make the journey, she said, turnout was expected to be high.

In California, US, where only one polling station was opened in Los Angeles, voters are also organising shared rides and accommodation. Milos Milenkovic, a Serbian citizen in San Francisco, told BIRN that organisers had recorded around 680 registrations across the state, while about 50 Los Angeles residents had offered their homes to travelling voters.

Voting in Los Angeles is scheduled from 11pm on October 24 until noon the following day, local time.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Kremlin Clings to Balkan Buddies Dodik and Vucic
World.content:
Over the past four and a half years, Russia’s war against Ukraine has devoured an immense number of human lives and resources but failed to lessen the Kremlin’s determination to pursue its aggressive tactics in hope of an eventual triumph. Vexed by the protracted stalemate at the front, Moscow is now annihilating Ukraine’s economic capacity with massive daily bombings. It has also embarked on a sabotage campaign in Europe to try to frighten Europeans into ending their assistance to Kyiv.

Now, as if being rewarded for its obduracy, Russia has scored a major diplomatic victory with the US. with Donald Trump’s administration temporarily suspending sanctions on Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down fuel prices ahead of US mid-term elections.

In the Balkans, the resilience of Moscow’s influence is also in evidence. Despite numerous setbacks in recent years, Russia is still eager to assist its local allies and ready to resort to intelligence operations in order to sabotage the region’s integration into the EU and NATO.

World.title: NATO’s ‘False Solidarity’: Fico Says Neutrality Would Better Suit Slovakia
World.content:
‘An invitation to Moscow’

Yet Fico’s comments could still have damaging effects in the real world and have been criticised both from within the governing camp in Slovakia as well as from the opposition and figures elsewhere in the region.

President Pellegrini, who was once the leader of the coalition Hlas party, said he accepted only one interpretation of the prime minister’s remarks: NATO members should avoid provoking Russia and risking an attack on an alliance country. “I do not accept any other interpretation and would reject it,” Pellegrini said, adding that Slovakia could not suggest it might stand aside during a conflict.

Parliamentary speaker Richard Rasi, from Pellegrini’s Hlas party, warned against treating collective-defence commitments as merely formal. “If we were to describe this commitment as merely formal or unenforceable, we would also have to accept that our allies might one day take the same position towards us,” he said.

Opposition politicians also inevitably criticised Fico. Progressive Slovakia leader Michal Simecka accused him of questioning the basic pillar of the country’s defence. Ivan Korcok, a former foreign minister, warned that publicly undermining confidence in NATO amounted to sending Moscow “an invitation”.

“If someone wanted to attack Slovakia, they know that they would not be facing a country of 5 million, but the strongest alliance in the world,” Korcok said.

Christian Democrat deputy leader Viliam Karas rejected neutrality as a realistic alternative, arguing that Slovakia lacked both the military strength and financial resources to defend itself independently.

“Whoever questions our readiness to help our allies also weakens their willingness to help us,” Karas said. “One day we may be the ones who need Article 5.”

The controversy also reached Prague. Czech President Petr Pavel, a former chairman of NATO’s Military Committee, called them “extremely serious” and warned against questioning solidarity between allies. It was not their first clash: the two have previously disagreed publicly over Russia’s war against Ukraine and how the conflict should be described.

Fico responded that Pavel, a former NATO general, “would like to fight”, while he preferred peace. Pavel said he had heard the same argument before, that a general wants war while others want peace, during the 2023 Czech presidential campaign.

Former Czech foreign minister Jan Lipavsky pointed to what Czech forces are already doing for Slovakia. Czech soldiers are serving in the country, while Czech aircraft have helped protect Slovak airspace. If Fico questions military assistance between allies, Lipavsky asked, why should the Czechs help defend Slovakia?

Prime Minister Andrej Babis said the Czech Republic was preparing to deploy two mechanised brigades if Russia attacked a Baltic NATO member. He had previously said Prague would respect Article 5, while declining to comment on Fico’s remarks.

Germany added its voice on September 29, when Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Bratislava for talks with his Slovak counterpart, Juraj Blanar.

“The greatest threat to freedom on our continent comes from Moscow. The greatest danger to Europe is Putin’s belligerent imperialism,” Wadephul said. “Questioning these facts is not only lacking in solidarity, but it would also be irresponsible.”

Wadephul warned that countries casting doubt on NATO’s collective deterrence put themselves at risk and weakened security guarantees for other alliance members.

Security analyst Radovan Branik says Fico is technically correct about Article 5’s obligations: the clause does not automatically require every NATO member to deploy combat troops when another member is attacked and governments can provide different forms of assistance according to capabilities and circumstances. “On the facts, he is right,” Branik says.

His concern is how Fico’s statements affect deterrence. A potential aggressor cannot know in advance precisely how NATO members would respond to an attack. Branik argues that publicly discussing limits on Slovakia’s possible involvement could weaken that uncertainty.

Retired Slovak general Pavel Macko also questions how Slovakia could defend itself without allied guarantees. With roughly 16,000 soldiers, he argues, the country could not defend even one major city alone against a large-scale attack.

Macko rejects neutrality as a guarantee of security, citing Belgium, whose neutral status failed to prevent German invasions during the world wars.

“Not every country has the same capabilities,” he says, pointing to Iceland, which has no standing army, and Luxembourg, whose armed forces are small. “It is still one for all and all for one, but everyone within their capabilities.”

Macko says Slovakia could restrict how its troops are deployed under NATO command, but limiting them to Slovak territory would be deeply at odds with allied solidarity.

Practical constraints remain, too: Slovakia still lacks the fully capable heavy mechanised brigade NATO expects under its force requirements. According to Macko, it may not be ready until 2035 or later.

Pavel Havlicek of the Prague-based Association for International Affairs (AMO) argues that Slovakia lacks the military capacity to repel a major Russian attack independently. Even a war that did not reach Slovak territory would bring refugees, inflation and economic disruption, he says.

Branik also questions who would determine whether a NATO member had “provoked” Russia, as Fico suggests. He noted that Moscow has already characterised Slovak arms production as provocative.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also recently raised concerns about the credibility of Article 5. Citing intelligence assessments, he warned that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against NATO countries on its eastern flank, cause damage and then portray the incidents as accidents rather than deliberate attacks.

He argued that such incidents could weaken NATO’s willingness to respond collectively and undermine confidence in its defence commitments. The aim would be to convince alliance members that Article 5 is “more theoretical than practical”, while giving politicians an excuse to argue that their countries should not have to fight for allies such as Latvia or Lithuania.

That confidence in Western hesitation was on display in a recent BBC interview with Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia’s Council for Foreign and Defence Policy. Asked whether Europe would retaliate against a Russian nuclear strike, Karaganov dismissed the possibility. “No, there will be no response from Europe,” he said, expressing confidence that neither the UK nor the US would risk nuclear retaliation.

Fico may have his own political reasons for questioning NATO solidarity, but his remarks give Moscow further reason to believe its strategy is working.

World.title: Trump Associates Attended Rally for Bosnian Serb Nationalist Party
World.content:
On October 6, two days after the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the New York Times reported that two Trump associates had been paid for a pre-election engagement in Republika Srpska. This paid trip came as electoral campaigns are in full swing for US elections in November.

The US media has since published more stories on this trip.

The New York Times later confirmed that at least six US advisers close to Trump had travelled to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The sources the reporting relied on claimed that Blair and LaCivita did not do work for SNSD and only worked for the government of Republika Srpska, which has paid lobbyists and consultants close to Trump and the Republican Party more than four million dollars since the beginning of last year.

According to the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) register, the lobbying firm Continental Strategy was paid almost 240,000 dollars from the Republika Srpska budget between February and the end of August.

The New York Times reported that Blair and LaCivita were each paid several hundred thousand dollars by the law firm Boies Schiller Flexner, which represents Republika Srpska. Smith also works at the law firm and was reportedly hired by the Republika Srpska government, which the New York Times wrote is “essentially one and the same” with the party that controls it.

The arrival of Trump’s advisers in Republika Srpska drew criticism from members of the Republican Party, with some officials criticising the president’s advisers for spending time making money from foreign consulting instead of devoting themselves to the Republican electoral campaign in the US.

Trump said that Blair and LaCivita do not work directly for him and that there is no obstacle to them being paid by others for their services as his outside advisers.

On October 7, Trump wrote on his social network Truth Social that he had no idea who else they worked for but would ask them: “If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

Later the same day, answering questions from the media, Trump said the two advisers were independent and that he did not think there was a conflict of interest.

“If I thought they had a conflict here, I would terminate,” Trump said.

Previous reporting in the US and Bosnia and Herzegovina relied on unnamed sources for the advisers’ trip to Republika Srpska. Of the firms involved, only Continental Strategy confirmed that its partner, Alex Garcia, was in Republika Srpska on October 4, election day.

In footage from local televisions stations and in photographs published by the SNSD from the Borik Hall rally, Garcia can be seen standing behind Dodik.

According to American media, Garcia is a partner at the lobbying firm Continental Strategy. Katie Wiles, the daughter of Trump’s current chief of staff Susie Wiles, also works for the firm.

Garcia did not immediately respond to a request from BIRN for comment.

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Continental Strategy, told The New York Times that the firm “meticulously complies with every ethical and legal requirement.” According to the newspaper, it was Garcia who recommended Blair and LaCivita to the government of Republika Srpska.

Asked by the online media outlet Semafor whether Continental Strategy had helped organise Blair and LaCivita’s trip, a spokesperson for the firm replied that Garcia was the only employee in Republika Srpska on October 4 and the only one who lobbies the US government on the firm’s behalf.

Citing three sources, Semafor reported that Continental Strategy had helped organise the trip. After publication, Stone said this information was incorrect.

None of the advisers answered BIRN’s question as to whether, apart from attending the party rally, they had advised the SNSD while being paid from the entity’s budget.

According to Transparency International’s Korajlic, “All this lobbying that Dodik financed from the budget, and which was actually for his personal interests – lifting sanctions and everything else – is questionable, but none of our institutions will deal with it.”

In mid-September, a few weeks before the elections, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina banned all payments from the Republika Srpska budget related to a consulting services contract concluded between the Republika Srpska representation office in Vienna and the company Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.

The ban also applies to other lobbying activities whose aims are contrary to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the decisions of the Constitutional Court and the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

State prosecutors had earlier decided not to open an investigation into a complaint about payments made through the Vienna office for lobbying for Republika Srpska’s independence.

Trump associates rally for Dodik

World.title: Journalists Targeted in Row over Croatian Football Fans’ Nazi Slogans
World.content:
The march by Torcida members in Split on October 15. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook.

Ivan Penava, president of the far-right political party Homeland Movement, which is part of Croatia’s governing coalition, held a press conference on Tuesday to denounce what he called a “political and media witch-hunt” against members of Torcida, a hardcore fan group supporting Hajduk Split football club.

Penava’s remarks came after members of Torcida chanted pro-Nazi and anti-Semitic slogans such as “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf” during a street march prior to a Hajduk Split match against the Dutch club Ajax.

Police identified 23 individuals suspected of publicly inciting violence and hatred; several were arrested and six remain in custody.

After the incident was reported, Torcida accused journalists of exaggerating it.

“From a fan fight with Ajax fans, with the selfless help of the media, you have created a first-class national scandal,” the group said.

Torcida published portraits of 12 journalists, presenting them in a format resembling wanted posters, accompanied by the caption: “Croatia has already seen all sorts of wonders, but it hasn’t found enough rope for so many Judases.” The group also posted a photograph of a banner reading “Worm Journalists” on its Facebook page.

The Croatian Journalists’ Association, HND called on the police and the State Attorney’s Office to respond, while the international media freedom organisation SafeJournalists urged the Croatian authorities to provide urgent protection to the threatened journalists and to prosecute those responsible.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who heads the ruling Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, also voiced support.

“We always stand up for journalists. We don’t have to agree with their views, comments or even with what is sometimes an undisguised bias; regardless, we still stand up for them,” Plenkovic said on Monday.

However, Homeland Movement leader Penava, whose party is in coalition with Plenkovic’s HDZ, strongly criticised the Interior Ministry and the media for publishing photographs of suspects who are being sought by the police.

While condemning the pro-Nazi chants during the supporters’ march, Penava claimed that the Interior Ministry “decided to pump up this topic”.

Interior Minister Davor Bozinovic, when asked about Penava’s remarks on Tuesday, said there was nothing unusual about the publication of photographs of wanted suspects.

“When the police are searching for someone and have a photograph, they release it. If they don’t have a photograph, they might release a composite sketch instead,” Bozinovic explained, adding that such procedures were prescribed by the Law on Police Affairs.

“Photographs of all suspects were not released – only those of individuals who are being sought, or who are on the run or in hiding,” Bozinovic said.

World.title: Croatia is the Leading Camping Destination by Quality in Europe for 2027
World.content:
October the 21st, 2026 – Croatia is the leading camping destination in terms of quality in Europe for 2027, following very significant improvement and offer diversity.

Croatian camping has significantly improved the quality and diversity of its accommodation offer, facilities and services over the past two decades, further strengthening its position on the European tourism market. Continued investment in quality, adaptation to market changes and responding to increasingly demanding guest expectations are key to the further development of the sector. Glas Istre/The Voice of Istria reports that these are the main topics of the jubilee 20th Croatian Camping Congress, organised by the Croatian Camping Association (KUH), taking place from the 19th to the 21st of October at the Well Hotel in Terme Tuhelj.

“This is a fantastic day for Croatian camping and the realisation of the dreams of all tourism workers who have worked for years to make Croatian camping the best in Europe in terms of quality. Recent research by PiNCAMP, the camping platform within ADAC, confirms that Croatia has become the leading camping destination by quality, which we can all be very proud of. This is an additional incentive for the further development of Croatian camping, and at the same time confirmation that investments, especially over the last ten years or so, pay off and that guests recognise them. Further development will also depend on the legal framework regulating camping activities in the areas of spatial planning, maritime domain and the sea, and tourism. We expect that conditions and frameworks will be defined in all three areas that will enable further investments. Without new investments there is no raising of quality, and I believe that in the coming years we will see an additional flourishing of Croatian camping and a new rise, especially thanks to the positioning of Croatia as the highest-quality camping destination in Europe,” emphasised Veljko Ostojić, President of the KUH Executive Board and Director of the Croatian Tourism Association.

croatia leads the european ranking

According to the announcement by PiNCAMP, the camping portal of ADAC (the largest German and European and the second-largest automobile club in the world), Croatia will for the first time lead the European ranking of campsite quality in 2027, while the number of Croatian campsites with the ADAC Superplatz label is rising to 29. ADAC PiNCAMP expects continued strong demand from the German and Dutch markets for the next season. How to maintain competitiveness on the European market and create conditions for sustainable growth of the sector is one of the key questions of this year’s Croatian Camping Congress.

“The next step in the development of Croatian camping is not only accommodation, but the complete quality of the stay – from the pitch, sanitary facilities and shade to service and facilities that give the guest a reason to come even outside the summer season. It is important to preserve the diversity of the offer, from places for tents and campers to mobile homes, as well as small family campsites and large resorts. Research should help us direct investments towards specific groups of guests, and technology should facilitate reservations and leave employees more time for the guest. For such development, professional people and clear, predictable business conditions are equally important,” said Adriano Palman, Director of the Croatian Camping Association.

These changes are particularly visible in the development of accommodation quality. According to data from the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, in 2007 Croatia had 13 four-star campsites, while there were no five-star campsites. By 2025 the number of four-star campsites had risen to 82, and nine had entered the five-star category. Thus, as many as 58% of the capacity of Croatian campsites falls into the 4- and 5-star category. This development reflects continuous investments in infrastructure, improvement of the existing offer and development of facilities, with which Croatian camping responds to the increasingly demanding expectations of guests.

a huge transformation over the last two decades

“The camping industry has transformed significantly over the last 20 years. Today, 50 percent of Croatian campsites have four or five stars, and they account for 20 percent of all overnight stays in Croatia. The level of their quality is also confirmed by guest loyalty, as shown by the latest research. As many as 50 percent of guests have returned to Croatian campsites seven or more times, which speaks of the competitiveness of this tourism segment,” emphasised Monika Udovičić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport.

From 1 January to 11 October 2026, Croatian campsites recorded almost 3.4 million arrivals and 21.4 million overnight stays, maintaining results at the level of the same period last year, which was a record year in the history of Croatian camping. Germany, Slovenia and Austria remain the leading markets, with more than 60 percent of total overnight stays in campsites, while domestic guests recorded 9.7 percent more overnight stays than in the comparable period last year. The importance of camping for Croatian tourism is confirmed by its 23 percent share of overnight stays in commercial accommodation, with an average stay of 6.2 days – the longest among all types of accommodation.

The continuation of the programme also includes European examples of campsite adaptation to climate change, from the arrangement of green areas and creation of shade to infrastructure adaptation. Business topics cover the development and retention of employees, energy efficiency, and a review of ten years of online reservations in Croatian campsites.

continued investment in the camping sector

A special part of the programme also opens the question of how Croatian campsites present themselves to guests through artificial intelligence. The research covered four leading AI assistants that were asked 100 questions about Croatian campsites on five source markets, with almost 2,000 answers analysed and the accuracy of the claims made and sources used verified. The results provide insight into the reliability of the information that potential guests receive and the opportunities for campsites to improve their visibility and the availability of accurate data in the digital environment.

The professional programme is accompanied by an exhibition of mobile homes, glamping tents, equipment and digital solutions for campsites. The Congress thus connects research and exchange of experience with a concrete offer for investment and business improvement. From the first edition in 2007 to last year’s Congress, around 5,200 participants from Croatia and abroad have taken part in these gatherings. As the central meeting place for representatives of campsites, the tourism sector, institutions and related industries, the Congress encourages the exchange of experience, presentation of innovations and discussion of trends and challenges that shape the future of camping.

The jubilee Congress ends tomorrow with the presentation of the Croatia’s Best Campsites and OK Mini Camps awards, as well as the Naj Kamp Adria 2026 award, which recognise the quality and development of the camping offer.

World.title: SafeJournalists Demands Official Croatian Reaction After Threats to Media
World.content:
October the 21s5, 2026 – The organisation SafeJournalists is currently demanding an official Croatian reaction after imagery of hanged journalists and other threats to the media have come to light.

Extreme condemnation of morbid threats made against journalists in Croatia have come from the international SafeJournalists network following their reporting on Nazi and antisemitic outbursts by Torcida members in Split, Morski reports. Specifically, the organisation has warned about the publication of journalists’ photographs, calls for their liquidation, and banners depicting hanged journalists from Croatian media.

They demand urgent protection of the threatened journalists from the Croatian authorities and prosecution of those responsible. SafeJournalists warns that a campaign of intimidation against journalists has since begun, with them being accused of creating hysteria and conducting a campaign against Torcida. Today, Interior Minister Davor Božinović himself spoke out, saying that the police have launched an investigation into messages aimed at intimidating journalists while they perform their work.

“I have some information about this, the police has launched a criminal investigation precisely because of inscriptions intended to intimidate journalists,” Minister Božinović said before the HDZ Presidency session. “No one has any authority to frighten or intimidate anyone in this country, especially not those who are merely doing their job,” the minister and Deputy Prime Minister stated.

On the 18th of October, the Facebook page Narodni reporteri published photographs of 11 Croatian journalists and one political analyst under the title “12 horsemen of the Croatian apocalypse.” According to SafeJournalists, some commenters called for the journalists to be expelled from Croatia and banned from working, while others suggested finding their home addresses, expressed a desire for their death, or mentioned compiling a liquidation list. The next day, the 19th of October, photos of new threatening messages appeared in the Facebook group Torcida Split 1950.

On one wall in Dalmatia, the following message was written: “Torcida remembers and does not forgive! Journalists are worms.” Particularly disturbing was a banner on which journalists were called “the greatest evil of Croatian society.” The banner showed a tree with hanged journalists from Slobodna Dalmacija, Index, Jutarnji list, Večernji list and 24sata.

The SafeJournalists network expressed particular concern about the political messages accompanying the incidents. They singled out a press conference that Domovinski pokret president Ivan Penava held today in Split. Penava condemned Nazi and fascist chants, but at the same time accused the police and the media of conducting a campaign against Torcida. He also questioned the publication of photographs of suspects sought by the police and criticised the Croatian Journalists’ Association for its warnings about threats against journalists.

SafeJournalists considers that such political rhetoric further worsens the atmosphere in which journalists are exposed to intimidation.

World.title: Vrsar Attracts Visitors from Around the World
World.content:
October the 21st, 2026 – Vrsar has done exceptionally well in attracting visitors from around the world this year. Tourists from 74 countries descended on the Istrian settlement in 2026.

From distant countries like Japan and Australia to Brazil, New Zealand and South Africa, this year, Vrsar attracted guests from as many as 74 countries around the world. As Istra Terra Magica writes, although at first glance it is a small Istrian destination, the tourist figures reveal its significant international reach: The growth in tourist traffic, especially during the months of May and September, follows the development of Vrsar’s multi-layered tourist offer, which is based on the natural and cultural heritage, tradition and local particularities of the destination.

vrsar’s investment in what it offers the world pays off in 2026

Over the first nine months of this year, Vrsar was visited by guests from 74 countries of the world, including those from Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Brazil and South Africa. At the same time almost 260 thousand arrivals and 1.84 million overnight stays were recorded, i.e. 4 percent more arrivals and 5 percent more overnight stays than in the same period last year. Behind these figures stands a destination that has for years been developing its tourist offer on the foundations of what makes Vrsar special, from the sea and the coast, through sculptural creativity, to the Kontija forest, the Lim Bay and local food and wine scene.

The multi-layered nature of the offer is precisely one of Vrsar’s special strengths. Guests who come for the sea and a holiday here have the opportunity to see, hear, learn and experience much more. What today constitutes Vrsar’s tourist offer stems from what the destination is and what it has been throughout its history. Its natural and cultural particularities, local stories and tradition have over the years received new content and become part of the tourist experience. Such an offer did not arise by chance, but is developing through long-term work, investment and the linking of the destination’s values with experiences that enrich the stay of guests.

The results achieved outside the peak of the summer season are particularly encouraging. In May 20 percent more arrivals and 32 percent more overnight stays were recorded, while September brought growth of 8 percent in both indicators. These results are important in the context of the development of content that gives guests additional reasons to come and stay in Vrsar outside the main summer months as well.

great traffic outside of the summer season

“We’re particularly pleased that we are recording good results outside the main summer months as well. We are developing content because of which guests can discover Vrsar in different parts of the year, and at the same time it is important to us what value tourism creates for the destination. That is why we look at the results through the total number of arrivals and overnight stays, their distribution throughout the year, the length of stay and the motives for which guests choose Vrsar,” emphasises Dr. Sc. Klara Trošt Lesić, director of the Tourist Board of the Municipality of Vrsar.

Germany, Slovenia, Austria and Italy remain the most important source markets for Vrsar, with almost 71 percent of all arrivals. At the same time, the fact that the destination was visited by guests from a total of 74 countries speaks of its international reach, which extends far beyond the traditional European markets, even though arrivals from more distant markets are of considerably smaller volume.

Germany remains the most important individual market with almost 740 thousand overnight stays, or about 40 percent of total overnight stays, with growth of 7.5 percent compared to last year. Among the four leading markets, Italy records the largest growth, with about ten percent more arrivals and overnight stays.

One of the most important foundations of Vrsar’s tourist offer remains camping. In the wider Vrsar area’s campsites, more than 1.34 million overnight stays were recorded by the end of September, or almost three quarters of all tourist overnight stays in the destination. The developed camping offer and Vrsar’s location provide guests with the opportunity to explore the wider region, while the multi-layered nature of local content further enriches their stay.

World.title: Velebit Positioned as a Sustainable Tourist Destination
World.content:
October the 21st, 2026 – A project involving cross-border cooperation has seen Velebit positioned as a sustainable tourist destination.

For the Croatian people, the mighty Velebit has always been much more than a rocky mountain rich in flora and fauna and hidden endemics. Marin Smolcic reports for Novi list that this mountain range’s imposing slopes are packed with speleological formations, many of which will never be accessible to human eyes. Apart from hiking enthusiasts, only a few have the privilege of being part of this mythical mountain.

The Public Institution Nature Park Velebit, within the framework of the REVERS project, held a two-day event on the 30th of September and the 1st of October entitled “From Protected Nature to a Sustainable Tourist Experience”. The programme included an international round table at the Cerovačke Caves Centre of Excellence in Gračac and a field tour of the Majstorska cesta (Master’s Road), Tulove grede and the area of the Zrmanja River.

The project was also presented at the “Autumn in Lika” fair in Gospić. This time the event brought together representatives of the public, private and civil sectors from across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro who work in the fields of nature protection, management of protected areas, tourism, local and regional development and science.

During both days, 30 participants took part each day, which opened space for the exchange of experiences and joint reflection on solutions for the sustainable management of protected areas. There is still a lot of work ahead for the organisers of this project because proud Velebit does not reveal its secrets all at once. This is best known by hikers who, during frequent ascents to the same peak, each time discover a new path, spring or viewpoint of a mountain that is too rich and diverse for us to “consume” it visually at first sight.

World.title: Changes to Dentistry Under Croatian Health Insurance Fund
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – There are changes to certain aspects of dentistry within the scope of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, with white fillings being part of the shakeup.

Instead of the previous amalgam fillings, the installation of white fillings at the expense of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) has been announced, even when they aren’t going to be placed on the front teeth. Poslovni reports that amalgam fillings entered history on the 1st of July, unless a dentist assesses that such a filling is necessary due to the patient’s particular health needs. This measure was introduced in Croatia on the basis of an EU regulation.

dentists are still charging…

In practice, however, the matter is somewhat different: the use of a white filling still comes with a cost if the patient wants a white composite filling of the kind that, according to HZZO rules, they should receive free of charge on their front teeth. The dentist will most often not offer a choice, but will allegedly place a composite filling and then charge the patient for it. Anyone who wants a free white filling must request it, but must also inform themselves beforehand, because each of the materials used has its own characteristics. We received information that the free white filling visually completely differs from the tooth base and looks “like cement”.

These are glass-ionomer and hybrid glass-ionomer cements, which have good characteristics for replacing the former amalgam fillings, but cannot match composite white fillings. Research in European countries where these materials have been used for about 20 years shows that the disadvantages of glass-ionomers are more frequent chipping, limited resistance to abrasion and erosion, and strength below the values for composite. Persons who had such fillings installed had a higher rate of fractures and abrasions of the fillings than with composites, as well as colour deviations.

economic status and purchasing power in dental medicine

“The key problem is the fact that white fillings do not cover all the indications in which amalgam can be used,” emphasises Irma Šavorić, president of the Association of Contracted Doctors of Dental Medicine MODDUS HR. This means that the choice of material should not be only a matter of aesthetics but also of the concrete clinical situation.

“Indications are key, and problems usually arise when something is not in a specific indication,” Šavorić states. Patients, she says, as a rule do not come with a request for a particular type of filling, but make the decision in conversation with the dentist. In this, the patient’s economic status, i.e. purchasing power, can play a role, especially when there is a choice between a filling covered by insurance and one that requires additional payment. The fact that a certain material is more expensive does not automatically mean that it is more suitable for every situation, this doctor of dental medicine explains.

“Materials have different characteristics and limitations, so the choice should primarily depend on the indication,” she concludes. The price of 30 to 80 euros per tooth will be important for a considerable part of citizens when deciding between the two types of white filling.

the right to free composite fillings until you’re 18

The right to a free composite filling for all teeth, regardless of which tooth is involved, is now held in Croatia by children up to 18 years of age, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. For all other citizens who do not want to pay extra for such fillings, the health insurance fund will, according to the announcement of the Ministry of Health, secure from 10 to 12 million euros annually.

The MODDUS HR Association was founded in order to clearly define issues related to materials, indications, financing and the position of dentists who work in different models of dental healthcare. From the HZZO they are requesting a correction of the financing model, warning that the existing model could lead to longer waiting times for patients and reduced availability of certain services.

World.title: HŽ to Invest €7.4 Million – Here Are the Croatian Cities Covered
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – HŽ is set to invest a fortune in the country’s future railway plans, with multiple Croatian cities covered by the plans.

HŽ Passenger Transport has issued a tender estimated to stand at a whopping €7.4 million excluding VAT for the arrangement and modernisation of six workshops for the maintenance of trains across the country. Poslovni reports that more specifically speaking, these will be located in Vinkovci, Solin, Osijek, Pula and Varaždin. The tender was published on Monday in the Electronic Public Procurement Notice, and offers can be submitted until the 26th of November.

According to the tender documentation, the most money is planned for Solin, where two workshops will be arranged for €2.73 million. For Osijek the estimate is €1.59 million, Varaždin €1.48 million, Vinkovci €998,000, and for Pula €606,000. At all those locations construction, electrical and mechanical works are planned, as well as the procurement and installation of equipment for the maintenance of trains.

For example, for one of the Solin workshops the project states that it is in poor condition and that it needs to be adapted for the maintenance of existing and new trains. Therefore inspection channels for examining trains from below and a platform for inspecting equipment on the roof will be made in it, and the roof, floor and lighting will also be renewed.

The works will be carried out gradually, beginning in January 2027 and continuing until January 2028, and at each workshop they should last 119 days. First in line are Vinkovci, which will take place from the 12th of January to the 10th of May 2027, and the final one is Varaždin, where the works should finish on the 3rd of January 2028, should all go as planned.

The deadlines have (at least according to the documentation) been set so that too many workshops don’t end up being closed at the same time and so that trains can be regularly maintained even during the works. Completed parts of the halls can be returned to use after they pass expert supervision. The most advantageous offer will be selected according to price and quality, and one of the criteria is also the length of the warranty period, which must not be shorter than two years. Bidders can compete for one, several or all locations.

World.title: Croatia Lagging Further and Further Behind on Innovation Ranking
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – Despite being the home of many successful startups, Croatia keeps on lagging further and further behind on the innovation ranking.

Croatia has unfortunately fallen six places on the Global Innovation Index ranking for 2026 and is now in 46th place among 139 countries. Index reports that the Academic Trade Union warns that such a result is a consequence of the Government’s poor economic and innovation policy, and particularly highlights the weak cooperation between universities and the economy. It is calling for the establishment of a special ministry that would deal with higher education, science and innovation.

According to the latest report of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), Croatia was in 40th place last year and this year has fallen to 46th. Of the 39 European economies covered by the research it is in 28th place. The Academic Trade Union considers this to be yet another warning that Croatia must change the way it develops the economy, science and higher education.

croatia is getting further behind european innovation leaders

The Global Innovation Index compares economies according to approximately 80 indicators, among which are investments in research and development, education, technology, the business environment and the application of innovations. Switzerland is in a highly impressive first place for the 16th year in a row, followed by Sweden and the United States of America.

In fourth place came South Korea, fifth Singapore, sixth the United Kingdom, seventh the Netherlands, eighth Finland, ninth Denmark, and tenth China. The Academic Trade Union warns that Croatia lags behind European economies in all the main areas assessed by the index.

croatia has nowhere near enough cooperation between universities and industry

According to the trade union, one of Croatia’s greatest weaknesses is the cooperation between universities and industry, for which they point out that Croatia is only in 84th place. Connecting research with production and entrepreneurship should, they believe, be one of the foundations of economic development. The trade union stresses that for years it has been warning the Croatian Government of the need for better linking of the academic community and the economy, but that its proposals are not being implemented. For these exceptionally poor results, they hold the responsible officials accountable, especially the leadership of the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth. They claim that the responsible persons insufficiently follow the results of international research and do not understand the importance of innovations for the development of the economy.

is a new ministry on the horizon?

The Academic Trade Union proposes the establishment of a Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation. The new ministry, according to their proposal, should coordinate the work of the National Innovation Council and encourage cooperation between universities, scientific institutions and companies. The trade union demands that innovation become the third fundamental task of universities, alongside education and scientific work. It also proposes the adoption of a Law on Innovation that would regulate the financing and functioning of the Croatian innovation system.

could croatia’s investment in r&d ever equal 3% of gdp?

Among the trade union’s proposals is an increase in investment in research and development to 3 percent of Croatian GDP. They also demand a doubling of the number of researchers employed in the economy, especially holders of doctorates, so that Croatia can reduce the lag behind the European Union average. The new ministry should also facilitate the coordination of different state institutions when it comes to innovation, the application of new technologies and their transfer from scientific institutions into the economy. The Academic Trade Union considers that such changes would enable stronger development of industry, increase its contribution to the economy and in the long term contribute to the growth of the standard of living. They called on the government to accept their proposals and change the previous policy of developing science, higher education and innovation.

World.title: Why Your Ancestor’s “Austrian” or “Italian” Passport Doesn’t Mean You Aren’t Legally Croatian
World.content:
October the 19th, 2026 – Croatia hasn’t always been the Croatia we know. You may have ancestors that are listed as being Austrian, Italian or Hungarian, but you might still be legally Croatian.

If you’ve curiously started digging into your family’s emigration history, you have likely unearthed a treasure trove of century-old documents: ship passenger manifests, American or Canadian naturalisation petitions, and faded, yellowed draft cards. However, for a massive segment of the Croatian diaspora, specifically those whose families left Europe during the peak migration waves between the late 1800s and the 1920s, these documents often bring a frustrating surprise.

Under the column labelled “Country of Origin” or “Nationality,” your ancestor’s record might not say “Croatia” at all. Instead, it might explicitly state “Austria,” “Hungary,” “Yugoslavia,” or even “Italy”. For many diaspora members, this feels like an immediate dead end. The common assumption by the mere mortal is as follows: If my great-grandfather left Europe as a citizen of the Austro-Hungarian Empire or the Kingdom of Italy, I must not qualify for Croatian citizenship by descent. Despite this being a common assumption, it’s fortunately totally incorrect. In the eyes of modern citizenship law, an imperial passport from 1910 doesn’t erase your legal right to a modern Croatian passport today. However, proving your lineage across a century of shifting borders requires navigating a complex historical and bureaucratic maze.

roots don’t recognise changing borders, but the ministry of the interior does

To understand why your ancestor’s old paperwork says “Austria” or “Italy,” you have to look at the tumultuous geopolitical history of not only Croatia but the wider region. Before the modern Republic of Croatia declared independence on October the 8th, 1991, the territory was repeatedly carved up, absorbed, and governed by various empires and federations, with a lot of bloodshed in between.

First we need to go all the way back to pre-1918 when Croatia was part of the once mighty Austro-Hungarian Empire. Emigrants from Zagreb, Slavonia, Dalmatia and even the furthest-flung islands all travelled on Austrian or Hungarian documentation. Then came the interwar period & WWII. Following the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920, sections of Istria, Rijeka, Zadar, and several Dalmatian islands (including Cres and Lošinj) were annexed by what was then the Kingdom of Italy. People from these regions suddenly became legal Italian citizens, changed their names to Italian variants, and emigrated under the documentation bearing the Italian flag. Then, from 1945 to 1991, Croatia and the countries of the region became part of the various iterations of Yugoslavia.

You can see how Croatian citizenship applications can often become very confusing territory, but the authorities are fully aware of Croatia’s blurry past and as such even blurrier documentation. When the Croatian Ministry of the Interior evaluates an application for citizenship by descent, they don’t care what a clerk at Ellis Island wrote down way back in 1912. They care about geographic reality that corresponds to modern-day Croatia and historical municipal tracking.

Under the current Croatian Citizenship Act, the key question is whether the specific town or village your ancestor emigrated from sits within the modern, legally recognised borders of Croatia as it is today. If your great-grandfather was born somewhere near Split back in 1905, he was technically born under Austro-Hungarian rule, but because Split is indisputably Croatian territory today, the bloodline connection remains legally valid, long after Austria-Hungary’s demise.

here’s where diy croatian citizenship applications often come to grief…

While the law very much allows for these problematic and complex geographical and historical shifts, the burden of proof rests entirely on the applicant. This is where DIY applications frequently fall apart, stall, and end up shoved to gather dust on a shelf somewhere. If you submit an application to a Croatian consulate with an American death certificate stating your grandfather was born in “Austria,” alongside a modern birth record request, the reviewing officers require a meticulous paper trail that bridges the historical gap. You must prove two things simultaneously in such cases.

The first is what’s known as the registry match. Initially, you need to locate the original historical birth or baptismal record in the local municipal registry or church archive within Croatia, confirming they were registered on that specific territory once upon a time. After you’ve cleared that hurdle, you need to deal witu name and identity reconciliation. What this means is that you need to prove that the “Giovanni” or “Giuseppe” listed on an Italian emigration record from Istria is legally the exact same person as the “Ivan” or “Josip” recorded in the local village archives. You can imagine how difficult this is without administrative help.

If your family came from an area like Istria or Zadar that switched between Italian and Slavic administration, records may be split between different archives, written in different languages (Latin, Italian, or old Croatian scripts), or filed under completely altered surnames.

solving the runaway border problem

Navigating various international treaties, century-old municipal border adjustments, and dual-language archives is a daunting task for anyone working from North America, South America, or Australia. It requires a level of historical expertise and local administrative access that standard translation services or internet databases simply cannot provide. This is where the specialised, ground-level infrastructure put in place by services like Croatian By Descent becomes an invaluable asset for the busy American diaspora.

Instead of letting your application get derailed and shoved to the back of a massive pile by a confusing historical paper trail, their team functions as both legal researchers and archival detectives. They know exactly how to trace your mysterious, multi-national ancestors through the shifting territorial registries, cross-referencing old land records and municipal books to establish an airtight geographic proof for the Ministry of the Interior. They dismantle Croatia’s age-old runaway border problem by making sure your ancestral files are organised, properly reconciled, and professionally translated, transforming deeply confusing geopolitical hurdle into a successful, legally sound submission package.

Skip the administrative confusion and verify your historical eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent, who can make sure changing borders and complicated political histories don’t come between you and your EU passport. This service uses knowledgeable lawyer partners who can readily assist clients with obtaining their family’s records from Croatia, as well as dealing with them after the fact throughout the process.
