World.title: Justice minister: Worst AI offenses should be equated with crimes against humanity
World.content:
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta calls for stronger international regulation of AI to protect national sovereignty, smaller languages and cultures.

Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta spoke Wednesday on ERR's "Otse uudistemajast" webcast about regulating artificial intelligence, protecting children's rights, safeguarding privacy, reducing bureaucracy, restricting overly powerful electric scooters, sex offender registries and the future of her party, Eesti 200.

The global push to regulate AI

Pakosta compared the challenges posed by artificial intelligence to those associated with nuclear energy, stressing the need for international regulation.

"Broadly speaking, the situation is more or less the same as with nuclear energy. Nuclear energy has positive aspects, but it also has the potential to cause catastrophes. And although it took some time in that case, from August 1945 until 1970, to establish international rules, we need to move faster here. We don't have that many years," she said.

Pakosta outlined three areas Estonia wants to prioritize in international AI regulation.

"First, we have proposed that the most harmful impacts of artificial intelligence should be treated as crimes against humanity. We already have that entire framework in place and we would extend it to cover AI's extremely harmful and destructive capabilities," she said.

Second, Estonia must ensure its digital infrastructure does not become dependent on technology controlled by foreign providers.

"We cannot build the Estonian state around AI solutions when someone in a third country could suddenly decide not to provide them to us or to add two zeros to the price, for example. This has become a matter of national sovereignty, which means that AI systems with a significant impact must have open-source options that we can build our services on," Pakosta said.

Liisa Pakosta. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Her third priority is protecting smaller languages and cultures in major AI systems.

"Large systems must be required to include small languages and cultures. This is something we are genuinely fighting for. Otherwise, the Estonian language and culture will disappear from the world," she said.

Pakosta also warned that Russia is deliberately financing automated online activity to influence the information used by AI systems.

"Russia is deliberately using and funding bots to ensure that its interpretation of imperialist history and everything associated with it is represented in AI systems, while Estonia's perspective is not," she said.

"Russia is not only destroying cultures with bombs on Ukrainian territory; it is also destroying our culture, our narratives, our stories and our identity in AI environments."

The minister warned that younger generations increasingly rely on AI rather than history books for information, making such manipulation a potentially effective investment for Russia.

She called for international agreements requiring AI systems to incorporate safeguards against disinformation and the distortion of historical narratives.

Pakosta also defended digital regulation, arguing that clear rules encourage rather than hinder innovation.

"When you have clear rules, you can build innovation around them. And businesses actually support this, too," she said, pointing to Estonia's experience with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation.

Businesses investing heavily in AI need predictable regulations to protect their investments, she added.

Another priority is developing sovereign AI solutions to protect Estonian residents' personal information.

"There are some very impressive large models in third countries, but we don't know exactly how our data moves through those systems. We don't know exactly what happens to that data afterward," Pakosta said.

She emphasized that Estonia has made a fundamental decision not to use AI for surveillance activities that would otherwise be considered unacceptable.

"We have decided not to use AI to surveil people in ways that technology makes possible but that we would not otherwise do as human beings. That is a very fundamental decision," she said.

Estonia currently uses AI in approximately 260 public sector services, relying on public or non-sensitive information, according to the minister.

As an example of locally developed technology, she highlighted an Estonian legal advice service that automatically deletes sensitive personal information entered by users seeking assistance.

Liisa Pakosta. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Protecting children

Turning to children's rights, Pakosta discussed legislative proposals being prepared by her ministry based on research conducted under the Mudila project.

The goal is to make it easier for parents and others to find assistance for children, something she described as currently "terribly complicated."

"This is not just about preventing crime. That is only a very small part of it. It is about the broader question of how, in a small, lovely country like Estonia, we can make sure help reaches every child," she said.

Pakosta said the aim is to prevent children from falling through gaps between different services and ensure they receive help as early as possible, potentially immediately after birth.

Containing red tape

On reducing bureaucracy, the minister said Estonia has made substantial progress, introducing a "one in, one out" principle in lawmaking and repealing or simplifying nearly one-fifth of legal acts.

She also highlighted efforts to prohibit the practice of "gold-plating" EU legislation where additional domestic requirements are attached to European rules.

According to Pakosta, this practice has allowed extra regulations to pass through the Riigikogu without sufficient democratic scrutiny.

"We have been successful both in Estonia and in Brussels in not only putting an end to this insane proliferation of bureaucracy, but actually beginning to reduce it," she said.

Illegal electric scooters

Discussing police proposals to confiscate electric scooters exceeding legal power limits, Pakosta acknowledged that legislative changes would be necessary but said they should follow public debate.

She raised the example of parents purchasing excessively powerful scooters for their children, potentially endangering both the children and other road users.

"The parent is putting the child's life at risk, but also endangering other people, including pedestrians. Would the right solution be to fine the parent? That would lead to enormous disputes, with parents saying, 'No, I only bought it for myself to ride somewhere on an off-road track and my child secretly took the scooter. I'm not to blame.' After all, we cannot really punish a younger child, and rightly so. Or do we place greater emphasis on protecting not only the life of the child, for whom the parent is responsible, but also the lives of other road users?

This is where society needs to discuss how to strike the right balance," she said.

Liisa Pakosta and Aleksander Krjukov. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Private offender lists

Pakosta also addressed controversy surrounding a privately created registry of sex offenders and domestic abusers launched at ettevaatust.ee by content creator Mallu Mariann Treimann-Legrant and her husband, Tomas Märten Legrant.

She encouraged people to report problems with existing government registries, saying Estonia has the most transparent and accessible criminal records registry among democratic countries.

She warned that privately maintained criminal records databases can contain inaccurate information, cause lasting harm to innocent people and victims and create a false sense of security.

"That registry contained around 400 people, but our national criminal records registry actually contains more than 11,000 people who are prohibited from having contact with children," she said.

The minister also announced that the government was expected to consider legislation Thursday extending the time available for victims of childhood sexual offenses to report crimes.

Currently, such offenses become time-barred when the victim turns 28. For the most serious offenses, the proposed amendment would extend that deadline until age 50.

"Victims need time to gather themselves, process what happened and report to the police that such a vile crime was committed against them," Pakosta said.

Sensitive health data

On medical privacy, Pakosta discussed a bill already before the Riigikogu that would allow investigative authorities to obtain certain medical information during criminal proceedings, subject to court authorization and strict conditions.

She emphasized that investigators would only be permitted to access technical descriptions of injuries, not patients' personal accounts of how those injuries occurred.

For example, authorities could obtain information about the depth of a knife wound or the path of a bullet, but not statements a patient made about a domestic dispute or other circumstances.

Liisa Pakosta. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"People must be able to tell their doctors openly and honestly what actually happened. That is essential because it is the only way a doctor can properly treat them," she said.

Hospitals and doctors would use a separate form to ensure that patients' accounts are not passed to investigators.

Pakosta also stressed that competent, sober adults who are not under guardianship would retain the right to refuse such disclosures and investigations, citing the privilege against self-incrimination. Different rules would apply to children, while exceptions would also exist in cases of suspected fraud by doctors or patients.

Eesti 200 and elections

Turning to politics, Pakosta declined to reveal her views on the future of Eesti 200, saying decisions rested with the party's board, of which she is not a member.

Her comments followed Sunday's decision by Eesti 200's council not to pursue a merger with the Estonian Greens ahead of the Riigikogu elections.

Nevertheless, Pakosta expressed support for party mergers, arguing that smaller parties can strengthen their influence and broaden their representation by joining forces.

"All the major parties we have today were formed from several parties coming together. There is nothing bad about it. In fact, it is entirely positive," she said.

She argued that parliamentary parties need sufficient size and geographic reach to represent voters effectively, including strong connections with local governments.

Although Eesti 200 has rejected a merger for now, Pakosta said she believes one will eventually take place.

Asked whether she would run in the next Riigikogu elections, Pakosta said the question was premature, noting that Eesti 200 had not yet decided whether it would participate.

"There are a whole range of other issues that I also feel very passionate about. It is not just politics," she added.

Pakosta also declined to express a preference on whether Eesti 200 should participate in the elections, saying she did not want to pressure the party's leadership.

She concluded by defending politicians across party lines, emphasizing the personal sacrifices and hostility that often accompany political work.

"I have seen how difficult it is to work as a politician. No matter which party you belong to, it is very difficult. You face a great deal of hostility, even physical attacks," she said.

"I respect every person who is willing to devote their time to participating in Estonian politics and doing this difficult work. Every person who does this work deserves respect."

Liisa Pakosta. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

World.title: Center for Defense Investments sells Seli Manor
World.content:
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has sold the Seli manor complex at auction. The new owner plans to preserve the manor estate and find a suitable use for it.

The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) sold the Seli manor complex in Rapla County at auction for €380,000, the starting price.

The Seli Manor property came under RKIK's management in 2019 when the Seli Health Center ceased operating as an independent institution and was merged with the Estonian Defense Forces. As the health center relocated to Raadi in Tartu, there was no longer a need to use the manor complex and it was put up for sale, RKIK media relations specialist Andra Nõlvak told ERR.

The complex was purchased by Eksfisk, whose owner, Maria Peetri, told ERR that the company views Seli Manor primarily as a long-term development project.

"The first priority, once the transaction is finalized, is to properly take over the manor complex, gain a comprehensive overview of the buildings' technical condition and initially focus on the work needed to preserve the property," she said.

Going forward, the new owner hopes to find a use and development strategy for the complex that will allow the historic manor estate to be preserved and gradually brought back into active use.

"It is still too early to announce more specific plans, as some matters require design work, planning reviews and approvals. This is not a project we want to rush through, but a long-term development where we want to do things in the right order," Peetri said.

Peetri added that although the auction has ended, the notarized sale transaction has yet to take place.

Eksfisk, which operates Peetri Lõheäri, is engaged in the retail and wholesale sale of fish products. The company posted a profit of €330,000 last year, compared with nearly €280,000 the previous year. According to its annual report for last year, the company had more than €1 million in retained earnings.

The manor complex includes the main building and several outbuildings, including servants' quarters and a hydrotherapy facility.

The earliest records of Seli Manor date back to 1474. The first buildings were wooden structures with straw or reed roofs, none of which have survived. The first limestone buildings at Seli Manor were not constructed until the mid-to-late 18th century. Of these, the manor house or main building, the estate manager's house and the horse stable remain standing today.

Main building of Seli Manor. Source: Varakeskus.ee

World.title: Estonia to revoke draft dodgers' driver's licenses without court order
World.content:
Young people who repeatedly fail to attend a medical examination after being summoned by the Defense Resources Agency could face financial penalties and ultimately lose their driver's licenses.

Undergoing a medical assessment at the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) is a prerequisite for entering compulsory military service and no one can be called up without completing it. Attendance at the assessment is therefore mandatory for anyone who receives a summons.

Under the current rules, if someone repeatedly fails to appear after receiving a summons, the KRA can issue an order or impose a coercive fine. If these measures prove ineffective, the agency can apply to an administrative court to have the conscript's driving privileges suspended.

Starting next year, the procedure will change and the KRA will no longer need to seek permission from an administrative court to suspend a person's driving privileges. Instead, the agency will be able to make the decision itself if the conscript has repeatedly ignored summonses for a medical examination, has been warned of the consequences and has received the warning.

Krismar Rosin, a communications adviser at the Defense Resources Agency, told ERR that the change is primarily procedural and formal, eliminating the judicial review currently required before a suspension can be imposed.

"The aim is to save the courts time," Rosin added.

Anneli Vilu, spokesperson for Tallinn's administrative and circuit courts, noted that applications from the KRA to suspend driving privileges are treated as urgent by the courts and must be resolved immediately.

"However, courts can ask conscripts about their position regarding the KRA application and generally do," Vilu said.

According to Vilu, some people mistakenly believe that paying a coercive fine releases them from their obligation to appear before the medical commission, but this is not the case.

"If a conscript fails to appear before the medical commission, a coercive fine is imposed to compel the person to fulfill their obligation, not as a substitute for appearing before the commission," Vilu emphasized.

Rosin noted that even under the current system, when courts grant the agency permission to suspend driving privileges, they do not make a substantive decision but merely verify that the legal requirements for granting permission have been met.

"So, broadly speaking, the only change is that this preliminary review will be eliminated," Rosin added, referring to the changes taking effect next year.

World.title: Estonian and Helsinki art academies hold joint exhibition in Finland
World.content:
A group exhibition will open at the Kuva/Tila exhibition space, bringing together students' work from the Estonian Academy of Arts (EKA) and the Academy of Fine Arts (KuvA) at the University of the Arts Helsinki.

The exhibition opens on Thursday (October 22) and is titled "Sild/Silta", meaning bridge in both Estonian and Finnish.

The gallery will showcase work from 22 students, and the idea behind the art show is to build relationships between the two neighboring countries.

The collaboration will continue in January 2027, when the same group of students will open a second exhibition at the EKA Gallery in Tallinn.

The organizers say the two exhibitions form a conceptual bridge between Finland and Estonia, allowing artistic ideas, working methods and cultural experiences to flow in both directions.

Participating artists: Eeva-Liisa Anttila, Cecilia Ebbe Belinskij, Vita Edvards, Denis Kudrjašov, Anetta Lukjanova, Sandra Marins, Daniel Niittymäki, Liisa Nurklik, Anna Ovtšinnikova, Jaakko Pennanen, Viljamaria Raittila, Ella Rahkonen, Paul Rannik, Kertu Rannula, Mahmood Salim, Kertu-Liisa Sarap, Marc Léger Sauvageot, Nora Schmelter, Kati Silo, Yiyang Sun, Hanna Vinter, Maria Wrang-Rasmussen.

The exhibition is curated by Merike Estna, Kristi Kongi, Kaisa Maasik, Päivi Takala, Salla Tykkä and Laura Wesamaa.

World.title: School head: Failure is also something one needs to learn
World.content:
"Parents are an incredibly important source of support for their children. A parent's role in supporting their child's self-esteem is to be a secure anchor. Parents need to reflect their child's worth back to them and that reflection should not change because of something bad the child has done or a mistake they have made. Nor should it change because of a bad grade at school, for example. A child is valuable and good enough no matter what and it is the parent's job to maintain that image at home. Our self-image begins at home," said school principal and trainer Cattre Hein.

A child's self-image can become more positive when we recognize their positive actions and efforts. "Working in a school, I see every day how easily children give up. What we want is for children to develop intrinsic motivation. Instead of simply telling a child 'good job,' we should praise the effort they have put in," Hein said.

If a child comes to help stack firewood, something they probably don't want to do, parents should acknowledge that the child came to help anyway and ask how they feel about the fact that their help made it possible to finish the job quickly.

"Similarly, we should recognize small achievements along the way. For example, we could praise a child for making an effort and asking their grandparents for advice, which helped them come up with a topic for their research project," Hein said.

According to Hein, everyone needs to experience failure. "Learning begins when things are difficult and we don't know how to do something. We should accept failure as a normal part of life. Some days everything goes really well, while on other days we can't seem to do anything right, everything goes wrong and nothing works out. But that doesn't make me a worse person. We all tend to give up very easily because failure is extremely uncomfortable. We also need to learn how to fail," Hein explained.

We should also learn to be more forgiving of ourselves. "Young children develop their sense of self through the feedback they receive from their families and at home, while teenagers get that feedback from their friends and social media. It's very easy to start feeling that you can't cope or that you're not good enough. But if we explain to young people how personal growth happens and they begin to understand it, they'll be better equipped to cope," the school principal said.

World.title: New communications cable to be laid between Estonia, Sweden and Finland
World.content:
A Swedish company is laying a new fiber-optic communications cable connecting Sweden, Estonia and Finland, which is expected to enter service next year.

Seabed surveys are about to begin near Saaremaa ahead of construction of a new communications cable connecting Sweden, Estonia and Finland.

The cable will run along the seabed from Gotland in Sweden to Saaremaa, then on to Hiiumaa and mainland Estonia, before continuing through Harju County and across the seabed to Helsinki, Finland. The overland section in Estonia will run from Haapsalu to Viimsi.

"In Estonia, the project includes both submarine and terrestrial fiber-optic communications cables," Tõnu Nirk, head of the communications markets division at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, told ERR. The overland cable route in Estonia is expected to total 250 kilometers, while the subsea connections to Finland, Sweden and Estonia's two largest islands will add another 300 kilometers.

Seabed surveys are planned in preparation for the new communications link. The surveys will identify a suitable route for the cable and map other factors that need to be considered during planning, Nirk said. According to Nirk, the findings will be used in the design process and to prepare a preliminary assessment of whether an environmental impact assessment is necessary.

Cable to be built and owned by Swedish company

The project developer and future owner of the infrastructure is GlobalConnect AB, a telecommunications company registered in Sweden. The company is also responsible for organizing the surveys needed to prepare for the project.

Estonia's Ministry of Climate has issued GlobalConnect AB the necessary marine survey permits, which are valid until the end of this year. Applications for the right to use the seabed and for construction permits for the submarine communications cable are being processed by the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA).

Preparations for the project began in 2025. Cable installation is scheduled for this year and next, with the connection expected to enter service in 2027.

There are currently two communications links between Estonia and Sweden and six between Estonia and Finland. However, various undersea cables and pipelines have been damaged by ships on several occasions in recent years, making a new, alternative connection necessary, Nirk said.

"For Estonia, it is important to establish an additional route that is physically separate from existing connections and to ensure that international data communications can continue even if cables are damaged," he said.

Demand for data transmission capacity is also constantly growing and the new Sweden-Estonia-Finland communications link will increase the capacity of data networks in the Baltic Sea region, Nirk noted.

The ministry declined to comment on whether the project would also include backup connections that could be used if the main connection were disrupted.

Construction of the Sweden-Estonia-Finland communications cable will cost approximately €40 million, of which €15.7 million will come from the European Union's Connecting Europe Facility Digital program.

"The Estonian government is not contributing financially to the project, but it has supported efforts to secure European Union funding and is facilitating the international and domestic cooperation needed to implement it. The project is important for Estonia because it diversifies our international communications links and those of our neighbors, while strengthening digital resilience," Nirk said.

Over the past year, Russia-linked vessels have damaged a gas pipeline and an electricity connection between Estonia and Finland, as well as several international communications cables in the Baltic Sea.

World.title: Reform Party leader: 20 seats in parliament enough to be a political player
World.content:
The Reform Party is aiming for 20 seats after the March elections for a strong team with which to defend the liberal worldview, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.

The Reform Party held a party council meeting over the weekend, setting a goal of winning 20 seats in parliament in next spring's Riigikogu elections. Host Arp Müller noted in his question that 20 seats would not be enough to win an election.

"You can get a strong team into parliament. I remember speaking with Siim Kallas a little while ago and his message was that even when times are difficult, populism is on the rise and the media often criticizes those in power rather indiscriminately, you still have to hold your head high and make sure there is a strong team in the next parliament. And a strong team means that our goal is to win 20 seats, which would give us a foundation to work from, remain a force in Estonian politics and defend what we believe in," Michal replied.

"Because the thing is, Social Democrats are not liberals, conservatives are neither Social Democrats nor liberals and liberals are neither Social Democrats nor conservatives. We are clearly a strong liberal party that stands for individual freedoms, economic freedoms and many other things and you can't get that anywhere else," he added.

'Scope for lowering income tax'

Asked whether the Reform Party plans to cut income tax during the next parliamentary term, Michal said there was scope to do so.

"We have already reduced the tax burden. Last year it was 36.2 percent and next year it will be 35.2 percent, so the tax burden is declining. We have cut income tax and we are cutting it this year. And I think it will be possible to do so in the next term as well, if we review how we do things. We will need to find ways to pay for it because my recommendation is to prioritize several things. First, defense spending must remain at 5 percent. Second, when it comes to the budget, we need to continue what we have been doing — reducing the deficit by half a percentage point a year. That will bring borrowing under control and should eventually start reducing it. At the same time, we can review public services or find other ways for the state to generate revenue, including through new technologies, whether by cutting costs or generating revenue from them. That would also create room to cut income tax," Michal said.

The prime minister declined to specify how large an income tax cut would realistically be possible.

"You'll have to wait a little longer and enjoy the suspense. It will take some time before the election platforms are unveiled, but perhaps I'll talk about it on the next show or the one after that," he said.

'Possibility to cancel next year's fuel excise hike'

Regarding a possible increase in fuel excise duty next May, Michal said it was important to consider developments in the global market more broadly.

"We don't know what fuel excise duties or fuel prices will be next spring. I've said this several times at government press conferences, but we're monitoring the situation quite regularly. At our last couple of Cabinet meetings, we've met with representatives of the Bank of Estonia, the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and the Ministry of Finance. Market participants, including Neste and Alexela, have also attended and shared their assessments of the situation. We're keeping a very close eye on the fuel market," Michal said.

"There are several factors we're monitoring. The first, and the state's main concern and responsibility, is ensuring that reserves are sufficient and security of supply is guaranteed. That means making sure there is enough fuel of every type, which is the responsibility of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency. Based on assurances from the agency's head, Ando Leppiman, I would say that our current reserves are sufficient to see us through," he noted.

"Why is this important? Because if we look at the current risks, the rise in fuel prices originated in the Strait of Hormuz, but now, according to market participants and experts, the bottleneck has shifted to refineries, which are unable to supply enough fuel to the market. We certainly need to ensure that any new disruptions do not lead to shortages of physical fuel supplies. Fortunately, at the moment, there appear to be no such shortages in any fuel category. The second thing we're monitoring is, of course, prices. When it comes to prices, we're looking at the potential risk of losing tax revenue to Latvia, for example. Latvia has repeatedly taken various measures concerning fuel and if we look at average pump prices, we're at virtually the same level. Generally, prices are higher in Latvia on one day, while occasionally it's the other way around and so on. We're fairly evenly matched. But if Latvia takes further steps next year, we'll certainly have to monitor the situation and make decisions about our own fuel excise duty rates accordingly. That's something we're assessing on an ongoing basis," Michal said.

Michal acknowledged that if the government planned to cancel next year's excise duty increase, it would have to take that into account when preparing the budget.

"But we certainly won't make that decision before next year because we don't currently know what fuel prices will be next year. How will the U.S. midterm elections turn out? What will happen next in the Strait of Hormuz? There is an enormous amount of uncertainty. What happens after that? Will fuel supplies recover? Will refineries be able to meet demand? Which direction will things go? We simply don't know yet. So we'll make our decisions accordingly. And I would remind you that this year when it became necessary and we in the government considered it appropriate to cancel the excise duty increases, we made that decision. We can do the same next year," Michal said.

Estonia's Rail Baltica cost sharing component could go up

Michal has previously said that delaying the Rail Baltica construction deadline would make the project cheaper for Estonia.

"When the infrastructure construction market isn't so overheated and overstretched, the cost per unit doesn't rise as much. If you inject a very large amount of money into a single market very quickly, each unit becomes more expensive. That's the first point. Second, from the Estonian state's financial perspective, if you can use more EU funding and other external financing for the project from the next budget period, which you otherwise wouldn't be able to use, you don't have to borrow money on behalf of taxpayers and pay interest on it later. So it's cheaper financially and cheaper in terms of construction costs — cheaper in both respects," Michal said.

However, Estonia's share of the project's costs could rise to 25 percent, with European Union funding covering the remaining 75 percent.

"Yes, the original plan, or the original approach, was an 85-15 split. The idea is that the European Union covers most of Rail Baltica's construction costs. I think the current split for Estonia is probably closer to 80-20, roughly speaking. And the European Commission's new proposal has been to reduce the EU co-financing rate to 75 percent. That would mean a ratio of about 75-25. That's what the debate is about," Michal said.

According to Michal, Estonia would still come out ahead even if it received less funding from the European Union.

"The benefit for us becomes clear when you compare it with completing construction by 2030. During the gap years in EU funding, we would have to contribute more of our own money. That would mean a substantial increase in Estonia's share of the costs, requiring us to borrow money and repay it with interest. On top of that, because we would be pouring so much money into the infrastructure construction market all at once, the cost per unit would also be higher. So spreading construction over a longer period means we can make greater use of EU funds, regardless of whether the co-financing rate is 75 or 80 percent at the time," Michal said.

"Even if it's 75 percent, that still brings money into Estonia's budget in any case," he added.

Passport functionality more important than color

Speaking about the Ministry of the Interior's plan to change the color of Estonian passports back to blue, Michal said he would discuss the matter with Taro on Thursday.

"That's a good question. We can certainly give it plenty of thought. There's a certain nostalgic appeal to blue and we've had blue passports before. But when you travel elsewhere in the world, border guards recognize the burgundy color as indicating an EU passport. In my view, what's far more important than either color is that, regardless of the color of the passport cover, it allows you to pass through all checkpoints electronically as quickly as possible. But to add a little good-natured discussion to the debate, why should it be blue? It might as well be blue, black and white, like the Estonian flag," Michal said.

World.title: Wise founder: AI will eventually reach every sector
World.content:
Estonia's industrial sector could use AI and information technology to improve its relatively poor productivity, investor and entrepreneur Taavet Hinrikus has said.

"I think AI will reach every sector. We are at the very beginning of a very rapid transformation. I think AI will already be helping you [host Andres Kuusk – ed.] prepare the questions in front of you in the coming months, and there is no field of work that it will not penetrate," Hinrikus, a shareholder in AI giant Anthropic, told Tuesday's "Esimene stuudio".

AI skills are important for improving the productivity of Estonian industry, he said.

"Our industrial productivity is below average, and I think that is embarrassing. But one way to look at it is that all the IT skills we have in Estonia are very heavily concentrated in our technology sector. And thanks to that, we have 12 unicorns, and everything is going well in that sector. But we have far fewer people with IT skills working in the traditional economy, and I think that is where we should be paying much more attention: how can we bring considerably more technological knowledge into the traditional economy?" the entrepreneur said.

"If we go back in time, you needed a team of five or six people to get something done. Say you have a manufacturing company. You need some software, you need a team of five or six people, and getting to that point, hiring them and managing them, is quite complicated. Today, you have one person who can do the same work with the help of AI, and I think we need to bring AI skills into everything – agriculture, tourism, energy and manufacturing," Hinrikus added.

He believes that the rapid changes AI is bringing to the world are not a negative phenomenon but rather the emergence of new opportunities.

"Perhaps some jobs will start to disappear. The statistics don't show that yet, but on the other hand, many new jobs will emerge, just as we now have new jobs such as YouTuber and drone pilot – things we didn't know about 10 years ago. And if we think 10 years ahead, what jobs will exist then? We don't know yet, but there will certainly be many of them," Hinrikus said.

Jaan Tallinn, also an Estonian shareholder in Anthropic, has warned about the dangers associated with the development and advancement of artificial intelligence. Hinrikus acknowledged that he shares those concerns.

"We have already seen dangers and accidents arising from AI, and there will certainly be more accidents. I have no doubt about that. We can only hope they won't be very serious. Perhaps I am a little more optimistic by nature and hope that human ingenuity will be able to save us from the worst," he said.

"On the other hand, we have faced dangerous situations in the world before and have managed to develop our way out of them. Perhaps nowadays we have paid too little attention to managing the risks of AI. Take Anthropic, for example: they are developing their capabilities very quickly, but they haven't put as much energy into developing safeguards. I think that if we put just as much focus into that, we can hope to avoid the worst," Hinrikus added.

Regarding Anthropic's planned initial public offering, Hinrikus noted that when it eventually happens, it will not necessarily have a significant impact on the development of artificial intelligence.

"It will not slow down or accelerate [development]. I think it might bring back some capital that can be invested in new companies," he said.

World.title: Iraq shuts Sheeb border crossing with Iran for security reasons
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has closed the al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran to all passengers, vehicles, and commercial transit until further notice.

An Iraqi border crossings official told Reuters that the sudden shutdown on Wednesday was implemented to review existing security procedures and install advanced detection equipment.

Officials mentioned that current security protocols at the busy Maysan province crossing were weak and inadequate to effectively halt the smuggling of prohibited materials.

Iranian security official Valiollah Hayati has advised passengers and cargo trucks to divert to the Shalamcheh crossing in Khuzestan province.

No official date has been announced for the resumption of operations. Local reports suggest the Iraqi government is currently evaluating security at other checkpoints and may gradually close additional borders with Iran in the coming days.

Iran’s Interior Ministry is currently in talks with Iraqi provincial authorities to coordinate a timeline for reopening the border.

In mid-September, Iraq announced the resumption of trade through its border crossings with Iran, following a brief closure due to security concerns.

Iraq closed several border crossings with Iran following a drone attack targeting a pipeline in Saudi Arabia, which Riyadh and Baghdad said originated from Iraqi territory.

Iraqi authorities had discovered drone launchers near the Iraqi-Iranian border in the remote al-Tayeb area in the ​​southern province of Maysan.

World.title: Five things to know about Chinese AI startup DeepSeek
World.content:
Beijing – The United States Department of Homeland Security ordered government agencies on Monday to stop using artificial intelligence tools from DeepSeek, citing concerns over data being transferred to China.

Here are five things to know about the Chinese AI startup following the new restrictions:

– ‘Sputnik moment’ –

Founded by Liang Wenfeng in the eastern Chinese tech hub Hangzhou, DeepSeek started life in 2023 as a side project of Liang’s data-driven hedge fund that had access to a cache of powerful AI processors made by US chip giant Nvidia.

It gained global attention in January 2025 with the release of its R1 deep-reasoning large language model, which sparked a US tech share sell-off.

Industry insiders were stunned by R1’s high performance — at a level similar to ChatGPT and other leading US chatbots — and DeepSeek’s claims to have developed it at a fraction of the cost.

Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen described it as a “Sputnik moment”, referencing the 1957 launch of Earth’s first artificial satellite by the Soviet Union that stunned the Western world.

– Censorship concerns –

Like other Chinese chatbots, DeepSeek’s AI tools eschew topics usually censored in the world’s second-largest economy, such as the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.

That and data privacy concerns have led DeepSeek AI to be banned or restricted on government-issued devices in several countries, including the United States, Australia and South Korea.

On Monday, the US went further by banning civilian government agencies from using products developed by DeepSeek and third-party tools created using DeepSeek.

China’s foreign ministry said it opposed that move and accused the US of “overstretching” the concept of national security.

DeepSeek’s low cost and ease of deployment have made it a popular choice in developing countries, analysts say.

The company holds around four percent of global market share for chatbots, according to web traffic analysis company Similarweb. ChatGPT dominates at 68 percent.

– Open source –

DeepSeek’s systems are open-source, meaning their inner workings are public, allowing programmers to customise parts of the software to suit their needs.

That is the same for other major Chinese AI players, including tech giant Alibaba, in contrast to the “closed” models sold by OpenAI and other Western rivals.

The Chinese government has trumpeted its lead in open-source AI technology, which it says can accelerate innovation.

“Chinese AI models are leading the way in the open-source innovation ecosystem,” National People’s Congress spokesman Lou Qinjian told policymakers in April.

– Startup boost –

The success of DeepSeek has galvanised China’s AI scene, despite hurdles posed by rivalry with the United States and fears of a global market bubble.

Shares in two leading Chinese AI startups, Zhipu AI and MiniMax, soared on their market debuts in Hong Kong this year, and it has been a similar story for Chinese chipmakers such as MetaX.

In June, investors valued DeepSeek at more than $50 billion in the company’s first funding round, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shi Yaqiong and her team at Beijing-based Jinqiu Capital told AFP there has been a “clear surge” in enthusiasm around Chinese AI — and competition among investors — since the DeepSeek shock.

– Chip smuggling reports –

DeepSeek’s rise has not been without controversy.

Reports, including in technology outlet The Information, say DeepSeek has been skirting a US ban on the export of top-end chips to China to train its new V4 model.

The Information said in December, citing six people with knowledge of the matter, that DeepSeek developed V4 using thousands of chips dismantled in third countries and smuggled to China.

DeepSeek did not respond to AFP’s request for comment at the time. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment but told The Information that they had not seen any evidence of this and that “such smuggling seems farfetched”.

In April, DeepSeek said it had used both Nvidia and Huawei’s domestically-produced Ascend chips for its new model.

Huawei, at the forefront of Chinese efforts to reduce reliance on US semiconductor technology, said in a statement that the full range of its Ascend products support DeepSeek’s V4 series.

Washington says DeepSeek’s latest model is about eight months behind the top offerings from US companies.

World.title: Iraq’s foreign reserves rise to $81.5 billion in August
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) revealed on Wednesday that the country’s foreign reserves rose to $81.53 billion by the end of August 2026, compared to $80.633 billion at the end of July.

Iraq’s foreign reserves increased by approximately $905 million during August but remained below the level recorded at the end of 2025, when they stood at $97.43 billion. Throughout the first eight months of this year, there has been a $15.89 billion decrease.

After reaching $101.08 billion at the end of January 2026, Iraq’s foreign reserves fell to $100.34 billion in March, $97.8 billion in April, $93.67 billion in May, $86.17 billion in June, and $80.63 billion in July before rising once again in August.

Last month, the CBI confirmed that its foreign currency reserves are entirely sufficient to meet all market demands.

Earlier in October, a Standard Chartered economist said that Iraq may resort to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) if oil revenues continue to fall and the currency’s devaluation fails to boost state finances as intended.

Standard Chartered chief economist for the Middle East and Pakistan Carla Slim said that any potential program with the IMF could entail structural reforms, particularly regarding the public sector wage bill, to enhance fiscal sustainability, Bloomberg reported.

If the current pace of depletion continues, Iraq’s foreign reserves might fall to roughly $60 billion by the end of the year, down from over $100 billion at the beginning of the year, according to Slim.

World.title: France’s tourism sector worried about impact of riots
World.content:
Paris – The images of France’s riots posted and broadcast around the world have cast a pall on the country’s important tourism sector, with many fearing worse consequences if violence returns.

“The surge of violence in the centres of Nice, Paris, Lyon — it’s catastrophic,” said Christelle Cassagne, head of the ADN Tourisme body covering the country’s tourism institutions.

“When you book a hotel for a week, it’s not so you stay stuck in the hotel,” she said.

The scenes of clashes with police, public buildings on fire, shops being looted and masked young men roaming the streets have, since last weekend, shocked and fascinated news audiences internationally.

The violence has usurped the usual curated footage of genteel cafes favoured by influencers, who have suddenly taken to asking “Is Paris safe?” — many using AI on thumbnails or even in their videos to boost click-through rates.

Even in Paris, some tourists who had front-row seats to the convulsion on the streets are looking for the exit. And others coming in were hesitant.

“Honestly, we were not certain that we’d keep our stay,” an Indian businessman in a pricey Paris hotel said, declining to give his name.

Already, hotel reservations are weakening in major cities such as Paris, Lyon and Marseille, according to Didier Arino, head of the consulting and research firm Protourisme.

For a country used to welcoming 100 million visitors a year — and the more than 70 billion euros ($80 billion) they spend — it’s a concern.

Arino and other observers questioned by AFP said the overall picture for France’s tourism industry would depend on whether new violence broke out in the coming weeks.

“The impact of a day of rioting and urban violence in the heart of Paris caused around a one-percent cancellation rate for the monthly count in the days following, and the same for the following weeks,” Arino said.

“For the 42 million hotel nights forecast for 2026, that’s not major. But watch out you don’t underestimate the effects from repeated incidents.”

That could also flow through to tourism revenues, as visitors from those countries often have more spending power than Europeans.

– Travel advisories –

The downward pressure on reservations comes as several countries, including the United States, China and Germany issued travel advisories for their citizens in France.

“The further away the clients are, the more sensitive they are to safety risks, and the stronger the impact,” said Arino.

Laurent Abitbol, head of the executive board of travel agency group Selectour, said: “If this lasts two weeks, that’s not so serious. However, if this continues for several months it will be catastrophic.”

“When you watch CNN, or Fox News, BBC, all that, you’d believe that France is at war. That’s not good…”

Another firm, MKG Consulting, said that, since last weekend, Paris hotels have lost potential bookings for the next six weeks.

Its data showed bookings had weakened sharply within a day.

Between October 19 and 20, the share of rooms booked for stays from October 20-29 fell from being 1.0 percentage point above the level recorded for the same period in 2025 to just 0.2 percentage points higher.

For stays between October 20 and 25, the increase over 2025 levels also narrowed significantly, dropping from 3.5 percentage points to 1.9 points.

“This slowdown is especially notable for near-term and high-end stays,” it said, drawing a parallel with a period in December 2018 when Yellow Vest street protests raged in the capital’s streets.

World.title: Iraq’s domestic public debt climbs to 113.5 trillion dinars in August 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s domestic public debt surged to 113.485 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $86.6 billion) by the end of August 2026, climbing from 109.516 trillion dinars at the end of July.

The monthly increase of 3.969 trillion dinars reflects expanding sovereign borrowing needs to finance fiscal obligations, according to official economic indicators released by the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI).

Economic data indicates that domestic debt expanded by roughly 22.97 trillion dinars compared to the end of 2025, when it stood at 90.515 trillion dinars.

This represents a steep expansion of 25.4% during the first eight months of 2026, driven by higher reliance on central banking liquidity and domestic sovereign debt instruments to cover budget spending.

The breakdown of domestic obligations at the end of August shows that Ministry of Finance claims held by the Central Bank constituted the primary component, rising to 76.499 trillion dinars from 72.499 trillion dinars in July.

Commercial and sovereign loans represented the second-largest portion at 18.945 trillion dinars, followed by domestic bonds at 9.330 trillion dinars and treasury bills at 8.711 trillion dinars, underlining the structured profile of the central treasury’s internal liabilities.

World.title: US Dollar climbs back above 169,000 IQD in Baghdad, Erbil, and Basra
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate of the U.S. dollar against the Iraqi dinar edged upward across parallel retail and wholesale counters in Baghdad, Erbil, and Basra on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, pushing market selling prices back above the 169,000 dinar threshold per $100.

In Baghdad, foreign exchange bureaus and trading desks quoted selling rates at 169,500 dinars per $100 against purchase bids of 168,500 dinars, gaining 500 dinars compared to Tuesday’s closing levels.

In Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, counters registered selling quotes at 169,300 dinars per $100 alongside purchase transactions accepted at 168,750 dinars. Across the southern port hub of Basra, cash counters listed retail selling prices at 169,000 dinars against buying rates of 168,500 dinars per $100.

The prevailing market rates sustain a marked premium over the Central Bank of Iraq’s official statutory cash price, which remains anchored at 152,000 dinars per $100 (1,520 dinars per dollar).

The current spread of up to 17,500 dinars per $100 highlights ongoing demand for physical foreign banknotes outside the official trade-financing and electronic clearance mechanisms.

World.title: Parliamentary committee unveils proposals to revamp Iraq’s public salary scale
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Details of a comprehensive overhaul proposed for Iraq’s public sector salary scale have been disclosed by Member of Parliament Mohammed Abu Al-Eis, outlining recommendations by a specialized ministerial committee to raise base nominal wages, standardize allowances, and eliminate discretionary bonuses.

The reform package aims to narrow persistent income disparities across state institutions and enhance job equity, particularly for civil servants in lower pay grades, though the draft measures have not yet received formal legislative or executive enactment.

According to statements delivered by Abu Al-Eis to the official gazette on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the recommendations stem from the Diwani Order Committee established in 2022 to review public compensation legislation. The committee’s framework proposes an updated salary grid that elevates baseline nominal salaries while setting standardized allowances at 50% and 30% pursuant to the State Employees’ Salaries Law.

Under this model, secondary and discretionary departmental bonuses would be abolished, capping aggregate allowances at a maximum ceiling of 50% of an employee’s revised gross compensation, with surplus funds redirected to the state treasury. No executive exemptions would be permitted, barring the armed forces and security apparatus due to their operational operational nature.

The review also addressed macroeconomic implications and data limitations across the state apparatus. Economic experts were consulted to evaluate potential inflationary pressures on basic consumer commodities and safeguard vulnerable demographics, including social protection beneficiaries.

Furthermore, the committee noted that while Table (C) of the federal budget law records 4,074,697 public sector personnel, verified payroll records for only two million civil servants have been submitted to date, underscoring the urgent need to finalize comprehensive civil service registry data.

The proposal stipulates that employees earning elevated compensation under stand-alone special legislation will be excluded from the standardized bonuses until the Council of Representatives enacts harmonizing legislative amendments.

The recommendations would also extend to civil servants in the Kurdistan Region upon final approval, contingent on the regional government providing complete institutional staffing rosters to the federal Ministry of Finance alongside funding requests, while simultaneously standardizing executive pay grades across the country’s sovereign presidencies and supreme constitutional bodies.

World.title: Iraq opens university classrooms for inmates in Susa and Amarah prisons
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Justice announced on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the establishment of university-level classroom branches inside Susa Central Prison and Amarah Central Prison, expanding higher education access for inmates across correctional facilities.

According to an official statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the initiative aligns with ministerial directives issued by Justice Minister Khaled Shwani and activates an inter-ministerial memorandum of cooperation concluded with the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research.

The implementation framework pairs Susa Central Prison with private higher education institutions in Sulaymaniyah, while Amarah Central Prison is partnering with specialized university faculties in Maysan Governorate.

Murad Mahdi Haidar, Director of Media at the Ministry of Justice, confirmed that the academic expansion represents an evolutionary leap in penal rehabilitation programs.

The initiative broadens inmate education beyond standard adult literacy and secondary equivalency classes, granting eligible candidates the opportunity to pursue recognized undergraduate degree programs and acquire professional skill sets during their incarceration.

The ministry emphasized that integrating academic tertiary education forms a foundational pillar of modern correctional policy, aimed at strengthening personal cognitive development and lowering recidivism.

By equipping inmates with accredited intellectual credentials, the penal system seeks to ease community reintegration and enable former prisoners to secure stable employment post-release.

World.title: 'Shouldn't have come if unwell': Subodh Uniyal defends public reprimand of Daler Mehndi
World.content:
Congress demands minister's apology

Artists rally behind Mehndi

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand minister Subodh Uniyal on Wednesday defended himself over reprimanding singer Daler Mehndi on stage during an event, saying the artiste should not have performed if he was unwell.Speaking to news agency PTI, Uniyal said Mehndi was only lip-syncing during the event and that, as a public representative associated with the event's organising committee, he came under pressure from people who wanted the issue to be questioned."Daler Mehndi, being a big name, was invited to the Kunjapuri Fair. But during the performance, it became apparent that he was only lip-syncing and not singing. I, being a local representative and also associated with the organising committee, felt the pressure from people who wanted this to be questioned," Uniyal said."Mehndi was not able to speak or walk. At that point, I thought he was under the influence of some substance. I don't know what, because a medical examination was not conducted," he added.Uniyal said he later learnt that Mehndi was unable to speak because he was unwell."Being such a big artiste, he should have informed us about this. This fact was revealed only when he was interrupted. If he was unwell, he should not have come to perform," the minister said."We were asked to make full payment of Rs 35 lakh in advance to the artiste; hotels were also booked in advance. I have nothing personal against Mehndi nor any intention to hurt him, but such a big artiste, knowing his condition, should have refused to perform," Uniyal said."I stand by the fact that if an artiste's respect must stay intact, they should also work accordingly. I did not use any foul language while speaking to Mehndi," he added.The controversy erupted after Uniyal went on stage and expressed displeasure while Mehndi was performing at the Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair, a cultural event organised by the Uttarakhand government at Narendra Nagar in the New Tehri area on Sunday night.The controversy also took on political overtones, with Congress demanding that Uniyal publicly apologise for the way the episode was handled.âThe treatment meted out to Mehndi is deeply unfortunate and runs counter to Uttarakhandâs glorious tradition of hospitality,â Amarjit Singh, general secretary of the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee, said.Meanwhile, several people from the entertainment industry, including actor Anupam Kher, stand-up comedian Vir Das and singers Shaan, Palash Sen, Gurdas Maan and Alisha Chinai, came out in support of Mehndi. They said the artiste, who has been singing for three decades, was unwell, did not drink and should have been treated with greater respect."Couple of days ago, I saw a video in which Daler Mehndi ji was singing on stage and some minister got up and spoke to him insultingly. I wasn't there so I don't know but I've known Daler ji for 25 to 30 years. I know that he does not drink and he is one of the finest human beings that I have met. I personally know that he has not been keeping well for two-three years," Kher said in a video on X on Wednesday."Nobody should speak to anybody like this and that also on a public forum. This is not fair. To publicly accuse someone like this is wrong. Daler ji I am so sorry," he added.Comedian Vir Das said his first international show was in Dubai at Mehndi's show."So not just music people, comedy people also have a lot to owe to this great man and this great artist. And he was humble, nice, supportive and amazing. Daler paaji, I hope you feel well in your corner. Thank you from a very young comedian," Das said on Instagram.Mehndi's brother, singer Mika Singh, confirmed that the artiste had undergone major surgery and challenged anyone to prove that his elder brother had ever consumed alcohol. Although there has been speculation about Mehndi's health, the nature of his illness and surgery remains unclear.

World.title: I&B ministry warns TV channels over communal rhetoric, violent visuals, AI use
World.content:
(Representative image): The committee stressed that âinappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised in telecastâ, and urged broadcasters to follow both the letter and spirit of existing rules.

NEW DELHI: Flagging repeated lapses in television content, the information and broadcasting ministry has asked private satellite channels to check communal rhetoric, sensational coverage of crime and violence and the misuse of artificial intelligence in news production, warning that violations of the Programme Code could invite action.In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the ministry said its Inter-Departmental Committee had found content aired by various channels ânot in conformity with the spirit of the Programme Codeâ. It also noted instances of similar news and visuals being broadcast across multiple channels on the same subjects.The committee stressed that âinappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised in telecastâ, and urged broadcasters to follow both the letter and spirit of existing rules.Taking particular note of television debates, the advisory said channels must ensure that discussions do not âpromote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudesâ. It called for careful selection and prior sensitisation of panellists, adequate editorial control and, where necessary, âimmediate remedial measures such as muting, disclaimers, interruption or discontinuation of feedâ to stop derogatory, abusive or inflammatory content from being aired.On AI, the ministry asked broadcasters to exercise caution while using it, including generative tools, for graphics and virtual news presentations. âThe use of AI tools may be limited to assistive capacity,â it said, stressing that accuracy, authenticity and sensitivity must not be compromised.The advisory reiterated the prohibition on live coverage of anti-terror operations by security forces, restricting such reporting to periodic briefings by authorised officers. Telecasts of related visuals should be time-stamped wherever necessary to avoid misleading viewers.It also urged channels to avoid graphic or disturbing visuals, unverified and sensationalised crime reports, excessive replay of violent footage and coverage that might glorify unlawful behaviour. Images from disasters and major accidents, it said, should be time-stamped where necessary to prevent panic.Broadcasters were further reminded to use only authentic maps issued by the Survey of India and protect the identities of sexual offence victims, including through indirect details.The ministry asked channels to strengthen editorial reviews and train news, production and transmission staff in the Programme Code.

World.title: All India Kisan Sabha threatens govt of 'militant resistance' if it goes ahead with US trade deal
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The All India Kisan Sabha on Wednesday threatened the Centre of "militant resistance" from farmers if it proceeds with the India-US trade deal.

In a statement, the farmer's organisation said that the concessions to Washington would threaten agriculture in the country and lead to greater corporate consolidation in the sector.

The farmers' organisation said that farmers in the country would be unable to compete with "heavily subsidised" American agricultural producers.

"The government will face militant resistance from the peasantry if it goes ahead with the anti-national trade deal," it said.

"The ongoing visit of US secretary of state Marco Rubio, and the negotiations he reportedly led with Indian authorities to 'finalise' a trade deal between the US and India, demonstrate that the RSS-BJP-led Union government will go to any extent to please their imperial masters," it added.

AIKS also accused the government of keeping the Parliament in the dark about the details of the proposed agreement, even as negotiations appeared to be nearing completion.

This comes after Rubio said that the deal is "very close", with the US demand to sell milk products in India emerging as the last hurdle, the AIKS said, adding that commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal had also said the agreement was in the final stage of legal drafting.

"Indian soybean farmers cannot compete with heavily subsidised industrial farmers in the US," it said.

"To put it simply, concessions to the US would result in a dangerous level of corporate consolidation in Indian agriculture," it added.

World.title: Delhi court orders release of CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A special executive magistrate (SEM) court in Delhi on Wednesday accepted the surety bonds of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders

and Ashutosh Ranka and ordered their release, officials said.

The court said they may be released from jail if they are not in custody in any other case. The order came after Delhi Police sought a three-day extension of their judicial custody.

The two leaders have been in police custody for 7 days.

On their way back, Saurav Das in the brief interaction with media responded to the court's order saying, "Truth has prevailed."

The CJP founder and leader Abhijeet Dipke shared his reaction to the court's release order. Taking to his X account, Dipke shared a clip from the climax scene of Shah Rukh Khan's movie

Chak De India.

High court asks activists to pursue alternative remedy

Earlier in the day, Das and Ranka challenged the extension of their custody before the Delhi high court. The court asked them to await the SEM's decision and approach the appropriate appellate or revisional forum if their grievance persisted. The activists subsequently withdrew their plea.

Delhi HC also questioned why they had invoked its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution when an alternative legal remedy was available.





âYour second incident. You are a person who has actually broken a bond. Your remedy actually lies in revision,â the court observed while hearing the challenge to the SEM's October 19 order.

The bench also questioned whether authorities could impose stricter surety conditions following an alleged second breach of a peace bond.

âOnce you have broken peace for the second time, are the authorities not entitled to insist upon everything?â the court asked.

The court further expressed concern that breaching barricades at Jantar Mantar could encourage others to violate prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).

âThe two petitioners here are at the forefront. When you go and break a barricade, the chances of 10 or 20 more people in violation of 163 are very high,â the court observed.

Advocate Abhik Chimni, appearing for the petitioners, argued that the SEM lacked jurisdiction to extend their custody and that their sureties had been wrongly rejected.

The High Court clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case before permitting the withdrawal of the plea.

CJP leaders detained after Jantar Mantar protest

Das and Ranka were initially remanded to five days of judicial custody on October 14 after being detained for allegedly entering Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a designated protest site, and violating peace bonds. Their custody was extended by two days on October 19.

The activists challenged the extension under Sections 126 and 170 of the BNSS, arguing that their continued detention was illegal and that the allegations did not establish an imminent threat to peace and tranquillity.

World.title: Kolkata stampede probe: SIT gets 3 months to uncover cause of tragedy
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government, in consultation with the Calcutta High Court, has constituted a

(SIT) to probe the October 17 stampede at the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata that claimed 19 lives and left 25 people injured.

The SIT will investigate the circumstances leading to the incident and recommend measures to prevent similar tragedies. According to an official government notification, the panel must submit its final report to the state government within three months of the order.

The committee will be chaired by retired Justice Anindita Roy Saraswati. Its members include the Principal Secretary of the Disaster Management and Civil Defence Department, the Director General and Inspector General of Police of the Special Task Force (STF), a police representative of at least Additional Director General rank, a Home and Hill Affairs Department representative of at least Joint Secretary rank, and a representative of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) based in Kolkata.

Preliminary findings indicate that the victims sustained multiple traumatic injuries as the crowd surged towards the pandalâs exit during evening rain. The deceased included 13 women and six minors. The youngest victim was seven-year-old Aayansh Srivastava, who had travelled from Bihar with his family.

The victims came from Kolkata, neighbouring districts and other parts of West Bengal. Among them were 14-year-old Sandip Bej from Purba Bardhaman, 13-year-old Pranjal Sarkar from Agarpara, and teenagers Priya Samaddar, 18, from New Barrackpore, Akriti Kumari, 17, from Bally, and Barnali Haldar, 17, and Tania Biswas, 18, from New Town.





Meanwhile, the Kolkata Fire Department has placed five Durga Puja pandals in South Kolkata under special scrutiny following the tragedy. The department has issued written instructions to the committees of Chetla, Tridhara, Deshapriya Park and Tollygunge Cultural, directing them to pay particular attention to entry and exit routes and implement additional fire safety measures.

The state government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a job for the family of each deceased victim.

The Special Task Force has also begun an investigation to establish accountability for the incident.

Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, along with the Chief Secretary, Home Secretary, Director General of Police and Commissioner of Police, is closely monitoring the situation.

World.title: 'Avoid airing anti-national content': Govt warns TV channels against inflammatory debates and AI misuse
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The ministry of information and broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to satellite TV channels, asking them to avoid live coverage of anti-terror operations, exercise caution while broadcasting violent visuals and refrain from airing anti-national content.In its advisory, the ministry asked channels to strictly adhere to the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994."The ministry of information & broadcasting has observed instances of non-compliance with the provisions of the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, by various private satellite television channels," the ministry said."Instances of similar news/visuals broadcast on multiple channels on similar topics were observed during the meeting of IDC. Therefore, IDC recommended that all private satellite television channels be advised to strictly adhere to the statutory provisions governing content broadcast on television. The committee also emphasised that inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalized in telecast," it added.The guidelines cover live coverage of anti-terror operations, violent visuals, crime reporting, natural disasters, the use of authentic maps of India, communal harmony and the protection of sexual assault victims' identities.On communal harmony and debate programmes, the ministry said channels must ensure that programmes, including live debates and panel discussions, "do not promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes".Broadcasters have also been cautioned to exercise due care while using artificial intelligence, including generative AI, in programmes such as graphics and virtual news presentations.The ministry said AI tools "may be limited to assistive capacity" without compromising the "accuracy, authenticity, or sensitivity" of news content.The ministry further asked broadcasters to strengthen their editorial and content-review mechanisms and regularly sensitise and train personnel involved in news gathering, editing, production, transmission and telecast.The ministry said violations of these guidelines may invite action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995.

World.title: OpenAI to train government employees in AI through Mission Karmayogi platform
World.content:
OpenAI will make approved learning resources from its OpenAI Academy available through iGOT Karmayogi, the government's digital training platform under Mission Karmayogi. The initiative will cover eligible personnel across central and state governments and Union territories.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: AI training is set to reach India's government workforce, with OpenAI partnering with Karmayogi Bharat to introduce AI learning courses on the Centre's iGOT Karmayogi platform, which already has over 1.7 crore government employees registered across the country.The two organisations on Wednesday signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to equip civil servants with practical AI skills, enabling them to use emerging technologies in their everyday work and improve public service delivery.OpenAI will make approved learning resources from its OpenAI Academy available through iGOT Karmayogi, the government's digital training platform under Mission Karmayogi. The initiative will cover eligible personnel across central and state governments and Union territories.While OpenAI will provide the course content, Karmayogi Bharat will facilitate access, encourage participation and coordinate with government departments.The collaboration marks an expansion of AI-focused capacity building within the government, moving beyond specialised technology professionals to include civil servants performing administrative and public-facing functions."As technology reshapes governance, civil servants need practical skills they can apply directly in their day-to-day work," said Chhavi Bhardwaj, CEO, Karmayogi Bharat.She said the initiative would help officials engage with AI confidently, use it responsibly and translate new capabilities into better public outcomes.Pragya Misra, head of strategy and government affairs, OpenAI India, said the country's AI opportunity depended not merely on access to technology but also on how effectively institutions and individuals used it."With more than 1.7 crore government employees across the Centre, States and Union Territories registered on iGOT Karmayogi, the platform offers a powerful way to build practical AI capability at scale," she said.The partnership comes amid the Centre's broader push to integrate AI into governance while developing skills needed to use the technology responsibly.However, the announcement does not specify when the courses will become available, how many will be introduced or what proportion of the platform's registered users will be eligible for training.Karmayogi Bharat, a government company under the department of personnel and training, operates the iGOT platform as part of Mission Karmayogi's programme for continuous professional development of civil servants.

World.title: Belagavi Sub-Registrar office shifted
World.content:
The district administration has shifted the Belagavi Sub-Registrar office to the Deputy Commissioner’s office premises.

The new office started functioning on Monday. The relocation clears the existing site for the construction of a proposed five-storey administrative building that will accommodate multiple government offices.

The existing Sub-Registrar office building will be demolished to make way for the proposed five-storey administrative complex.

The plan is to bring various government offices under one roof, making it easier for citizens to access multiple government services at a single location, said a release.

World.title: Telangana to fill all police vacancies by 2028, recruit 5,000 more personnel: CM Revanth Reddy
World.content:
Telangana government will fill all existing vacancies in the Police Department by 2028, with steps already initiated to recruit another 5,000 personnel, Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy announced on Wednesday while reiterating the government’s commitment to strengthening policing and improving the welfare of personnel and their families.

Addressing the Police Commemoration Day parade, also observed as Police Martyrs’ Day, at the Police Martyrs’ Memorial in Goshamahal Police Stadium, Hyderabad, the Chief Minister said maintaining law and order is essential for the State’s development and that the government has accorded the highest priority to the Police Department.

He said the government had already appointed 112 Deputy Superintendents of Police (DSPs), describing the recruitment as unprecedented, and initiated steps to fill another 5,000 vacancies.

Paying tributes to police personnel who lost their lives in the line of duty, Mr. Reddy said 154 police personnel had died across the country during the year. He remembered Telangana Assistant Sub-Inspector D. Devi Singh, constables Empalli Pramod Kumar and Seelam Kamalakar, and Gajula Soumya of the Excise Department, who lost their lives while on duty.

Assuring the families of the deceased personnel of continued government support, he announced that the ex-gratia for Home Guards who die in the line of duty would be increased from ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh and directed Director General of Police C.V. Anand to take the necessary steps.

The Chief Minister also highlighted the enhanced compensation for police personnel who die during duty. The ex-gratia for constables has been increased from ₹40 lakh to ₹1 crore, while that for Head Constables and ASIs has been raised from ₹45 lakh to ₹1 crore.

For Sub-Inspectors, the compensation has been increased from ₹45 lakh to ₹1.25 crore, and for Inspectors, from ₹50 lakh to ₹1.25 crore. Families of DSPs and Additional SPs would receive ₹1.50 crore, compared with the earlier ₹50 lakh, while the compensation for SPs and IPS officers has been doubled from ₹1 crore to ₹2 crore.

Modern policing must retain humane approach

Highlighting the changing nature of crime, Mr. Reddy said the government was working towards modernising the Police Department and equipping personnel with advanced technology to tackle emerging challenges. However, he cautioned that technological advancement should not come at the cost of the humane approach expected of police officers.

Mr. Reddy also highlighted the appointment of transgender persons as traffic assistants, stating that the initiative had helped strengthen their dignity and self-respect. He said ensuring women’s safety was not the responsibility of the police alone and called upon society to play an active role in preventing crimes against women.

DGP flags cybercrime, drugs and organised crime as emerging challenges

Speaking at the programme, Mr.Anand said the sacrifices of police personnel who fought terrorism, Naxalism, Maoism and other threats had contributed significantly to maintaining peace and enabling development in Telangana.
