World.title: Russell Brand treated 21yo woman 'like an animal' after rape, court hears
World.content:
The jury in Russell Brand's criminal trial has heard from a woman who claims the celebrity raped her at his London home in 2009 and treated her "like an animal".

Warning: this article contains details some readers may find distressing.

The actor and comedian is before London's Southwark Crown Court on three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to six women in the United Kingdom across a decade from 1999.

Mr Brand, 51, has denied all the charges against him and previously told police that he never took part in non-consensual sexual activity.

On Wednesday, local time, the jury was played more of the police interview of a woman who is the youngest of the six accusers.

She was 21 at the time of the alleged rape and Mr Brand was 33.

In the video, she tells a detective she met Mr Brand after one of his live shows at the Hammersmith Apollo, and engaged in a consensual sex act with him in his dressing room.

She said Mr Brand took her number and invited her to his house the following week.

In the video and in court, she said that when she arrived they went upstairs to the bedroom, but he asked her to shower first.

"He asked me to shower because he said my hair smelt funny ... when I came out, he asked me to brush my teeth," the woman said.

She said that what started as consensual sex, then changed suddenly into an activity she did not consent to, and she begged him to stop.

This picture taken by a real estate agency in 2009 was tendered as evidence in court, and shows Russell Brand's bedroom. (Supplied: Metropolitan Police)

Under cross examination by Mr Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC, the woman agreed that in 2009 she was a "huge" Russell Brand fan.

"I completely adored him, I was obsessed with him," she said of the famous comedian.

Mr Winter put to her that those feelings and thoughts "clouded" her judgement and caused her to do things she would not have otherwise done.

The woman acknowledged she went to his home willingly for what she expected to be consensual sex but added, "I didn't consent to what happened to me, I have said that repeatedly in the questioning ... I made it clear throughout all of my statements."

The woman told the court that after Mr Brand raped her, the entertainer looked "horrified" and "told me to clean up the mess that I made", before pointing her to wet wipes kept in the bathroom.

The jury was also played the video of the woman's second police interview where she speaks about a text message Mr Brand sent her after he spotted her at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival a few months later.

The woman told police she could not remember what Mr Brand's first message said but she replied, "why are you even messaging me?".

She said he wrote back, "because you are dirty and I want to push you further".

"I said, 'I think you pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal', and I remember his response was immediate, he said 'I'm sorry'."

Mr Winter put to her: "You did not reply, did you, that 'you raped me'?" She replied: "No."

Mr Winter then said, "You replied, 'you pushed me far enough and you treated me like an animal'. And that's because he had pushed you and probably had treated you like an animal, but he didn't rape you."

"I didn't consent," the woman replied.

After the alleged assault, the woman said she told her close friends and her parents, who took her to a clinic for treatment, but she decided not to report the incident to police at the time.

The trial continues.

World.title: Macron calls Trump's comments on French riots 'stupid'
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron has described comments by US President Donald Trump and other world leaders blaming immigration for riots in France as "unacceptable" and "stupid".

The French president said foreign leaders, including those “on the other side of the Atlantic”, had been exploiting unrest in France for their own political agenda.

Thousands of people have been arrested in France as protests over the soaring cost of living has led to widespread looting.

Why protests are spreading across Europe Protests are sweeping across Europe, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets in dozens of cities across the content. This is what you need to know.

Mr Trump has used the violence and riots gripping France to make unsubstantiated claims that immigration is responsible for the unrest, urging Mr Macron to "close your borders and take control before it is too late".

On Wednesday, Mr Macron said there had "been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath” of the looting.

“And that has led to comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said.

Asked by a reporter if he was referring to Mr Trump, Mr Macron replied: “Among others."

Thousands of people have been arrested in France as protests over the soaring cost of living has led to widespread looting. (Reuters: Stephane Mahe)

Mr Macron went on to say that AI-generated images had been circulating online depicting scenes that "never actually happened in France".

"We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false," Mr Macron said in Qatar at the end of a tour of energy suppliers.

“The fact is, all the people who are speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country.

“When I see leaders who are in the middle of election campaigns, whether in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic ... they’re using our country for their own political campaigns. And we don’t need that.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said its office can provide the countries concerned with the necessary clarification, "to help them avoid spreading or amplifying false information and making baseless claims on social media".

AP

World.title: E-scooter hospitalisations more than tripled since 2019
World.content:
Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).

The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25.

Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall.

It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified.

The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the last decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable.

New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said.

AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices.

"Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said.

" This report provides the first national view on this topic, while also highlighting where more data is needed. "

What can improve safety?

E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research.

E-bike explainer When Barnaby Joyce was deputy prime minister and transport minister in 2021, his assistant minister Kevin Hogan made a quiet, but hugely significant change to the Road Vehicle Standards Act.

Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth.

"Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said.

Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns.

Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices.

"It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said.

"But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide."

Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation.

People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence.

Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision.

New laws for e-mobility devices in effect from today: what you need to know Laws for e-bike and e-scooter riders come into effect from July 1: we've unpacked the changes for you

Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations.

It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public.

"So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said.

Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people.

"Ideally we can get into schools and teach them how to ride a device safely. That's probably going to take out the majority of the problematic behaviour," he said.

"Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40.

"That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode."

World.title: House prices across capitals post steepest quarterly decline ever: Domain
World.content:
House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain.

Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record.

The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent.

Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction".

Houses and units dropped in price for a second consecutive month. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

Australia's biggest property markets of Sydney and Melbourne recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent respectively.

Unit prices also dropped by 3.5 per cent, the second consecutive quarter of both property types declining.

It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist.

Nicola Powell says conditions have shifted to be more favourable for buyers. (Supplied)

"What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said.

"The balance of power has shifted towards buyers.

"Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations."

The cumulative impact of the rate rises, lower affordability and cost of living pressure has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality.

"It's been a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said.

Gerard Burg says the fall in prices has been driven by lower demand. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

Australia's most valuable homes falling the most

While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities.

Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality.

In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile.

Nationwide, lower value homes have experienced much slower drop in prices, Cotality said.

Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile.

Cameron Kusher says fewer buyers and higher interest rates are pushing down the prices of more expensive properties. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The heavier downturn in the more expensive properties is a result of fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher.

"They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said.

However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable.

Mr Burg agreed, saying the lower-priced homes remained affordable to a higher number of buyers.

"The median house really appears kind of out of reach of the median income household across much of the country," he said.

Prices were falling before federal budget

The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher.

House prices peaked last year, and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, both Mr Kusher and Mr Burg noted.

While the changes to the budget have been a factor, house prices were decreasing before the budget. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and the three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened confidence in the market.

New underquoting laws take effect The real estate industry says new laws targeting agents underquoting a house price are well-intentioned but poorly designed.

Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved compared to last year, with a total of 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality.

"Confidence has really evaporated. Affordability is very stretched and borrowing capacity is reduced dramatically," Mr Kusher said.

" People just aren't in a position or able to pay the prices that a lot of these properties are worth at the moment. "

He said home ownership rates had not moved much since the May budget changes, as a result of lower buyer confidence and stretched affordability.

"The first time is pretty scary as it is, and I think a lot of them are looking at it and saying, 'Well, prices are falling, why would I jump in now when there's quite a lot for sale, if I wait another six or 12 months properties will probably be cheaper,'" he said.

AI use in real estate industry The real estate industry is "one of the fastest adopters of AI", experts say.

" I just don't think first home buyers have that urgency anymore. "

He said prices would be unlikely to return to their previous heights, at least not in the short term.

"I think this downturn is probably going to drag on a bit longer than people expect, and it probably will until it looks like interest rates are going to actually be reduced again," he said.

World.title: Comedian hit with car in Taiwan after criticising Xi, prosecutors say
World.content:
Five people have been indicted in Taiwan for allegedly plotting to mow down a comedian with a car after his shows made fun of the Chinese government, including President ​Xi Jinping.

The Taiwanese defendants were hired by a Chinese person and began tracking comedian Huang Yi-hao in July and planned to break his arms and legs so he could not perform, according to the New Taipei Prosecutors Office.

Mr Huang was hit and injured ​by a car as he rode home on his scooter last month, leaving him with a bruised pelvis.

"This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist Party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence," the prosectors said.

Two of the defendants have admitted their involvement in the plan to injure the stand-up comedian, according to prosecutors.

Mr Huang said he only criticised Mr Xi for two and a half minutes - and his only fear at the time was that the audience would not laugh.

"Yet I was subsequently targeted with both a faeces-throwing attack and a deliberate vehicular assault," he wrote in a statement on Facebook.

In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a comedy club ​in Taipei hours before ​Mr Huang's scheduled performance.

Two people were prosecuted after vandalising a comedy club ​in Taipei earlier this year. (Facebook: Taipei Comedy Club)

Mr Huang thanked prosecutors and police for their work on the case and publicly invited them to his upcoming shows.

"If people can already be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist Party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?" he posted.

China's government is not tolerant of criticism of its leadership.

Taiwan, which China views as its own territory, has complained that Beijing is ‌trying to use "transnational repression" to go after people in Taiwan who the Chinese government views as separatists or are otherwise politically suspect.

Chinese student deported from Taiwan after controversial 'pinching' video A Chinese exchange student has been deported from Taiwan after posting a controversial video in which he used an illusion to make it look like he was pinching the Taiwanese president.

Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said anyone who accepted orders from China's Communist Party or its collaborators to take part in transnational repression would be "pursued to the end, with no leniency".

But Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to a request for comment.

Organisation Keep Taiwan Free said "intimidation must never become the price of speaking freely in Taiwan" following the alleged attack on Mr Huang.

"Whatever the target—a comedian, an activist, a journalist, or an ordinary citizen," it wrote.

"Taiwan's democracy depends on people being able to speak, criticise, joke, and disagree without fear."

ABC/AFP/Reuters

World.title: Putin announces release of imprisoned US citizen during meeting with Witkoff
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said that Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old US citizen held in Russian custody since 2022, had been freed and was at Pulkovo Airport in St Petersburg.

Mr Putin did not give further details in comments published by Russian state media on Wednesday, local time.

He made the announcement during a meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.

Mr Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher from Michigan, had been serving a nearly seven-year prison sentence in Russia after being convicted of mercenary activity at a closed-door trial.

Stephen Hubbard has been freed amid a US special envoy's visit to Russia. (Reuters)

He was arrested in April 2022 in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum, where Russian prosecutors alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint.

Russian state media reported he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Although his US-based lawyer, Martin De Luca, previously told Reuters Mr Hubbard had said the charges were false and that he was not part of any combat or military unit.

At the time of his release, Mr Hubbard was the only US prisoner held by Russia who was designated by Washington as "wrongfully detained".

Mr Witkoff, who is in St Petersburg for talks, thanked the Russian president for the gesture of goodwill.

The visit marks the ninth time that Mr Witkoff has met Mr Putin in person and comes more than two years after US President Donald Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.

Mr Witkoff urged Mr Putin to consider reviving US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and to review new ideas on ending the war amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War II.

"One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States," Mr Witkoff told Mr Putin.

" Even if we don't have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that. "

The meeting comes amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.

Ukrainian interceptor systems grounded by Starlink restrictions Ukraine is grappling with Starlink restrictions vital to operating its interceptors.

Mr Witkoff flew into Russia's second city on Wednesday morning local time, a day after conducting what a US official called "constructive" talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and NATO representatives, as Mr Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing".

US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Mr Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States.

High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections.

Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Mr Zelenskyy said that the Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.

White House denies interference with Starlink satellite capabilities

Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday local time that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that ​Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Reuters could not ​immediately verify the report.

Diesel deal unlikely to lower prices US President Donald Trump says his deal with Russia will drive down the cost of fuel but experts say its effect will be minimal.

Mr Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Mr Trump has said he was not responsible.

US Defense Secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said ​the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed ​to comply with.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Mr Witkoff's meeting with Mr Zelenskyy was positive and that Mr Witkoff would share the results with Russia.

He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let's see if we can make some progress," he said.

Reuters

World.title: Man arrested for allegedly making threats at WA MP's office with nunchucks
World.content:
Police have arrested a man after he reportedly made verbal threats while armed with "nunchucks" at state MP Hannah Beazley's electoral office in the inner-city Perth suburb of Victoria Park.

In a statement, police said they responded to reports of a man causing a disturbance at the electorate office on Albany Highway in Victoria Park about 1:15pm today.

They said he was armed with nunchucks — a weapon used in martial arts made of two short sticks connected by a short chain.

Police found the 56-year-old man in nearby Bentley, where he was apprehended. He is assisting police with their inquiries.

No-one was injured in the incident.

Man 'demanded to see MP'

Speaking outside parliament, Ms Beazley said the man had allegedly demanded to see her.

She said he was asking for her by name and "demanding access" to her while brandishing "home-made" nunchucks.

Police say the man made verbal threats at Hannah Beazley's electorate office. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"But apart from that, when he was escalated, [they] couldn't actually understand what he was saying," she said.

Ms Beazley said it was especially concerning due to the "heightened environment" following the alleged attack on Helen Haines in Victoria.

Hannah Beazley's electorate office is in the inner-city suburb of Victoria Park. (ABC News: Madigan Landry)

"I immediately jumped to concerns for [my staff], and to be honest concerns of getting home and being able to have a conversation with my kids before they found out from anyone else," she said.

"Often times my local police say to me I should be calling them more often with some of the stuff we see in the electoral office.

"I'm a highly accessible member of parliament, I love that … every time I walk down the street I'm stopped for a conversation — I do not want to see that change at all."

Staff upset

Earlier, Ms Beazley described the incident as a "confronting situation".

"I have spoken to my staff, who are understandably shaken and upset by what took place," she said in a statement.

"At this time, I do not know the motivation behind what occurred today."

Ms Beazley is the daughter of former federal opposition leader Kim Beazley, who was also a former US ambassador and WA governor.

Witness heard screaming

Olivia Nelson witnessed the incident from a business across the road.

"We heard some screaming, and that's not uncommon here along this strip," she said.

"But we heard it pretty prevalently so we went out there.

"And this guy was just screaming, cussing, going crazy."

Olivia Nelson said she heard screaming, which she described as "scary stuff". (ABC News: Madigan Landry)

Ms Nelson said the incident was different from what she ordinarily might witness along the highway.

"It was scary stuff," she said.

"He was much louder than the usual crowd that we see."

Safety discussion

The incident comes just two days after an attack on the federal member for Indi Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition in hospital after being run over outside her electoral office.

Leaders of the state's political parties are due to meet with representatives from government, police and the parliament tomorrow to discuss safety issues in the wake of the attack on Ms Haines.

Roger Cook said safety at electorate offices is under discussion. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Premier Roger Cook said yesterday it would offer an opportunity to talk about recent improvements, as well as "what further actions can be taken to improve the security arrangements".

"There's three elements here: there's the parliamentary precinct, where we're already undertaking significant upgrades in security," he said.

"There's electorate offices, and they've changed significantly since I was an electorate officer back in the 1990s, and obviously there's people's homes as well."

World.title: 18yo charged over alleged Alice Springs hit-and-run that left man dead
World.content:
Police have charged an 18-year-old man with dangerous driving causing death five months after an alleged hit-and-run that killed a 57-year-old man in Alice Springs.

In a statement this afternoon, an NT Police spokesperson said the man was arrested at Alice Springs police station today. He was also charged with hit-and-run "and multiple other offences relating to the fatal crash".

Police have previously said the 57-year-old was found unresponsive on Len Kittle Drive at about 9:30pm on May 20 and was "believed to have suffered head injuries consistent with a vehicle strike".

"The 57-year-old male victim received catastrophic injuries and died at the scene," the spokesperson said.

A week later, police announced a taskforce had been formed to investigate the man's death involving major crash and regional crime detectives after he was captured on dash cam footage walking south near the BMX track.

"It is believed he was struck and killed by a vehicle about 350 metres south of this location, near the Men’s Shed building at Blatherskite Park," the spokesperson said at the time.

In the statement today, the spokesperson said the investigation had involved "a coordinated effort by specialist police units from across the Northern Territory".

"Police acknowledge and appreciate everyone who came forward and assisted investigators," they said.

The 18-year-old man has been remanded in custody to appear in the Alice Springs Local Court tomorrow.

World.content:
PropertyNewsProperty prices Perth house prices suffer record fall in unprecedented market reversal Indigo Lemay-Conway October 22, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Perth has had a record-breaking plummet in house prices and the largest fall of any capital city in the country. Domain’s House Price Report, released on Thursday, showed Perth prices fell by 7.4 per cent ($88,664) in the September quarter to $1.115 million, marking the largest quarterly decline on record. House prices have now fallen for two consecutive quarters which is the longest downturn since 2019. Perth unit prices also declined by 6.5 per cent ($45,487) in the September quarter to $659,561 which was also the largest decline of any capital city and steepest quarterly fall on record.



Domain’s chief of research and economics, Dr Nicola Powell, said the report shows a “sharp turnaround” in pricing conditions across Perth. “When you think about what we’ve seen over recent years, we have seen really strong rates of price growth, and what occurred over the September quarter was a really strong reversal of that trend,” Powell said. She says the context of how fast and steep prices rose over the year was a key factor for what caused the steep drop. “We’ve seen an awful lot of headwinds collide over a short period of time this year. Rate hikes, another one just in September and the prospects of another rate hike, so that’s reduced borrowing capacity,” Powell said.



“We have seen changes to the way we tax investment housing, and that’s given investors jitters, and we’ve had new investor activity pullback. “We’ve also got cost of living pressures placing additional pressure on Australian households, and I think all of these things together have really switched the dynamics of Perth’s housing market. “Ultimately, what we have seen is probably demand is now weakening, and overall supply is now rising.” Property expert Mark Hay said the 7.4 per cent house price fall was “a bit more drastic” than what he was seeing on the ground.



“I think we’re just doing a fundamental correction,” he said. “My business does everything from $300,000 apartments to $30 million farms and everything in between. So we have a broad cross-section and I think if you look at the statistics, there’s just over 8000 listings on the market today. “What we call a balanced market is somewhere between 12 and 15,000 listings, and another good statistic is a balanced rental market is somewhere between 3 and 5 per cent vacancy factor and that is under 2 per cent currently, and rents are increasing. “So it’s a bit of a strange conundrum … most properties in the last three years went up nearly double, depending on where you are. So we’re just making an adjustment now.” Domain data shows that the only suburb to see a median house price decline over the year was Applecross which had a downturn of 7.7 per cent.



The suburbs that saw the biggest price increase across the year were Leederville with an annual increase of 32.8 per cent, followed by Madora Bay (30.8 per cent) and Kalamunda (30.5 per cent). Powell said that the shifting market was having a positive and negative effect on first home buyers. “I think for a first home buyer, there would be absolutely the dynamics of the fear of missing out when you place it in the context of how fast house prices have risen over recent years,” she said. “When you look at house prices over the last five years, they’ve risen 82 per cent in Perth, which is an extraordinary rate of growth over a five-year period. And when you look at unit prices, it’s 64 per cent. So I think for first-time buyers hearing the news that property prices are now falling in Perth, that might give an element of hope that they now have a market that they can actually try and keep up with.



“But I think the flip side of that is when you do have property prices falling, this can also make first home buyers nervous because you don’t necessarily want to be buying into a market where property prices are pulling back, and that ultimately your home could be worth less tomorrow than today.” Hay echoed similar sentiments, noting that first home buyers on the ground were more likely to sit and watch the market then try and jump in. “It’s fair to say that the majority of first home buyers are sitting on the sidelines and waiting. And this is what uncertainty does,” he said. “It’s the biggest fear, and we have a herd mentality. And when the chips are down, people say, ‘Oh, we’ll wait and see’ so everybody, including just normal people, are waiting and seeing.”



He said that drastic market fluctuations are not appealing to any audience. “Nobody likes a booming market or a down market. We all like it slow and steady, and in a slow and steady market you should see five to 10 per cent growth a year.” As for what the market will look like over the next few months, Powell said to expect a continued fall. “[This data] means that Perth isn’t immune to the change in economics and those macro factors that are influencing our other housing markets,” she said. “I think it’s very clear that Australia’s slowdown in pricing is now not isolated to our big major capital cities, as in Sydney and Melbourne. It is geographically broadened, and we’re seeing all of our capital cities fall. “So I think that the dynamics that are happening for our housing market, do indicate that prices are likely to continue to fall, and we are likely to continue to see prices fall for the rest of this year and probably into early next as well.”

World.title: I love Apple’s iPhone Duo. But here’s why you shouldn’t buy one
World.content:
TechnologyGadgets Opinion I love Apple’s iPhone Duo. But here’s why you shouldn’t buy one David Swan Technology editor October 21, 2026 — 11:00pm

October 21, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Apple’s iPhone Duo is the most exciting iPhone in nearly a decade, but most people shouldn’t buy one. Not yet, anyway. I’ve spent the past week with Apple’s first folding phone, which hits shelves on Friday, and it’s a genuine “oh wow” device. My mother-in-law wanted to hold it. So did friends who usually couldn’t care less about a new phone. After years of upgrades built on faster chips and slightly better cameras, it’s refreshing to see Apple try something different, even if Samsung and Motorola have been selling folding phones for years. Apple’s iPhone Duo is the most exciting iPhone in nearly a decade. But most people should hold off. Buyers are keen, too. Within hours of pre-orders opening on October 16, delivery dates on Apple’s online store had slipped to January, and Apple said demand had been “extraordinary”.





One big catch is weight. At 254 grams, the Duo is heavier than a standard iPhone and outweighs the taller iPhone 18 Pro Max, which weighs 249 grams. It feels dense in your pocket. Unfold it, and you get a 7.6-inch screen, a touch smaller than an iPad mini’s, with a matte finish that Apple says cuts glare and makes the crease harder to see. Here’s the thing, though: I barely used it. On a typical day, I’d open the Duo four or five times, and use it closed probably 100 times. That’s about 20 pick-ups as a regular phone for every one as a tablet. The iPhone hasn’t felt this new since the iPhone X ditched the home button in 2017. But most people will be perfectly happy with a regular iPhone, for a lot less money. Blame the apps. Apple sorts them into three tiers. Apps built for the Duo stretch the whole inner screen, with their controls moved to the side; Netflix and Slack do this. The next tier fills most of the screen. The oldest apps float in the middle surrounded by black space, and while a zoom button blows them up, in my testing they often came out soft and a bit blurry.



Multitasking doesn’t help either. You can run only two apps side by side, while Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 runs three, plus floating windows. To be fair, things are moving quickly. During my week with the Duo, Facebook, Instagram and Threads were all updated and look and work great on the big screen. My news apps, the AFL app, my banking apps and my public transport apps? Still waiting. When so much of what you use every day isn’t ready, unfolding the phone hardly seems worth the effort. You can run only two apps side by side, while Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 runs three, plus floating windows. Where the Duo shines is on the move. On a three-hour flight to Cairns for a family trip to Port Douglas, my toddler and I watched bits of Finding Nemo on the inner screen, which was vivid and looked fantastic. Over the flight, the battery dropped 10 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Phones Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone? It’s the same on the tram home from work, where Netflix or the NBA on the Duo beats a regular phone by a mile. This is its killer app: a tablet that folds into your pocket. Battery life is excellent. I’d typically go to bed with about half a charge left and not need to plug in until lunchtime the next day. That’s a day and a half between charges. Just don’t buy the Duo for its camera. It’s good, but no match for Apple’s Pro models. Zoom tops out at 2x, and there’s no variable-aperture main camera like the one on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Most of the time I didn’t notice. At the zoo I did, when my photos of faraway animals came nowhere near what I could see with my eyes.



The Duo does have one trick no other iPhone can match. Kid Cue plays animations on the outer screen to get small children looking at the lens, and my toddler looked right at the camera. But if photos matter most, buy the Pro Max. It’s the better camera phone, and much cheaper. Which brings us to price. The Duo starts at $3499 for 256GB and runs to $5899 for 2TB, the highest price Apple has charged for an iPhone. At every storage tier, that’s a whopping $1200 more than the equivalent Pro Max, and Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $2699. On Apple’s Afterpay financing, the base Duo costs about $146 a month over two years. About $50 of that, every month, is the price of the fold. It’s also eSIM-only, so if you’re still using a physical SIM card, check that your telco can switch you over. A demonstration of Apple’s iPhone Duo at Apple Park in Cupertino, California on September 19. Dominic Lorrimer So who is it for? I love this phone and the iPhone hasn’t felt this new since the iPhone X ditched the home button in 2017. But most people will be happy with a regular iPhone, for a lot less money.



Frequent flyers and people with long commutes will get the most out of it. Artists and note-takers will too, eventually: Apple Pencil support arrives later this year, but only for the cheaper USB-C model, and there’s nowhere on the phone to attach it. Either way, I’d wait a year for the second generation, when most apps should be optimised and the rough edges sanded down. I’m convinced the Duo will sell. I’m less convinced everyone needs one, or that foldables will overtake the humble smartphone slab. For now, the Duo is a brilliant support act, but the regular iPhone is still the headliner. The writer was loaned an iPhone Duo by Apple. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter. Sign up to receive it every Wednesday.

Executive chef Alejandro Saravia has crafted a flavour-packed itinerary across Latin America, right in the heart of Martin Place. First stop: Mexico. Slices of raw swordfish and crisp cucumber are rested in a cold, citrusy broth that hints of winter melon. The bluefin tuna belly tostada is a smoky and spicy affair with fiery salsa macha tempered by roasted avocado cream.

Next up is Argentina, with a well-charred and attentively seasoned Black Market Denver steak, melting gracefully on the palate and paired with tangy chimichurri.

A quick journey to Brazil calls for hearty, coconut-scented moqueca, the stew loaded with cod, prawn, scallop and squid, paired with steamed rice and toasted cassava flour.

The elegant dining room may be inside the heritage-listed former Sydney General Post Office, but with such a roving menu, and a wine list that follows the brief, you could well be in Buenos Aires.

Must-order dish: Black Market Denver steak with chimichurri.

World.content:

Judging by the flocks of locals loading up with Ciro’s takeaway boxes, Thirroul residents are quite aware their town has some of the best pizza in the state. The base is thin, blistered and subtly sour, and you can also have it in flatbread form to run through stracciatella with pistachio vinaigrette, or whipped ricotta underneath charred butternut pumpkin.

A pizzeria is only as good as its margherita, of course, and this one has the ideal balance of San Marzano tomato sweetness and creamy dollops of fior di latte. The white-sauced pizzas are just as good, including the garlicky, earthy “Shroom” number, which goes great guns with a house orange wine made by co-owner Joel Mucci’s label Benson and Mooch.

House-made limoncello also feels essential, and if you’re in the market for something more protein-heavy, ask about the wood-fired rice with confit chicken.

Good to know: On Mondays, only pizzas are available, but all of them are $20.

World.content:

David Prest of Thrumster writes: “When I started my Mechanical Engineering Certificate in 1975, I was forced to get a calculator as the rest of the class were worried that my use of logarithm tables and slide-rule (C8) wouldn’t be fast enough during the exam. I still have that calculator but the logarithm table book and the slide-rule have since gone.”

Perhaps Valerie Bray of East Killara can help: “I still have my old slide-rule and book of logarithm tables. The problem is, I’ve forgotten how to use them.”

“I once sat for an exam with an array of jelly beans (for sugar),” says Pasquale Vartuli of Pennant Hills. “I noticed an examiner looking at them to see if I had inscribed any messages on them. ”

Ian Nicholls of Baulkham Hills makes a good point “Years ago, during an engineering lecture, the topic of exam nerves came up. Our stern old school professor said self-control was important and went on to tell us that when he had a panic attack during an exam, he had to stab his hand with his pair of compasses to regain control.”

Edward Loong of Milsons Point (C8) has a fair bit to unpack regarding his new-found fame: “No, Graham Lum, I ain’t Edmund – he’s my older brother! Loong story. But, yes, Maureen Lysaght, Nancy is my older sister. Small world, indeed.”

World.title: Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park The powerhouse restaurant group makes a strategic play and giving the ’burbs what they want – a beautifully presented, Amalfi-inspired bistro, boozer and sun-kissed courtyard. Matt Shea October 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Finally, Alfi Eatery & Bar is here. This Mediterranean-influenced venue in the Everton Plaza precinct was intended to open in the winter. Given its ginormous size, though – 350 seats spread across 800 square metres – 80 or 90 days doesn’t seem so bad, especially when Ghanem Group only just came off the launch of the similarly large-format Hotel Terminus on Fish Lane. Alfi opens Thursday in Everton Park. Markus Ravik “There are elements that get easier about opening these venues, and elements that remain challenging,” managing director Nehme Ghanem says. “You can’t expect it to be smooth sailing ... But it also gets a little easier in some ways – back when we opened Byblos [in 2006], I was literally sleeping there, working 20 hours a day.” “We’re definitely more versed in what to expect now,” Nehme’s brother and co-director, Adonis Ghanem, adds. “You learn something with every opening and that experience helps, but every venue has its own challenges, team and audience, so you can never assume what worked somewhere else will automatically work again.”



Related Article Get Brisbane Times for $3 (plus free coffee) at some of the city’s top cafes Alfi encapsulates all of Ghanem Group’s accumulated experience after opening some of Brisbane’s buzziest venues – including Byblos, Donna Chang and Iris Rooftop – over the past 20 years. You can see it in the shrewd location in the middle of a suburb going through a significant demographic shift, and the Amalfi-inspired treatment, which flows effortlessly from a low-key, airy bistro into an expansive drinks garden. It’s a venue intended for locals and well designed for their needs. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “[These] larger venues definitely have another layer of complexity,” Adonis says. “With somewhere like Alfi or Hotel Terminus, you’re bringing together a lot of moving parts, from the kitchen and service through to the bar and the different spaces, and making sure they all work together. Alfi’s Amalfi-inspired fitout effortlessly flows from inside to the outdoor courtyard. Markus Ravik “The dining experience is still at the heart of what we do, but there’s more to think about when you’re operating a venue on this scale.”



Overseeing the design was regular Ghanem partner Space Cubed. It features Italian stone and marble, flashes of light timber and pastel upholstery, and arched windows and curved ceiling features. Inside, there’s a series of booths that can be curtained off from the dining room; outside, crazy pave tiling and a timber banquette that’s framed by greenery. Porchetta rolled with garlic, fennel and pepper with a rosemary jus. Markus Ravik For food, group executive chef Jake Nicolson and head chef Roberto D’Anna have written a menu that presents a selection of tweaked pub classics alongside pastas, pizza and larger Italian plates to share. Diners can expect char-grilled baby octopus with potato, celery and olives with a salmoriglio dressing; chicken parmigiana; slow-roasted porchetta rolled with garlic, fennel and pepper with a rosemary jus; spicy vodka parmesan rigatoni; beef ragu Napoletano; baked barramundi with potatoes, garlic, white wine and an acqua pazza broth; whole char-grilled heritage chicken with devil sauce and roast capsicum; and a selection of woodfired pizzas made with Alfi’s signature in-house dough that’s slow-fermented over 36 hours and cooked in an imported Valoriani Forte pizza oven that’s the centrepiece of the kitchen. Seafood scialatielli with capers, chilli, tomato, lemon, parsley-pangrattato. Markus Ravik



For drinks, there’s a punchy wine list that generally favours Australian wines made in a European style; short spritz, digestivo and signature cocktail menus; and nine beers on tap. “We’d love Alfi to become part of the local community,” Adonis says. “Somewhere people can bring their family, meet friends for a pizza and a drink, or spend a few hours enjoying the live music with a few drinks in the courtyard. Prosciutto pizza with rocket and cherry tomato. Markus Ravik “Good food is obviously a big part of that, but hospitality matters just as much. We want people to feel comfortable, well looked after, and enjoy themselves from the moment they walk in.” Open Tue-Wed 10am-10pm, Thu-Sat 10am-late, Sun 10am-10pm



Park Lane, Everton Plaza, 7 Sizer Street, Everton Park alfieatery.com.au

Unfold it, and you get a 7.6-inch screen, a touch smaller than an iPad mini’s, with a matte finish that Apple says cuts glare and makes the crease harder to see. Here’s the thing, though: I barely used it. On a typical day, I’d open the Duo four or five times, and use it closed probably 100 times. That’s about 20 pick-ups as a regular phone for every one as a tablet. The iPhone hasn’t felt this new since the iPhone X ditched the home button in 2017. But most people will be perfectly happy with a regular iPhone, for a lot less money. Blame the apps. Apple sorts them into three tiers. Apps built for the Duo stretch the whole inner screen, with their controls moved to the side; Netflix and Slack do this. The next tier fills most of the screen. The oldest apps float in the middle surrounded by black space, and while a zoom button blows them up, in my testing they often came out soft and a bit blurry.



Multitasking doesn’t help either. You can run only two apps side by side, while Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 runs three, plus floating windows. To be fair, things are moving quickly. During my week with the Duo, Facebook, Instagram and Threads were all updated and look and work great on the big screen. My news apps, the AFL app, my banking apps and my public transport apps? Still waiting. When so much of what you use every day isn’t ready, unfolding the phone hardly seems worth the effort. You can run only two apps side by side, while Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 runs three, plus floating windows. Where the Duo shines is on the move. On a three-hour flight to Cairns for a family trip to Port Douglas, my toddler and I watched bits of Finding Nemo on the inner screen, which was vivid and looked fantastic. Over the flight, the battery dropped 10 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Phones Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone? It’s the same on the tram home from work, where Netflix or the NBA on the Duo beats a regular phone by a mile. This is its killer app: a tablet that folds into your pocket. Battery life is excellent. I’d typically go to bed with about half a charge left and not need to plug in until lunchtime the next day. That’s a day and a half between charges. Just don’t buy the Duo for its camera. It’s good, but no match for Apple’s Pro models. Zoom tops out at 2x, and there’s no variable-aperture main camera like the one on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Most of the time I didn’t notice. At the zoo I did, when my photos of faraway animals came nowhere near what I could see with my eyes.



The Duo does have one trick no other iPhone can match. Kid Cue plays animations on the outer screen to get small children looking at the lens, and my toddler looked right at the camera. But if photos matter most, buy the Pro Max. It’s the better camera phone, and much cheaper. Which brings us to price. The Duo starts at $3499 for 256GB and runs to $5899 for 2TB, the highest price Apple has charged for an iPhone. At every storage tier, that’s a whopping $1200 more than the equivalent Pro Max, and Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $2699. On Apple’s Afterpay financing, the base Duo costs about $146 a month over two years. About $50 of that, every month, is the price of the fold. It’s also eSIM-only, so if you’re still using a physical SIM card, check that your telco can switch you over. A demonstration of Apple’s iPhone Duo at Apple Park in Cupertino, California on September 19. Dominic Lorrimer So who is it for? I love this phone and the iPhone hasn’t felt this new since the iPhone X ditched the home button in 2017. But most people will be happy with a regular iPhone, for a lot less money.



Frequent flyers and people with long commutes will get the most out of it. Artists and note-takers will too, eventually: Apple Pencil support arrives later this year, but only for the cheaper USB-C model, and there’s nowhere on the phone to attach it. Either way, I’d wait a year for the second generation, when most apps should be optimised and the rough edges sanded down. I’m convinced the Duo will sell. I’m less convinced everyone needs one, or that foldables will overtake the humble smartphone slab. For now, the Duo is a brilliant support act, but the regular iPhone is still the headliner. The writer was loaned an iPhone Duo by Apple. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter. Sign up to receive it every Wednesday.

Executive chef Alejandro Saravia has crafted a flavour-packed itinerary across Latin America, right in the heart of Martin Place. First stop: Mexico. Slices of raw swordfish and crisp cucumber are rested in a cold, citrusy broth that hints of winter melon. The bluefin tuna belly tostada is a smoky and spicy affair with fiery salsa macha tempered by roasted avocado cream.

Next up is Argentina, with a well-charred and attentively seasoned Black Market Denver steak, melting gracefully on the palate and paired with tangy chimichurri.

A quick journey to Brazil calls for hearty, coconut-scented moqueca, the stew loaded with cod, prawn, scallop and squid, paired with steamed rice and toasted cassava flour.

The elegant dining room may be inside the heritage-listed former Sydney General Post Office, but with such a roving menu, and a wine list that follows the brief, you could well be in Buenos Aires.

Must-order dish: Black Market Denver steak with chimichurri.

World.content:

Judging by the flocks of locals loading up with Ciro’s takeaway boxes, Thirroul residents are quite aware their town has some of the best pizza in the state. The base is thin, blistered and subtly sour, and you can also have it in flatbread form to run through stracciatella with pistachio vinaigrette, or whipped ricotta underneath charred butternut pumpkin.

A pizzeria is only as good as its margherita, of course, and this one has the ideal balance of San Marzano tomato sweetness and creamy dollops of fior di latte. The white-sauced pizzas are just as good, including the garlicky, earthy “Shroom” number, which goes great guns with a house orange wine made by co-owner Joel Mucci’s label Benson and Mooch.

House-made limoncello also feels essential, and if you’re in the market for something more protein-heavy, ask about the wood-fired rice with confit chicken.

Good to know: On Mondays, only pizzas are available, but all of them are $20.

World.title: No wonder exam results are on the slide
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

David Prest of Thrumster writes: “When I started my Mechanical Engineering Certificate in 1975, I was forced to get a calculator as the rest of the class were worried that my use of logarithm tables and slide-rule (C8) wouldn’t be fast enough during the exam. I still have that calculator but the logarithm table book and the slide-rule have since gone.”

Perhaps Valerie Bray of East Killara can help: “I still have my old slide-rule and book of logarithm tables. The problem is, I’ve forgotten how to use them.”

“I once sat for an exam with an array of jelly beans (for sugar),” says Pasquale Vartuli of Pennant Hills. “I noticed an examiner looking at them to see if I had inscribed any messages on them. ”

Ian Nicholls of Baulkham Hills makes a good point “Years ago, during an engineering lecture, the topic of exam nerves came up. Our stern old school professor said self-control was important and went on to tell us that when he had a panic attack during an exam, he had to stab his hand with his pair of compasses to regain control.”

Edward Loong of Milsons Point (C8) has a fair bit to unpack regarding his new-found fame: “No, Graham Lum, I ain’t Edmund – he’s my older brother! Loong story. But, yes, Maureen Lysaght, Nancy is my older sister. Small world, indeed.”

World.title: Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park The powerhouse restaurant group makes a strategic play and giving the ’burbs what they want – a beautifully presented, Amalfi-inspired bistro, boozer and sun-kissed courtyard. Matt Shea October 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Finally, Alfi Eatery & Bar is here. This Mediterranean-influenced venue in the Everton Plaza precinct was intended to open in the winter. Given its ginormous size, though – 350 seats spread across 800 square metres – 80 or 90 days doesn’t seem so bad, especially when Ghanem Group only just came off the launch of the similarly large-format Hotel Terminus on Fish Lane. Alfi opens Thursday in Everton Park. Markus Ravik “There are elements that get easier about opening these venues, and elements that remain challenging,” managing director Nehme Ghanem says. “You can’t expect it to be smooth sailing ... But it also gets a little easier in some ways – back when we opened Byblos [in 2006], I was literally sleeping there, working 20 hours a day.” “We’re definitely more versed in what to expect now,” Nehme’s brother and co-director, Adonis Ghanem, adds. “You learn something with every opening and that experience helps, but every venue has its own challenges, team and audience, so you can never assume what worked somewhere else will automatically work again.”



Related Article Get Brisbane Times for $3 (plus free coffee) at some of the city’s top cafes Alfi encapsulates all of Ghanem Group’s accumulated experience after opening some of Brisbane’s buzziest venues – including Byblos, Donna Chang and Iris Rooftop – over the past 20 years. You can see it in the shrewd location in the middle of a suburb going through a significant demographic shift, and the Amalfi-inspired treatment, which flows effortlessly from a low-key, airy bistro into an expansive drinks garden. It’s a venue intended for locals and well designed for their needs. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “[These] larger venues definitely have another layer of complexity,” Adonis says. “With somewhere like Alfi or Hotel Terminus, you’re bringing together a lot of moving parts, from the kitchen and service through to the bar and the different spaces, and making sure they all work together. Alfi’s Amalfi-inspired fitout effortlessly flows from inside to the outdoor courtyard. Markus Ravik “The dining experience is still at the heart of what we do, but there’s more to think about when you’re operating a venue on this scale.”



Overseeing the design was regular Ghanem partner Space Cubed. It features Italian stone and marble, flashes of light timber and pastel upholstery, and arched windows and curved ceiling features. Inside, there’s a series of booths that can be curtained off from the dining room; outside, crazy pave tiling and a timber banquette that’s framed by greenery. Porchetta rolled with garlic, fennel and pepper with a rosemary jus. Markus Ravik For food, group executive chef Jake Nicolson and head chef Roberto D’Anna have written a menu that presents a selection of tweaked pub classics alongside pastas, pizza and larger Italian plates to share. Diners can expect char-grilled baby octopus with potato, celery and olives with a salmoriglio dressing; chicken parmigiana; slow-roasted porchetta rolled with garlic, fennel and pepper with a rosemary jus; spicy vodka parmesan rigatoni; beef ragu Napoletano; baked barramundi with potatoes, garlic, white wine and an acqua pazza broth; whole char-grilled heritage chicken with devil sauce and roast capsicum; and a selection of woodfired pizzas made with Alfi’s signature in-house dough that’s slow-fermented over 36 hours and cooked in an imported Valoriani Forte pizza oven that’s the centrepiece of the kitchen. Seafood scialatielli with capers, chilli, tomato, lemon, parsley-pangrattato. Markus Ravik



For drinks, there’s a punchy wine list that generally favours Australian wines made in a European style; short spritz, digestivo and signature cocktail menus; and nine beers on tap. “We’d love Alfi to become part of the local community,” Adonis says. “Somewhere people can bring their family, meet friends for a pizza and a drink, or spend a few hours enjoying the live music with a few drinks in the courtyard. Prosciutto pizza with rocket and cherry tomato. Markus Ravik “Good food is obviously a big part of that, but hospitality matters just as much. We want people to feel comfortable, well looked after, and enjoy themselves from the moment they walk in.” Open Tue-Wed 10am-10pm, Thu-Sat 10am-late, Sun 10am-10pm



Park Lane, Everton Plaza, 7 Sizer Street, Everton Park alfieatery.com.au

World.title: Armed Offenders Squad storm Massey property after man reported with firearm
World.content:
The Armed Offenders Squad have stormed a property in the west Auckland suburb of Massey following reports of a man with a firearm.

An RNZ reporter at the scene said police used a battering ram to enter a house on Manutewhau Road about 10.45pm on Wednesday. They said several loud bangs were heard, accompanied by bright flashes.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407175242112

An ambulance was then seen driving through a cordon towards the property.

Another ambulance arrived later, and a man sitting up on a stretcher was brought out of the house and loaded into the back of a waiting ambulance soon after 11pm.

RNZ understands his injuries are not life-threatening.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Earlier, about 10pm, police said they were at a property in Massey following reports of a male with a firearm.

"Specialist Police staff are at the scene and are working to speak with the male to bring the situation to a safe conclusion.

"The scene is currently contained to the property on Manutewhau Road, and people are asked to avoid the area."

They said no one was believed to be injured at that time.

Police are in the west Auckland suburb of Massey following reports of a man with a firearm. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

The police Eagle helicopter began circling the area before 9pm.

Hate Hone St John confirmed it was called at 7.49pm and had an ambulance, rapid response and manager on standby.

It said the operations manager and ambulance were stood down by 10.15pm, but the rapid response remained on standby.

An online aviation tracker shows a Police helicopter circling above Massey. Screenshot / adsbexchange.com

RNZ's reporter said several armed police were blocking Manutewhau Road at the intersection of George McWhirter Avenue at 10pm.

Armed Offenders Squad (AOS) and police vehicles could be seen further down Manutewhau Road where they were focusing attention on a property near Orowaru Avenue.

Members of the AOS were coming and going up the front steps of a block of units.

What looked like a communications or negotiation unit, where several police staff were located, had also been set up on George McWhirter Avenue, the reporter said.

About 10.30pm, another police vehicle arrived and officers were seen removing and preparing rifles from the boot.

World.title: Blindspott cancels Auckland show after singer lands in hospital
World.content:
Blindspott's one-off show in Auckland has been cancelled after vocalist Damian Alexander landed in hospital.



The alternative metal band was due to host a release party for its new single Stitches on 7 November at The Powerstation.



In a post on social media, the band announced the event's cancellation.



"Last week, Damian experienced a serious vascular health issue that will require some time to heal and ongoing specialist follow-up," it said.



"He's doing well and is in good hands, and is incredibly grateful to the team at Auckland Hospital for the care he's received.



"Unfortunately, this means our November 7 show at Auckland's Powerstation has been cancelled, not postponed. All ticket holders will be advised of the refund process."



The release of Blindspott's upcoming album would also be put on hold until Alexander was medically cleared "to return to the studio and stage to put the finishing touches on the record".



"Damian wants to thank everyone who has reached out and checked in on him. He's incredibly grateful for the support and is focused on getting well," the band said.



"As a band and a family, Damian's health and wellbeing are our absolute priority. We're all behind him and wishing our brother a full and speedy recovery.



"Thank you all for your understanding, love and continued support."



Blindspott was formed in the late nineties in West Auckland.

World.title: Silver Ferns beat Australia again to take commanding Constellation Cup position
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have put themselves in the best possible position to win the Constellation Cup for just the fourth time after beating Australia 62-50 in Christchurch.

After losing the first Test in Auckland by six goals, the Diamonds came out stronger but the Silver Ferns managed to weather the storm to go 2-nil up before the series heads to Australia for the final two Tests.

The Silver Ferns have now beaten Australia four times in a row, going back to last year's annual series, while the Diamonds surprising losing streak on New Zealand soil now sits at 12.

Peta Toeava returned to the black dress for the first time in a year, starting at wing attack, where she quickly resumed her telepathic connection with her former Mystics team-mate Grace Nweke.

The Diamonds welcomed vice-captain Kate Moloney back, after a finger injury and the more traditional Australian shooting line-up of Sophie Garbin and Kiera Austin provided good structure for the visitors.

New Zealand led 17-14 at the end of the first quarter, where a few turnovers were the difference.

Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich made several changes throughout the game, particularly in her defensive end.

The Silver Ferns patiently absorbed the pressure of a more clinical Australian side, and were able to bide their time before finding opportunities to bomb it into Nweke.

The circle defensive pairing of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger built across the game and the Ferns extended their lead 33-26 at half-time.

Mila Reuelu-Buchanan came on at wing defence at half-time, which saw Kate Heffernan and Maddy Gordon shift one position up the court.

Grace Nweke of the Silver Ferns and Courtney Bruce tussle for the ball. John Davidson / www.photosport.nz

The Silver Ferns went out to an 11 goal lead in the early stages of the third quarter before the visitors launched a fightback.

Jessie Grenvold, who made her Diamonds' debut in the first test, was able to make some inroads at goal keep.

The Diamonds managed to cut New Zealand's lead to just three heading into the final turn but the home side held their nerve.

Te Paea Selby-Rickit entered at goal attack for the final quarter and Toeava returned, which saw Gordon shift back to centre, and Kate Heffernan went to the bench.

Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua told Sky Sport some changes needed to be made as "tired errors" came into the game.

Shooter Donnell Wallam made a long-awaited return for Australia and faced the Silver Ferns for the first time in her career, when she came on during the final quarter.

Toeava had an impressive 45 minutes on court. Nweke had a brilliant game finishing with 49 from 55.

Gordon, who maintained a high work rate in the midcourt, came away with MVP honours.

The Diamonds penalty count of 84 was significantly higher than the Silver Ferns.

Despite the bigger score line, the Diamonds posed more challenges for the Silver Ferns in the second Test.

The Silver Ferns have found playing in Australian a challenge, winning just one of their last nine tests across the Tasman.

If the series ends with two wins each, the winner will be decided by goal percentage.
