Tech.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
Tech.content:
Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle.

As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men.

The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.”

Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.”

The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution.

Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated.

Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.

A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels.

Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy, which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire, TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring.

Tech.title: Roku Pro Series OLED TV Review (2026)
Tech.content:
From there, Roku’s friendly UI walks you through the usual configuration steps, many of which you can complete on your phone (as opposed to navigating onscreen menus with the remote, always a slower process).

Photograph: Rick Broida

Four well-marked HDMI ports reside on the left side of the Roku Pro Series, set close enough to the edge that they’re easy to reach. The top one, clearly labeled “eARC,” is painted with Roku’s trademark purple for quick at-a-glance identification, while the bottom two—120-Hz ports intended for gaming—are white. (Why two? It’s a bit unusual, yes, but splendid for those who operate more than one console.) The TV also supplies the usual coaxial input for a traditional cable or antenna hookup, an optical audio input for older soundbars and an Ethernet port if you want to bypass Wi-Fi.

Speaking of which, it’s a bit disappointing that Roku opted for Wi-Fi 5 here instead of Wi-Fi 6 or later. That said, my Eero Pro router also tops out at Wi-Fi 5, and it’s likely the same situation in plenty of other households. I encountered zero issues in terms of connection reliability, stability, or performance.

The Roku operating system continues to offer the most intuitive and novice-friendly TV viewing experience, marked by its colorful, oversize app icons and simple menus. There’s a bit more UI customization available now than in Rokus past, like the option to display icons in four columns instead of three. And there’s a sense of whimsy here not found elsewhere, including the lively “Roku City” screensaver that appears when the TV is idle. You can also opt for Roku Backdrops, an art-themed screensaver that does a solid Samsung The Frame impression.

Tech.title: A Design Flaw in Share Links Exposes Users’ Personal Conversations With Meta’s Muse
Tech.content:
Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.

Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

Tech.title: I’m Baffled by Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max, but I Love It Anyway
Tech.content:
It feels a bit weird to be writing about Oppo’s new Find X10 Pro Max flagship phone. I only reviewed the company’s last flagship, the Find X9 Ultra, back in June. But as the larger number in the name suggests, the X10 Pro Max is the first of Oppo’s next generation of Android phones, packing a whole suite of new tech, from fancy new camera sensors to the new MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing it for the past week or so, and there’s no question it’s a powerhouse phone that’s well worthy of its flagship title. But I said much the same about the Find X9 Ultra, with both phones boasting incredible Hasselblad-branded camera setups and potent processors. Both also make use of detachable telephoto zoom lenses for shooting long-distance photos.

It’s not that I have any problem with the X10 Pro Max so far — it’s great in every respect — it’s just that I don’t know why it needs to exist so soon after the X9 Ultra debuted. I’ve already been quite vocal about companies launching new flagships every year and the X10 Pro Max doesn’t seem to have moved the story on all that much since the X9 Ultra. And at a starting price of £1,499 in the UK (roughly $2,010) the Pro Max costs roughly the same as the X9 Ultra, too. It does come with a “complimentary accessory” in the form of either the detachable telephoto lens or an Oppo smartwatch.

More from CNET

The glass and metal design looks classy. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Between the Find X9 Pro launched last October and the X10 Pro Max seen today, there are clear upgrades across the board. But between the more recent Find X9 Ultra and the Find X10 Pro Max it’s less clear-cut. Right now, I can’t tell you which has the better camera — both the X10 Pro Max and the six-month-old X9 Ultra have awesome setups, and I’ve taken great photos with both.

The Ultra phones have traditionally stood apart from the Pro phones by having better screens, processors and camera systems. With the X10 Pro Max matching — or beating — the X9 Ultra’s performance across the board, I’m struggling to understand why you’d pick one over the other. Maybe this distinction will become clearer later.

Or for a more positive spin, I find myself in a situation where both these phones appear so equally superb that I can’t choose between them.

If you live in the US, this is something of a moot point. Oppo doesn’t officially sell its phones in your country, so you can’t buy either of them. If you’re still keen to know more about this phone, here’s what I like so far.

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Great cameras with new tech

I’ve been impressed with the cameras on Oppo’s recent phones, and the Find X10 Pro Max is no exception. It echoes some of what I saw in the Find X9 Ultra (200-megapixel main and telephoto lenses), but it bumps the ultrawide to 200 megapixels and adds an interesting upgrade to its main camera sensor.

There are a whole bunch of cameras and sensors on the back. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The main camera uses a Samsung Isocell HPC sensor with something called DeepPix technology. What this essentially does is allow for more light information to be captured, resulting in a dynamic range (the difference between the brightest and darkest parts of an image) of around 17 stops. That’s up there with professional cinema cameras, but it also sounds like similar technology to the LOFIC (lateral overflow integration capacitor) sensor seen in phones like the Leitzphone by Leica and Xiaomi and in the recent DJI Osmo Pocket 4P.

Because I’m neither an image sensor engineer nor a physicist, I can’t tell you exactly how these technologies differ — or if it really matters, as fundamentally they aim to achieve the same thing: better-looking images with more light information captured.

Technicalities of the sensor aside, I’ve been pleased with many of the images I’ve taken with the phone so far. Dynamic range is (perhaps unsurprisingly) excellent, with colors that look punchy yet natural in both tone and saturation.

Taken with the main camera, this shot has great dynamic range, with bold colors that still look realistic. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And again, I love the vibrant but natural tones of this scene from the main camera. It’s pin-sharp, too. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I like this shot, but I do think it looks a bit too “HDR” from the image processing. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

This shot is a little drab, but it’s still packed with detail. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While some images can look a bit overprocessed, with unnaturally lightened shadows, I think the phone gets the balance right better than many Android cameras. Oppo also says it’s taken a lighter-touch approach with artificial image sharpening, instead giving images a more natural appearance when it comes to fine details. I think this has worked for the most part, although I sometimes find it goes too far the other way, with some highlights having a noticeable haziness and lack of definition around them.

I shot this in the Master mode in order to take manual control of the white balance, as well as make extra edits in Adobe Lightroom. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I used Master mode here too to choose my own white balance as well as use manual focus to ensure focus was on the owl and not on the bars of the cage. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Like with the Find X9 Ultra, I found that some of my favorite shots were taken using the Master mode where I took manual control of settings, including white balance, and in some cases shot in DNG raw to apply my own edits in Adobe Lightroom.

The ultrawide has been bumped to 200 megapixels and its shots are crystal clear. I used one of the color filters here to add some drama to the scene. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Taken at 6X zoom, this shot of a man with his falcon looks great. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

At 3X optical zoom this shot is vibrant, with rich colors. There is a softness to the highlights around the yellow pylons in the middle, however. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There’s little color shift between the main and ultrawide lenses, and the 3x optical telephoto camera captures crisp details, with almost no noticeable drop in quality when you push the zoom to 6x by using digital cropping.

With the telephoto lens attached I could snag this shot of a seagull needlessly trying to ride a boat. Surely it knows it can fly? Andrew Lanxon/CNET

You can go right up to 40X zoom, though the details become noticeable softer at this point. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

If you want to take the zoom even further, slap on the physical telephoto zoom lens to achieve an optical zoom up to 10x and a digital zoom up to a whopping 40x. I’ve used these lenses on the X9 Ultra and the X9 Pro before and they’re good fun, especially if you’re into wildlife photography and want to capture a bird off in the distance.

The quality isn’t great when you push it right to 40x, and the phone uses AI to upscale some of the details, but it’s far better than what you’d achieve with the phone by itself. I don’t know exactly how much the X10 Pro Max’s telephoto lens will cost, but keep in mind that the Hasselblad lens for the Find X9 Ultra was a princely $400 accessory.

I used one of the camera’s color profiles to give a slight filmic look to this scene. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are a variety of new filters to choose from, all of which use a grid-based adjustment system, not unlike Apple’s Photographic Styles. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I love taking panoramic images like this. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The camera comes with extras like the Hasselblad XPAN mode for taking wide, narrow panoramic images, along with a new color filter tool that’s basically identical to the color and tone grid Apple uses in its Photographic Styles. Still, I’m not complaining — it works well and it’s easy to craft a more creative look for your image. I suspect Apple may not be thrilled at the similar interface.

I’m overall impressed with the camera on the Find 10 Pro Max. It’s more than capable of taking stunning images, especially if you’re into your zoomed-in shots. But I can’t say if it’s any better than the Find X9 Ultra, or even if it’s supposed to be. The new sensor technology should mean it’s the better camera, but the Find X9 Ultra has a second telephoto zoom camera, a longer telephoto accessory and it’s covered in Hasselblad branding and colors.

To understand the minute differences between their camera capabilities, I need time to put the two phones side-by-side. I also want to test it against the Leitzphone to see how the DeepPix sensor compares to the LOFIC one. The Leitzphone’s sensor is also physically larger, and the phone itself offers unique photography tricks like its continuous telephoto zoom, its physical settings wheel and its variety of Leica film profiles, all of which make it the camera phone to beat, in my opinion.

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Solid performance, too many apps

The Find X10 Pro Max is powered by the latest MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chip, rather than a Qualcomm chip as you’ll find in the Find X9 Ultra. There are some differences in performance between the two processors, with the X10 Pro putting in better processing scores on Geekbench 7, while the Find X9 Ultra’s Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip consistently outperforms on 3DMark’s graphics benchmark test.

It’s a high performance phone in every sense. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

In everyday use, the X10 Pro Max was capable of handling everything I could throw at it, from demanding games like Genshin Impact to editing images in Adobe Lightroom. I honestly can’t say I find the phone to be any more (or less) powerful than the X9 Ultra, so if you were hoping to choose between the phones on benchmark tests alone, then you’re out of luck.

What continues to bug me with Oppo’s phones is the needless amount of junk you’ll find preinstalled the first time you turn it on. There are third-party apps such as Temu, TikTok, ChatGPT and LinkedIn, and apps I’ve never heard of, including Bigo Live and iQiyi. Throw in the wealth of Oppo’s own apps, shopping services and theme stores, and the phone feels cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to download anything of your own.

This is nothing new, though — I leveraged the same criticism at the Find X9 Ultra, and indeed many other Android phones. Yes, you can uninstall any of the garbage you don’t want, but it irks me that these expensive phones feel ad-supported because of the casserole of nonsense clogging your app library.

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Battery life and other features

The Find X10 Pro Max packs a whopping 8,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, at least in my test version; some EU regions will have a slightly smaller 7,150-mAh battery. After an hour of our YouTube streaming rundown test, the phone had dropped from full to 98% remaining and by the third hour was only down to 89%.

I don’t love the amount of preinstalled junk on the phone. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

That’s not bad at all, putting the phone in line with top performers like the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra although not quite troubling the epic stamina of the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It also didn’t quite beat the scores achieved by the Find X9 Ultra. Still, it’s a great effort and you should comfortably expect the phone to offer at least a full day of demanding use with enough spare to get you a fair way into day two.

The phone supports 80-watt wired fast charging which should make it extremely quick to put some juice back in the tank if you’re running short before heading outside. Though you’ll need to get a compatible fast charger. Oppo also reckons the battery is optimized for longevity, promising the battery capacity will only drop to 80% after five years.

While I obviously haven’t been able to test this, I’m pleased that there’s a focus on longer-lasting hardware to keep your device going for longer. Oppo offers five years of software updates and six years of security updates, which is a step behind the seven years Google and Samsung offer, but I suppose it could be worse.

Oppo Find X10 Pro Max: Should you buy it?

As I mentioned at the start, I find this phone’s existence confusing. It’s a camera powerhouse, but it comes right off the back of another Oppo camera powerhouse — there’s a huge amount of overlap in what these phones offer and who might be interested in buying them. They’re both superb, no question about that, but it’s like inviting two Michelin Star chefs to cook the same meal for your party — there might be subtle differences that mean some like one over another, but at the end of the day, why have both?

I rarely wish for companies to offer less in their product lineups, but in this instance I feel Oppo might have been wise to hold back some of its camera innovations — especially the new sensor tech. Instead, the Find X10 Pro Max could have been more focused on general lifestyle, productivity and gaming, giving the Find X9 Ultra a bit more breathing room.

Everything is great about this phone from its vibrant display to its awesome cameras. But I loved the same about the X9 Ultra, too. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Then, after Spring next year, the company could launch the Find X10 Ultra, packed with incredible camera tech that totally changes the game and makes it feel fresh and exciting. Instead, the X10 Pro Max feels so close to its six-month-old sibling that I’m struggling to work out which one is actually better and, more importantly, why both need to exist at the same time.

Early adopters who shelled out the high price for the Find X9 Ultra specifically for the camera performance may well feel a little cheated that the company has so quickly launched a phone with brand-new, superior image sensor technology. It feels like Oppo is at risk of diluting its impact, cannibalizing sales of its own products and potentially even alienating existing customers.

But company strategy aside, the X10 Pro Max is excellent, offering everything you’d need from a flagship phone right now. It’s got enough power for any of your daily tasks and the camera is well-equipped to capture your world as you see it. How it compares to the competition remains to be seen.

Tech.title: The iOS 27 Setting That Can Flag a Scam While You’re Still on the Phone
Tech.content:
Two-factor authentication stops a stranger from logging into your bank account. It does nothing when a scammer on the phone convinces you to log in and send the money yourself. Apple’s answer in iOS 27 is Impersonation Risk Detection, a privacy setting that lets supported apps request a quick risk check before you complete a payment or account change. Your iPhone analyzes signals such as timing and interaction patterns on the device, then gives the app a simple rating without sharing the data behind it. It’s off by default, and turning it on takes a few taps.

The tool protects against active social engineering scams, which try to scoop up money or account information by posing as trusted entities, such as your bank or a government agency. Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes factors such as interaction patterns, timing and context to indicate one of three risk levels:

Unknown: There’s no evidence or detection of suspicious activity. This doesn’t mean the action is confirmed safe.

Medium: The action shows some signs of suspicious activity.

High: There are significant signs of suspicious activity.

The analysis happens on-device, which means your personal data is never sent to Apple or the app you’re using. The app — not Apple — receives only the determined threat level and can decide any necessary actions to take. Based on the risk level, the app might show a warning, add a delay or ask you to verify your identity.

Here’s how to enable Impersonation Risk Detection for an extra layer of scam protection. But note that it’s only available in supported apps, so it won’t work with everything.

How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection

1. Open Settings.

2. Tap Privacy & Security.

3. Tap Impersonation Risk Detection.

4. Enable the Share with App Developers toggle.

CNET/Apple

After enabling or disabling this toggle, Apple notes it can take up to 24 hours for the feature to activate or deactivate. That delay serves as a barrier against scammers who might tell people to turn off the feature so they can keep their schemes moving. Once the feature is active, you can return to this menu and see which apps have requested a risk assessment and why.

This feature won’t catch everything, so you should stay vigilant. For example, if someone wants you to turn this feature off, they could be trying to scam you.

CNET/Apple

If you find yourself bombarded with constant requests to verify your identity, or you want to turn off the feature for any other reason, just toggle off the Share with App Developers option. You can also disable access to individual apps by following the above steps, tapping the individual app and then tapping the toggle next to the app.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and what iOS 27.0.1 fixes on your device.

Tech.title: PHP Vulnerabilities Could Put Much of the Internet at Risk, Experts Warn
Tech.content:
An agency that monitors the programming language PHP issued a severe warning on Tuesday that it had identified two major cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Fixes should have been deployed on Wednesday at 10 a.m. ET, but security experts are urging website administrators to take immediate notice and precautions.

PHP is a free, open-source programming language that much of the web is built on. The warnings are unusually severe, rated 9.2 out of 10. While we don’t have many details about the specifics of the vulnerabilities yet, the concern is that the exploit could be used by bad actors to hack into websites. The vulnerabilities could affect 70% of the world’s websites, according to the Wall Street Journal. That’s why security agencies around the globe, including the US National Security Agency and the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, are urging website administrators to install the updates or take their sites offline until they are able to patch them.

Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or… — NSA Cyber (@NSACyber) October 21, 2026

Cloudflare’s chief technology officer Dane Knecht said Wednesday morning that the company has deployed a fix to its firewall, but it’s still seeing early attacks emerging.

More from CNET

OpenAI said in a blog post on Wednesday that the vulnerabilities in PHP were discovered with its AI model, GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz, an AI cloud cybersecurity company, also independently identified the vulnerabilities, according to the ChatGPT maker. This incident “highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” OpenAI said.

This is a developing story. Check back often for additional updates.

Tech.title: My Favorite Budget Camera Brand Is Finally Getting 4K Plus and a Mile-Long Range
Tech.content:
Amazon’s Blink is one of my go-to security brands for long battery life and affordability. It also sports one of the easiest security camera apps to learn and has one of the lowest subscriptions if you want to add cloud or AI features. But those benefits come with restrictions, and Blink has focused on only a few camera lines with relatively few choices. Today, that changed.

Blink has announced five new security cameras that significantly expand its current offerings. Not only are they all available for preorder right now, but they include features Blink hasn’t dabbled in before. Prices may be a bit higher than usual for this new tech, but they’re still affordable compared to alternatives, and I can’t wait to test them all out. Here are the features I’m most interested in trying.

4K resolution at last

Blink’s new Mini cams have tricks, like a boosted 4K resolution. Blink

Blink only recently updated its cameras to 2K resolution, but now it’s time for another leap. The Blink Mini 4K Plus ($80) is made for both indoor and outdoor use, packing in more detail than any other Blink camera. It has a 115-degree field of video and two-way audio, too. Most major security companies have at least a couple of 4K models available for those seeking better visuals, and now Blink joins them with a cam more compact than most high-resolution offerings.

More from CNET

The Mini 4K Plus is still larger than the other Blink Minis I’ve tested and a bit more expensive, as well. That’s one change these fine cameras have in common — prices that push most of them out of the budget range, although these are still generally affordable compared to many similar alternatives.

Extra long-range models for Wi-Fi worries

Blink’s new model offers a huge range for off-site and large property monitoring. Blink

Another significant evolution comes with Blink’s two new XR Plus cameras, made to be used with a Blink Sync Module XR Plus hub to reach extra-long distances beyond your usual Wi-Fi range. The first is the Fronter XR Plus ($200), with a shape similar to Blink Outdoor cams but with an antenna and optional trunk strap for mounting on a tree. It can reach a range of up to 7,000 feet in the right conditions.

Accompanying the Fronter XR Plus is a new Blink Outdoor 2K XR Plus ($150). It’s a more compact version with a lesser 2,700-foot range, but it is still able to connect to watch areas standard Wi-Fi can’t reach, like the end of long driveways or detached sheds and garages.

Chris Liguori, general manager at Blink, told CNET, “With XR, we’re extending that same approach beyond the reach of ordinary home Wi-Fi. The Frontier XR Plus brings a new option to the trail camera category, combining extended-range connectivity with the features and experience customers expect from Blink.”

It’s interesting Blink is calling the Frontier model a “trail camera” since this usually makes people think of viewing wildlife or mountain trails in remote areas. But the brand makes it clear this cam is focused on more property-oriented tasks. If your property entrance is half a mile away at the end of a road, the Frontier could keep an eye on it. It could also watch distant activity on farms or monitor a remote job site, as long as the XR Plus hub is placed correctly.

A compact and completely wireless spotlight camera

A battery spotlight camera requires careful testing, but Blink’s model intrigues me. Blink

While Blink has dabbled in floodlight cameras before, it’s now releasing its first spotlight cameras, the Blink Spotlight Cam 2K Plus ($110), with a unique design unlike any spotlight model I’ve seen. This cam is entirely wireless, so you can mount it nearly anywhere without worrying about junction boxes or outdoor outlets.

Blink didn’t give any info on the total lumens of this spotlight model, but the brand did say the spotlight is controlled via the motion detector. If it’s like the floodlight versions, you’ll be able to control the brightness, motion sensitivity and other settings to change how the lights work.

However, I really want to test this model to see what the battery life is like, since LED lights can drain batteries quickly. Frequent activations of Ring’s new Spotlight Cam, for example, quickly brought battery life down, which is why I was glad that model came with room for two battery packs. Blink doesn’t appear to have any design changes made to mitigate battery loss.

Pan/tilt features on a particularly versatile camera

Blink’s final new camera has broad coverage. Blink

Finally, Blink is releasing a pan/tilt camera, the Blink Mini Pan-Tilt 2K Plus ($50), the most budget-friendly of this new crop with an indoor/outdoor design and 350-degree panning plus 115-degree tilting for more coverage. Like many pan/tilt cams these days, it autotracks when it picks up significant movement, like following a figure across the yard.

I like this coverage solution much better than the awkward, unnecessary experiment with the dual-cam Blink Arc. Note that outdoor use requires an outdoor adapter, which isn’t included in the sales price.

If you’re interested in any of these new camera preorders, you should know Blink’s cloud storage plans start at $4 per month, or you can spend a few dollars more if you want AI features, like video descriptions. Blink does sell certain types of Cync Modules you can connect to flash drives or microSD cards for local storage, although I’m not sure this approach is compatible with the XR Plus models. Finally, as an Amazon company, Blink has excellent compatibility with Alexa but typically doesn’t offer support for Siri or Google Home.

I’ll let you know what I think of these new cameras and details like these when I get a chance to test them out.

Tech.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends Soon. Here’s When the Clocks Go Back an Hour
Tech.content:
Daylight saving time ends in less than two weeks, with the clocks officially changing at 2 a.m. While it’ll still be light enough for trick-or-treating on Halloween, the time change will hit the day after, when most of the US adjusts back one hour.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March.

More from CNET

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time Sunday, Nov. 1. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, March 14, 2027. The end of DST has the motto “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates.

Daylight saving time vs. standard time

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located. Time.gov/Screenshot by CNET

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.



Sleep experts seek year-round standard time

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Will we ditch these time changes for good?

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

"You're in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally." Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation

Adjust your body clock to daylight saving time

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

Tech.title: Minecraft and Domino’s Team Up for Block-Shaped Pizza, In-Game Freebies
Tech.content:
The computer game Minecraft offers plenty of in-game food, from steak and cake to, uh, rotten flesh. Now, a popular real-world food is being mixed with Minecraft.

Beginning on Monday, Domino’s Pizza will offer Minecraft-themed tie-ins, including in-game extras, when customers buy “the Domino,” a recently launched Detroit-style pizza for one. The pizza is cut into two pieces to resemble Minecraft blocks, in connection with the new game Minecraft Dungeons II, a spin-off of the 2020 game Minecraft Dungeons.

Minecraft Dungeons II came out Sept. 29 for PC, Xbox Series X and S, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.

More from CNET

One of the six themed pizza boxes resembles a Minecraft zombie. Domino's

As part of the Minecraft collab, the rectangular Detroit-style Domino pizza will come in one of six game-related boxes, each featuring a different Minecraft Dungeons II character: the classic Creeper, Corrupted Creeper, Zombie, Pig, Prime Enchanter and the main protagonist, Valorie.

When you buy the pizza online, you can unlock a code for one of three randomly awarded in-game items to use in Minecraft Dungeons II: a Domino’s skin, a Slice Slayer Cape, and a Cheesy Cube pet.

Between Monday and Nov. 4, customers have a chance to win a free download of the game (for PC and Xbox only), normally priced at $30. Domino’s says 20,000 downloads will be given away. To enter the lottery, after purchasing “the Domino,” submit your proof of purchase on its dedicated web page.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Will Run iOS 27.1 at Launch on Friday
Tech.content:
Apple told CNET in an email in September that when the tech giant launches the iPhone Duo this Friday, Oct. 23, the foldable will launch with iOS 27.1, skipping right past iOS 27.

“When iPhone Duo first becomes available on October 23, it will run iOS 27.1,” Apple said. “This version of iOS builds on the foundation of iOS 27 but introduces features that were purpose-built for the new foldable design.”

Because of those iPhone Duo-specific features, and the fact that Apple began the beta process for iOS 27.2 on Wednesday, Sept. 16, you may not see iOS 27.1 on your device unless you were able to preorder the iPhone Duo.

The Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, a long-anticipated move into a device category that’s still pretty niche. Launching it alongside a version of iOS tailored to that foldable design could help smooth out the debut of what is likely to be many buyers’ first foldable phone.

However, Apple did say all devices, including the iPhone Duo, will be able to update to iOS 27.2 later this year. So Apple likely won’t stagger iOS releases in the future in this way. And since Apple released the iOS 27.2 release candidate on Monday, Oct. 19, folks likely won’t have to wait long for that update to land on their foldable and non-foldable iPhones.

For more on Apple, here’s everything the company announced at its September event and what you should know about iOS 27. You can also check out what iOS 27.2 might bring to your iPhone in October.

Tech.title: Investigation Reveals How TikTok Executives Ignored Internal Child-Safety Warnings
Tech.content:
Court documents on some of the inner workings of TikTok paint a picture of a tech company repeatedly warned by its own staff about the dangers its platform posed to minors — and then ignoring many of those warnings.

According to an investigation from NPR, unsubmitted depositions from an ongoing multistate trial against TikTok, Meta, Google and Snap reveal that TikTok executives knew that underage users were circumventing its age restrictions. Internal documents also reportedly show that some minors were engaging in sexually exploitative acts using TikTok’s own platform features, including its Live video streaming tool.

The NPR report cites the deposition of Reagan Maher, who worked in safety at the company in the early 2020s, addressing the fallout from a damning 2022 Forbes story about child exploitation on the platform. Maher said she informed senior leaders at the company that kids aged 13 to 15 were accessing features meant for adults, such as monetized live video.

More from CNET

A spokesperson for TikTok told CNET in an email that the information in the NPR report was “clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works.”

TikTok also said that NPR ignored “numerous documents and resources” that would demonstrate how the story’s claims mischaracterize the platform’s features. The spokesperson stated that the company has spent significant amounts of money on safety and introduced over 50 default protections for young users, including Family Pairing tools for parents, and that it was steadfast in its “commitment to the well-being of our community.”

Child-safety reckoning on tech platforms

TikTok is one of a growing group of major tech platforms that have faced lawsuits, scrutiny from parents and financial penalties over how they regulate the safety of younger users. Others include the gaming platform Roblox, AI companies such as OpenAI, streaming video services like Google-owned YouTube and social media companies such as Meta.

Online dangers like predators, cyberbullying and inappropriate content aren’t the only risks for kids. Tech companies are also facing lawsuits for making their platforms addictive and harmful to young users. In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement over those issues in a landmark lawsuit brought on by multiple US states.

TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance — which still holds a stake in the company despite some government-mandated divestment to the US for its American operations — were sued in 2024 by the Department of Justice over violations of child privacy laws, resulting in a $400 million settlement. Last month, TikTok settled a $100 million lawsuit in Alabama and agreed to limit daily child usage in the state.

The NPR report shows not only that TikTok was made aware of these problems by its own staff. It also reveals that the company — among other alleged violations of the law — may have directly profited from the sexual exploitation of minors. Youth were reportedly rewarded with gifts online that could be converted to cash, with TikTok earning a cut of those profits.

Devastating, but predictable

Child-safety advocates told CNET that the NPR report exposes safety gaps in the way platforms such as TikTok were designed.

“These court documents are nothing short of devastating, but for those of us fighting child exploitation every day, they are tragically predictable,” said Michael Medoro, chief operating officer of Childhelp, which focuses specifically on online safety.

Medoro said that active monitoring, the elimination of safety loopholes and stronger age verification will require cooperation between tech leaders, advocates and law enforcement.

According to Shanna Marzilli, CEO of Plan USA, an advocacy group for girls that is part of Plan International, the TikTok documents confirm what young people, especially girls, have been saying for many years. “Online spaces are not safe for them,” she said.

Marzilli said that young people are clued into the idea that tech companies can’t protect them. In a research study conducted among US young people aged 10 to 19, only 14% of them trust social media companies to take sexual harassment and assault seriously.

“Voluntarily implemented parental controls and self-reported age limits are demonstrably ineffective when platforms leave these structural loopholes open,” Marzilli said.
